The wish attributed is a thousand years. Then the argument, and it turns on a rare verb meaning to shift something a little to one side. Being granted that span would not budge a person away from what follows, not because the span is short but because length and what comes after it are not measured on the same scale.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the challenge in the preceding ayat and functioning as its explanation. Classical commentators read the ayah as accounting for the reluctance just described rather than as a fresh charge, and note the careful comparison it draws, which sets one attachment against another rather than making an absolute statement about anyone.

keyTerms.note: The superlative of a word for avid, clutching desire. It describes wanting that has stopped weighing what it wants, which is why the object of it here is left as bare life without qualification.
From the root behind the word for a lifespan, which also gives the verbs for building up and inhabiting a place. A life in Arabic is something constructed and dwelt in rather than merely elapsed.
A rare doubled form meaning to budge something a small distance. The word makes the denial exact: not that long life is insufficient rescue, but that it does not move a person even slightly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long life was genuinely rare and genuinely admired. Infant mortality was high, fevers and raids took adults without notice, and a man who reached great age became a source of history for everyone younger, since he remembered droughts and battles nobody else had seen. Wishing for a very long life was not a strange wish in that world. It was the most reasonable thing a person could want.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere gives a figure close to the one wished for here, saying that Noah remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty. So the number in this ayah sits just beyond the longest span the Quran itself records for anyone, which suggests the wish is being stated at the outer edge of what could be imagined rather than chosen at random.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats attachment to life as evidence rather than as a fault, reading a preference as a report on what a person expects. Its argument is then about scale. Extension does not alter a relation, however far it goes, because the thing extended and the thing that follows are not commensurable. That is why the verb chosen is one of tiny movement, since even a nudge would imply the two were on a single line.

crossReferences.why: Gives the span of a thousand years less fifty for Noah's time among his people.
Describes the gathering as though they had lingered only an hour of a day.
Has people asked how long they remained on earth, and answering a day or part of one.

studies.applyIt: Work out roughly how many weeks you have been alive. It takes a minute with a calculator and the number is smaller than most people expect. Do not draw a conclusion from it. Just let the figure sit for a moment, since this ayah is arguing about scale and a real number is more useful here than a feeling.

studies.title: Brought Down Upon Your Heart
studies.meaning: An objection aimed at the carrier of the revelation is answered without any defence of the carrier. The ayah states what he did, adds that he did it by God's leave, and then lists three things about what was brought: it confirms what came before, it is guidance, and it is good news. None of those concerns the messenger. The place of delivery is also worth noticing. Not to the ear or the eye but upon the heart, which is where the Quran consistently locates the receiving of revelation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentators report that this ayah answers an objection raised about which angel had brought the revelation, with hostility directed at the bearer rather than at the message. The reports vary in detail and the commentaries generally give the substance without pressing the particulars, since the ayah's reply works by redirection rather than by settling any question about the angel himself.

keyTerms.note: Named directly, which the Quran does for only a few angels. Elsewhere the same figure is called the Trustworthy Spirit and the Holy Spirit, and commentators identify all three with one another.
Permission, from a root that also gives the word for an ear. Lexicographers connect the two through listening, so granting leave in Arabic carries the sense of having given something a hearing.

The place the revelation is said to have been brought down to. The Quran uses the same phrase elsewhere for the same event, so the heart rather than the ear is consistently named as the point of arrival.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The person carrying a message and the person who sent it were sharply distinguished in that world, and everyone understood the distinction. Envoys moved between clans under protection, and an envoy could be disliked without the message being answered. Refusing to deal with a message by objecting to its bearer was a recognised evasion, common enough that people could name it when they saw it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran says the revelation was brought down upon the heart, and uses the same phrasing in another surah describing the same descent. Commentators note that the heart is consistently named as the place of reception rather than the ear, which is why revelation is described throughout as something settled inside a person rather than handed over to him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply refuses to treat an angel as an independent party who could be an object of enmity in his own right. What is stated instead is agency: he brought it, by permission, from the one whose permission it was. That establishes something about how the Quran presents the unseen servants of God, who are never described as having interests of their own. The three descriptions that close the ayah then move the discussion back to the content.

crossReferences.why: Describes the Trustworthy Spirit bringing the revelation down upon the heart in clear Arabic speech.
Attributes the same descent to the Holy Spirit, sent down in truth to make the believers firm.
Describes the bearer as a noble messenger, possessed of power, obeyed and trustworthy.

studies.applyIt: Notice one message you have discounted this week because of who delivered it. A colleague you find tiresome, a family member you have stopped listening to. Separate the two once, deliberately: write down what was actually said, without the person attached, and read it back.

studies.title: Tossed Aside Every Time
studies.meaning: Three ayat, each narrowing something. The first gathers God, His angels, His messengers and then two named angels into one object of hostility, refusing to let opposition be directed at a part while sparing the rest. The second says the signs sent are clear, so refusal cannot be explained by obscurity. The third turns from incident to pattern, asking whether it is not the case that every time a covenant is made, some of them throw it away. Even there the wording limits: a group of them, not everyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the answer to an objection about which angel brought the revelation. Classical commentators read these three as the widening of that answer, moving from one angel to the whole chain and then to a record of undertakings made and discarded. The surah has by this point recalled several covenants, so the question at the end has a series of specific instances already behind it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to run past or overstep. An enemy in Arabic is one who goes beyond a boundary toward you, which makes hostility a movement rather than a state of feeling.
The verb for throwing away something judged worthless, casually and without looking. It appears again in the next ayah of the surah, where what is thrown is described as landing behind their backs.
A word of proportion rather than of totality. The surah uses such limiting terms repeatedly in this section, and commentators lean on them when explaining how far any of these statements reach.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Treaties between clans were public, spoken before witnesses and renewable, and a group that repudiated one did it openly because there was no other way to do it. Everybody in a region knew which families' word held and which did not, and that knowledge determined who would trade with them, marry into them or stand beside them in a dispute. Discarding an agreement was a visible act with a long memory attached.
studies.didYouKnow: Gabriel and Michael are named individually immediately after the general phrase for His angels, even though both are included in it. Arabic rhetoric recognises this as a device, naming a particular right after a general term in order to single it out for emphasis, and commentators identify this ayah as a standard instance of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By gathering God, the angels and the messengers into a single object, the passage treats revelation as a chain that cannot be broken selectively. Objecting to one link is treated as objecting to the whole, which is why the answer to a complaint about one angel arrives in this form. The third ayah then makes a further point: a single broken undertaking is an event, while a pattern of them is a disposition, and the question is put about the pattern.

crossReferences.why: States the believing counterpart at the end of this surah, making no distinction between any of His messengers.
Describes accepting some messengers while rejecting others as an attempt to find a way in between.
Names those who break their covenant every time one is made, without any wariness about it.

studies.applyIt: Look at agreements rather than intentions. Pick one small commitment you have made repeatedly and dropped repeatedly, to a person or to yourself. Do not renew it today. Instead write down how many times the cycle has run. A pattern counted is different from a pattern felt, and the counting is the exercise.

studies.title: Thrown Behind Their Backs
studies.meaning: The verb from the previous ayah returns and is given a direction: thrown behind the back, the ordinary Arabic gesture for discarding something as worthless. Commentators differ on which book is meant, some reading it as the scripture they already held and others as the one that had just arrived, and either reading works, since the ayah has just described the second as confirming the first. The last clause is the careful one. Not that they did not know, but that they acted as if they did not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the account of how the arrival of a new revelation was received among communities that possessed an older one. The wording again limits the scope to a faction, as the surrounding ayat repeatedly do. Classical commentators read the passage as describing a response rather than assigning a permanent character, and note that the same phrase about throwing something behind the back appears elsewhere in the Quran.

keyTerms.note: Throwing away what has been judged worthless. The word carries no anger, which is what makes it worse than a rejection: something is not argued with but simply dropped out of the hand.
A fixed Arabic idiom for putting something out of consideration. The gesture behind it is real, a thing tossed over the shoulder without turning to see where it lands.
A particle of comparison, not of statement. It says they behaved in the manner of people who did not know, which quietly keeps the knowledge in the account rather than removing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Throwing something over the shoulder was a real gesture with a settled meaning. A broken tool, a stone turned up while digging, a thing not worth the weight of carrying went behind you without a look, and Arabic poetry used the phrase for treating counsel as nothing. Anyone hearing this ayah saw the movement, and saw that it is done without argument and without a second glance.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah does not say they were ignorant. It says they acted as though they were, using a particle of comparison, and commentators lean on that particle when explaining the passage. It matters because the surrounding ayat have repeatedly insisted that recognition was present, so a straightforward statement of ignorance would contradict what has just been established.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A performance of ignorance is treated here as a distinct condition, separate both from not knowing and from disputing. Knowledge placed behind a person is still knowledge, and the grammar keeps it on the account. The passage also makes the two scriptures inseparable in a specific way. Since the new one is described as confirming the old, discarding either amounts to the same act, which is why commentators can read the ayah both ways without changing its sense.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about throwing a covenant behind the back and taking a small price for it.
States earlier in this surah that what arrived confirms what its audience already possessed.
Says those given the Book recognise it as surely as they recognise their own children.

studies.applyIt: Find something you know perfectly well and have arranged your life not to look at. A bill, a result, a conversation you owe someone. The ayah's gesture is throwing it behind you without argument, which is exactly how this works. Take it out and look at it once today, without acting on it yet.

studies.title: Solomon Did Not Disbelieve
studies.meaning: The ayah's first move is a denial on Solomon's behalf, clearing a name before explaining anything. What follows is unusually hedged at every turn. The two at Babylon warned each person before teaching, saying they were a trial. Nothing learned could cause harm except by God's leave. What was acquired is described as harming its holders and benefiting them in nothing, and they are said to have known this already. Commentators record differing accounts of the details and generally keep close to what the wording states.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentators report that stories attaching sorcery to Solomon's reign were in circulation, and read the ayah as answering them directly, which is why the denial comes first. Babylon was a real name to that audience, a ruined ancient city on the northern trade route with a long reputation for old learning. The commentaries differ on the details of the two figures named and are cautious about going beyond the text.

keyTerms.note: From a root suggesting the turning of a thing from its reality. The same letters give the word for the last hour before dawn, when shapes are present but cannot be made out clearly.
Originally the assaying of gold by fire to see what is genuinely in it. A trial in this sense does not create a quality; it brings out what was already there and makes it visible.
A person's allotted part of something. The Quran uses it for a share in the hereafter, so the phrase denies a portion rather than describing a punishment inflicted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Charms and knot-tying were widespread across the region, and a great deal of it was aimed at exactly what this ayah names: separating a husband and wife, or joining them. Practitioners were paid, and clients came to them privately with domestic grievances. The Quran refers elsewhere to those who blow on knots, which was a recognised technique rather than an image, familiar to everyone who heard it.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning is inside the account rather than added by the commentators. The two at Babylon are described as teaching nobody until they had said that they were a trial and told the person not to lose his faith. So the passage records a caution being given first, every time, which is a detail readers often miss because the ayah is long and moves quickly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Every clause removes something. A prophet is cleared, a warning is recorded, harm is placed under permission, and the learners are said to have known the cost. What is left is a picture in which nothing operates independently of God, including what appears to be a power in its own right. The passage also returns to the surah's commercial image, and states the exchange in its harshest form, with the sellers and the goods being the same.

crossReferences.why: Names seeking refuge from those who blow on knots, the practice this ayah describes people learning.
States that whatever a practitioner of such arts contrives, he does not succeed wherever he comes.
Describes what Solomon was actually given, knowledge and understanding, and his response of gratitude.

studies.applyIt: Notice something you have been drawn to that you already know does not help you. Not a vice, necessarily. A conversation you keep re-entering, a feed you keep opening. The ayah says twice that they knew. Say the sentence about your own case out loud, in the past tense: I knew this did not help.

studies.title: Change The Word, Not The Tone
studies.meaning: The first of these states what would have been better, and the second gives a very small instruction with a well attested background. A word the community had been using to ask for the Prophet's attention was open to two senses in Arabic, one respectful and one demeaning, and some were exploiting the second while remaining deniable. The remedy given is not a rebuke about tone or intention. It is a replacement word with no second meaning available, followed by the instruction to listen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and one of the passages for which classical commentators do report a specific occasion with reasonable agreement. They describe a term in ordinary use among the believers that could be turned, by a slight shift, into something insulting, and record that the alternative supplied here closed the ambiguity. The same word is mentioned again in another surah in a passage about speech being twisted.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for tending a flock, so the plain sense is a request for care and attention. A nearby form of the same letters carries heedlessness, which is the second reading that made the word usable as an insult.

keyTerms.gloss: look at us, wait for us
keyTerms.note: The replacement offered. It asks for exactly the same thing, a moment of the listener's attention, and carries no second sense that could be exploited by anyone saying it.
From a root meaning to return, which also gives the ordinary word for a garment, understood as cloth returning to its shape. A reward in Arabic is what comes back to you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic culture prized double meaning and rewarded it. Poets built reputations on lines that wounded while remaining defensible, and a phrase that insulted deniably was a recognised instrument rather than a rare trick. In a society where a direct insult could open a feud between clans, the ambiguous form was the safer weapon, and everyone present could hear it working without being able to name it.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction given is a change of vocabulary rather than a correction of attitude. The community is not told to be more respectful. It is told to stop using a word that had become available for misuse and to use a different one meaning the same thing, which is a strikingly practical way of handling a problem of intention.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility for ambiguity is placed on the speaker rather than on how a hearer chooses to take it. That is an unusual allocation and it has a consequence: a word that has been turned is a word to be set down, regardless of what any individual speaker meant by it. The passage also shows a general principle handled by a specific and small remedy, which is a pattern in how the Quran addresses friction inside a community.

crossReferences.why: Mentions the same word again, in a passage about speech twisted with the tongue while listening.
Addresses the community about mockery and offensive nicknames, the same terrain at a different scale.
Instructs believers to say what is best, since ambiguity is exactly where discord is sown between them.

studies.applyIt: Think of a phrase you use that has become loaded between you and one particular person. It may have started harmless. Replace it with a plainer one for a week and see whether the exchange changes. This passage suggests that swapping the word is a real remedy and not merely a cosmetic one.

studies.title: God Singles Out Whom He Wills
studies.meaning: A wish is reported and then bypassed rather than argued with. Notice how total the wish is made in the Arabic: an indefinite word for good placed inside a negation, a construction that sweeps a whole category, so what is described is not the withholding of some great favour but of any good at all. The reply does not dispute that the wish exists. It observes that the wish is addressed to a party who has no part in the distribution, and closes on a name meaning overflow.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The wording again limits its subject, naming those who disbelieve among the People of the Book rather than the whole, alongside those who associated others with God in Mecca. Classical commentators note the qualification, which the surah uses consistently in this section, and read the ayah as describing an attitude found among some in both groups toward the young community in Medina.

keyTerms.note: An indefinite noun inside a negation, which in Arabic makes the denial cover the entire category. The construction is a standard way of making a negation total rather than partial.
From a root meaning particular as opposed to general. The verb describes picking something out for a specific recipient, which places the distribution wholly with the one doing the picking.
What exceeds a measure, the part beyond what was required. The same root gives the ordinary words for a remainder and for something spare, so bounty in Arabic is by definition surplus.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a world of hard limits, one party's good season often was another's loss. Grazing, wells, caravan routes and market share were finite, and a rival's strong year genuinely reduced your own. The instinct that another's gain costs you something was not irrational there; it described the economy accurately. What this ayah answers is that instinct applied to something which does not work that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic construction here makes the negation absolute. Placing an indefinite word for good after a negative sweeps the whole category, so the sentence says not that they begrudge some particular blessing but that they wish no good of any size to reach its recipients. Grammarians treat this construction as the standard way of making a denial complete.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is described as singled out according to God's will, which removes the distribution from the reach of anyone's preference, including the recipients'. That is the answer the passage gives, and it is not a reassurance about outcomes but a statement about jurisdiction. The closing name then reframes the whole exchange, since bounty in Arabic means an overflow, and an overflow given to one party is not withdrawn from another.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same statement, that God singles out for His mercy whomever He wills, in a similar setting.
States that the People of the Book may know they hold no power over any of God's bounty.
Asks whether they envy people for what God has given them of His bounty.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you treat someone else's good fortune as arithmetic, as though a fixed amount were being handed out. Most of us do this without ever forming the thought. Pick one person doing well in an area you care about and say something specific and true about their work today.

studies.title: Better Than It Or Like It
studies.meaning: A rule is stated with a guarantee attached: what replaces is better or equal, never less. Commentators differ widely here. They differ over whether the word for what is replaced means a verse of scripture or a sign given to a prophet, and the second verb is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions, one meaning to cause something to be forgotten and the other to defer it. The scope of all this has been discussed at great length, and the range of classical views is genuinely wide.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering objections about a revelation arriving in instalments over years, with later guidance sometimes replacing earlier. Classical commentators connect the ayah to that general situation rather than to a single occasion. They note that it is followed immediately by a second question opening with the same words, and read the pair as one argument, the first about power and the second about ownership.

keyTerms.note: The verb means both to cancel something and to copy it out. The ordinary Arabic word for a manuscript copy comes from this root, so one word holds replacing and transcribing together.

The same word covers a natural sign, a miracle granted to a prophet and a unit of the Quran. Commentators divide over which is meant here, and the ayah's reach differs considerably depending on the answer.
The lower limit of the guarantee. Better or equal exhausts the options offered, so the sentence rules out replacement by something lesser as a matter of the rule itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that world was learned in stages from a person. A boy learned a trade, a route or a set of poems by being given as much as he could hold and then more, and a teacher's later instruction routinely replaced an earlier simplification without anyone thinking the first had been a mistake. The community hearing this ayah had been receiving guidance in instalments for well over a decade.
studies.didYouKnow: The second verb in this ayah is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions. One reading means to cause something to be forgotten and the other means to defer or postpone it, and both are preserved in the standard works on recitation. Commentators explain the ayah with each reading, and the difference between them is a single vowel.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah answers an unsettling idea by attaching a guarantee to it. Replacement is not loss, because what arrives is equal or better by the terms of the rule itself. It also closes on power rather than on knowledge, which commentators notice, since the objection being met is not whether God knows what to send but whether He may change what He has already given. The closing question treats that as settled by what God is.

crossReferences.why: Describes one sign put in the place of another, and the accusation of invention that followed.
States that God effaces and confirms what He wills, with the source of the Book held with Him.
Notes that the Quran was divided into portions to be recited to people gradually, sent down in stages.

studies.applyIt: Think of an instruction you were given that was later revised, by a teacher, a doctor, a manager. Notice whether you experienced the revision as the first version having been wrong. Usually it was not. It was as much as you could use at the time, and the revision is evidence of attention rather than of error.

studies.title: No Guardian Besides Him
studies.meaning: The second of two consecutive questions opening with the same four words. The first attached its question to power, this one to ownership, and the pair works as a single argument delivered in two steps: what God can do, and what God holds. Then a consequence is drawn that does not follow automatically from ownership. Two supports are named and both are denied, one that stands behind a person and one that comes to his aid, which between them covered everything a person in that world relied on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately following the statement about replacement and completing its argument. Classical commentators treat these two ayat as a unit, since the repeated opening formula joins them in the Arabic. The ayah is addressed in the singular, which they read as directed to the Prophet and, through him, to anyone reading, before its second clause switches to the plural.

keyTerms.note: The same root gives the words for a king and for possessing something outright. Ownership and rule are not distinguished in it, which is why the sentence can move from holding to protecting without a step in between.
From a root meaning nearness. A person of this kind stands close enough to act on your behalf, which in that society was a formal position rather than an affectionate description.
From the verb for coming to someone's assistance in a fight, and the root behind the Quran's word for victory. It names intervention from outside rather than a standing relationship.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone needed a protector and everyone knew who theirs was. A clan answered for its members, a patron stood behind a client, and a stranger arriving in a town sought someone's protection before doing anything else, because a person without it could be wronged with no consequence to the wrongdoer. The two words used in this ayah name the two things such an arrangement actually provided.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one before it begin with exactly the same four words in Arabic, forming a matched pair that translation tends to obscure. Commentators read them as two halves of one argument rather than as separate statements, with the first grounded in what God is able to do and the second in what belongs to Him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Joining sovereignty to protection is a real move and not a truism. Owning everything does not by itself mean that nothing else can shelter a person, and the ayah asserts both in one sentence so that the second reads as following from the first. Using the exact vocabulary of the social order also matters. The passage does not say protection elsewhere is inferior. It says the position does not exist.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this ayah almost word for word, adding that He gives life and causes death.
States that you cannot escape on earth, and have no guardian or helper apart from God.
Places the same sovereignty of the heavens and the earth beside God's power over all things.

studies.applyIt: Write down who you would actually call if something went badly wrong tomorrow. Three names at most. Then notice that the list is short, that it has changed over the years, and that you did not build it deliberately. The ayah is not asking you to value them less. It is asking you to see the list clearly.

studies.title: Questioning Your Own Messenger
studies.meaning: The warning identifies itself by a precedent rather than by a description, which assumes the reader has just been given the precedent. This surah has supplied two: an escalating series of questions about an animal that made a simple instruction expensive, and a demand to be shown God plainly. The closing clause then names the risk in the vocabulary of trade, calling it an exchange rather than a drift, and describes the result as leaving a road that the Arabic calls level.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing this stretch of the surah before it turns to other matters. Classical commentators connect the warning to the episodes already recalled in this same surah rather than to a particular incident in Medina, and read the questioning in view as the kind that seeks to delay or to test rather than to understand, since the surah has just shown both varieties at work.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for asking, with no negative sense of its own. The Quran elsewhere instructs people to ask those who know, so what is warned against here is a use of the act rather than the act.
A form meaning to take one thing in place of another. It makes a change of position a transaction with two sides, so something is handed over as well as received.
Built on the root for evenness. A level road in that country was one a loaded animal could take without unloading, so the phrase was navigational before it became a way of speaking about conduct.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Routes were graded by ground. A level way could be taken by a loaded camel at pace, while broken country meant unloading, longer days and real risk of loss. Guides were paid for knowing which was which, and the difference between the two showed up in the arrival date and in what was still intact when you got there. Straying from the level way was an expensive mistake before it was ever a metaphor.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the level way is built from the same three letters that appear near the start of this surah, where warning and no warning are said to stand equal for certain listeners, and again where the heavens are described as brought into proportion. Evenness is the shared idea across all three, once as a comparison, once as a making, and here as a road.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes between questions that seek understanding and questions that function as resistance, and it makes the distinction by pointing at cases rather than by defining terms. That is a practical choice, since the two are hard to tell apart from a description and easy to recognise in an example. Naming the risk as an exchange also matters, since it implies that nobody arrives at a new position empty-handed.

crossReferences.why: Warns about questions whose answers would burden the asker, and notes that people before asked them.
Records the demand to be shown God plainly, one of the two precedents this ayah points back to.
Instructs those who do not know to ask the people of remembrance, which shows what kind of asking is meant.

studies.applyIt: Sort your next few questions into two piles as you ask them: the ones whose answers will change what you do, and the ones that will not. Only the first pile is enquiry. Doing this once, for an afternoon, is usually enough to show you which pile you have been filling.

studies.title: Pardon And Turn The Page
studies.meaning: A hostile wish is reported, its motive is located inside those holding it rather than in anything done to them, and the truth is conceded to have been clear. Then, having built the least sympathetic case available, the passage instructs pardon. Two verbs are used and they are not synonyms. The first is to give up a claim; the second, built on the word for the flat side of a thing, is to turn away from the matter so it is not brought up at all. Commentators treat the second as the wider of the two.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to a community under real pressure in the years after the migration. The instruction is given with a horizon attached, until God brings His command, and classical commentators discuss at length what that phrase refers to and when it was met. Their views differ considerably, and the commentaries set them out rather than settling on one, so the clause is best read as the text leaves it.

keyTerms.note: The word for wanting a good thing to leave someone else. The phrase after it places the source inside the people themselves, which rules out the reading that they had been provoked into it.
The root describes wind wiping out tracks in sand. Pardon in this word is giving up a claim so completely that nothing remains to be followed, rather than deciding not to press it for now.
From the word for the broad flat side of something, and later for a page. To do this is to present your side rather than your face to a matter, and to stop raising it altogether.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds ran on the obligation to answer. A slight left unanswered was read as weakness, poets recorded which clans had responded and which had not, and a family's safety depended in part on being known to reply. An instruction to pardon and then to leave the matter unmentioned, given to a community that was outnumbered and under pressure, cut directly against the machinery everyone lived inside.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs of pardon in this ayah are not a doubling for emphasis. Commentators distinguish them carefully: the first gives up the claim, while the second stops the matter being raised at all. A person can do the first and still bring something up, which is why the second is described as the more demanding of the pair.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is placed after every mitigating factor has been removed. The motive is named as envy, the knowledge is conceded, and the wish is described as active. Restraint is therefore asked for in the hardest available case, which is a deliberate arrangement. Attaching a horizon to it also matters, since the passage frames the restraint as an interval rather than as a verdict, and closes on power rather than on patience.

crossReferences.why: Uses the second of these two verbs on its own, instructing an overlooking that is gracious.
Tells believers to forgive those who do not look forward to the days of God, with a similar horizon attached.
Describes repelling with what is better, and the enmity that turns into warm friendship as a result.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between letting something go and stopping yourself from mentioning it. Pick one grievance you have officially forgiven and count how many times you have raised it since. Then try the second thing for a week: not raising it at all. Most people find the second harder and more useful.

studies.title: You Will Find It Waiting
studies.meaning: Two practices are named and then something is said about all good generally, using an image of dispatch. Whatever you send forward, you find with God. The phrase for whose benefit it is sent is the one to notice: for yourselves. Nothing here is presented as a service rendered upward. The passage describes a deposit lodged for later collection rather than a payment made, and it closes with a name of seeing rather than of receiving, so the one who is watching is not the one being paid.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed immediately after the instruction to pardon, so that restraint toward others is followed at once by an instruction about one's own practice. Classical commentators note that the surah repeatedly pairs these two acts, and that the image of sending good ahead appears in almost identical words in another surah, which is why they read the two passages together.

keyTerms.note: The verb for standing something up so that it stays standing. Applied to prayer it describes maintaining a thing in place over time rather than performing it on a given occasion.

From a root meaning both to grow and to be pure, used of a plant thriving. One word therefore carries increase and cleansing together, which is a claim about the remainder as much as about the portion given.
Putting something forward in advance. The surah has already used this verb for deeds sent ahead in a passage about reluctance, and here the same image is turned the other way round.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There were no banks and no way to carry value safely over a long road. A merchant left goods with a trusted agent in a town he expected to reach, or consigned them ahead with an earlier caravan, and found them waiting when he arrived. The whole arrangement ran on reputation. Saying you will find it with God uses exactly that vocabulary, of something lodged and later collected.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic name for what is given away comes from a root meaning to grow and to be pure at the same time, and the same root is used of a plant thriving. Neither sense is a metaphor derived from the other; the dictionaries list both as primary, so increase and cleansing are held together in the word itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The phrase saying that good is sent ahead for yourselves relocates who benefits. God is described in this ayah only as seeing, never as receiving, so nothing here is a transaction with Him. That makes the practices named an investment in the person performing them, and it explains the image chosen, since a deposit is retrieved by the one who lodged it rather than handed to someone else.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same clause almost word for word, adding that what is found is better and greater in reward.
Contrasts wealth put out to increase through people with what is given seeking God's face.
Describes the same movement later in this surah as a loan advanced and multiplied on return.

studies.applyIt: Give something small away today that you will not see again and will not be thanked for. Money, an hour, a thing you were keeping. Do not tell anyone. The image in this ayah is a deposit lodged ahead of you, and the exercise is simply to have made one deposit you cannot check on.

studies.title: Produce Your Proof
studies.meaning: A claim about who is admitted is quoted, described as a wish, and then met with a single instruction: bring your evidence. The reply makes no counter-claim at all. It applies a standard, and the standard applies in every direction, including back at anyone else asserting who is admitted and who is not. The word used for the claim is the same one the surah used earlier for a scripture held as things merely hoped, which quietly classifies the statement before the demand for proof is even made.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's long address. The ayah immediately following supplies the Quran's own answer to the same question, and states it as a condition anyone may meet rather than as a name anyone may hold. Classical commentators read the two together, since a demand for evidence about entry is only coherent if the criterion being offered in its place is one that can be checked.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for something hoped for, used earlier in this surah for scripture held as hearsay. Applying it here classifies the claim before any argument about it begins.
One of a small group of Arabic verbs that exist only as commands. There is no past tense of it, which gives the demand an abrupt conversational quality that translations tend to smooth away.
A word for conclusive evidence rather than a supporting reason. It later became the standard term for a formal demonstration in Arabic philosophy, and it carries that weight already here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in that society were settled by evidence and then by oath, in a fixed order that everyone knew. The claimant produced witnesses; if he could not, the matter passed to the other party's oath. Demanding a proof was therefore not a rhetorical flourish but the opening move of an actual procedure, and every person hearing this ayah knew exactly what happened next when none was produced.
studies.didYouKnow: The imperative used for produce your proof belongs to a small set of Arabic verbs that occur only in the command form. Grammarians treat these as defective, since they have no past tense and no ordinary present, and the word functions in speech simply as hand it over, which makes the demand sound closer to conversation than to argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering a claim with a demand for evidence rather than with a rival claim sets a standard that binds whoever uses it. Anyone asserting the boundaries of the next life is asked for grounds, and the ayah after this one accordingly offers a criterion in place of a label. That is the shape of the argument: not a different group named, but a condition stated that can in principle be met or failed by anyone.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the answer immediately after, stating a condition rather than naming a community.
Uses the identical demand for proof after a series of questions about who creates and provides.
States earlier in this surah that reward follows belief and good action rather than membership.

studies.applyIt: Take one confident claim you made this week and ask what would count as evidence against it. If nothing would, you were not making a claim about the world. Doing this once, on something small and low stakes, is the cheapest way to learn the difference between a conviction and a wish.

studies.title: The Condition Stated In Full
studies.meaning: The line answers a claim made two ayat earlier that Paradise belongs to one group alone. It replaces the claim with a condition in two parts, and both are required. The first is inward, surrendering yourself to God, which the Arabic renders as handing over your face. The second is outward, being a doer of good. Reward is then attached to the person rather than the label, and the sentence ends by lifting both fear and grief.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line sits in a stretch dealing with disputes between the town's religious communities. Each side made claims about who alone could be saved. The ayat just before quote such a claim and answer it by asking for proof. Early scholars tie this line to no single reported occasion. They read it as the surah's own reply to the argument it has just recorded.

keyTerms.note: The verb shares its root with peace and with wholeness. It carries handing something over intact and undamaged. So the surrender described is a giving over, not a defeat.
In Arabic the face stands for the person and for their direction of attention. Surrendering the face means the whole of you turned one way, not a part of you kept back.
The root joins beauty and benefit. It describes work done well and generously, not merely correctly. So the second condition asks for quality, not only compliance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The gesture behind the wording was familiar. You handed over a thing with both hands, face turned to the person taking it. That is how a debt was settled in front of witnesses. It is also how a surrender was made. Turning your face toward someone in a crowded gathering marked who you were talking to, and whose judgement you accepted. The phrase borrowed a public act to describe something inward.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause that closes this ayah says they have nothing to fear and will not grieve. It comes back more than a dozen times across the Quran. Each time it is attached to a different group. The steadfast, those who give without wounding, those who declare God their Lord and hold to it. Early scholars treat the repetition as a deliberate refrain. It gathers those descriptions into one promise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pairing inward surrender with outward good refuses two shortcuts at once. Sincerity without action is one. Action without direction is the other. The passage also removes group membership from the sum, which is the argument the surrounding ayat are having. What remains is a standard anyone can be measured against and nobody can inherit. The promise is stated in the negative: two specific fears will not survive.

crossReferences.why: States the same criterion at greater length across several named communities.
Uses nearly the same phrase, surrendering the face to God while doing good, of Abraham's way.
Repeats the image of handing the face over and calls it grasping the firmest handhold.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you did well this week and ask which half of this line it satisfied. Was it good work aimed at nobody in particular, or was it turned toward God without much care taken over the work itself? Most of us lean one way. Spend this week strengthening the side you lean away from, in one ordinary task, and see whether it changes how the task feels.
studies.explainEasier: You do not get into heaven by belonging to the right group. You get there by giving yourself to God and doing good to people. Then your reward is safe, and you have nothing to fear.

studies.title: Both Of Them Read Scripture
studies.meaning: Two communities are quoted dismissing each other in identical words, an Arabic idiom meaning to have no ground at all to stand on. The clause that follows is the aggravating one: both of them recite scripture. Then the sharpest line. People with no book at all said the same thing, which flattens the very distinction the disputants were relying on, since the form of the dismissal turns out not to require a text. The passage does not adjudicate. It names a day and a judge and stops.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a city where several religious communities lived alongside one another and disputes of exactly this shape were audible in ordinary conversation. Classical commentators describe the setting generally rather than reporting a single exchange, and they note the ayah's closing clause, which defers the matter rather than resolving it. The same deferral appears in several other places in the Quran wherever communities differ.

keyTerms.note: An idiom meaning to have no standing whatever. It is a total dismissal, not a criticism of a position, which is what makes the two quoted sentences mirror images of each other.
One verb means both to read aloud and to come along behind. Reciting in Arabic is following a text word after word, in the way a person follows a track across ground.
From a root meaning to come after or to take another's place, so difference in Arabic is pictured as two parties standing in succession rather than as an opposition of views.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Asserting precedence and denying it to others was a recognised literary form. Every tribe kept a poet whose work included boasting of his own people and stating that a rival had nothing, no lineage worth naming and no standing worth counting. Audiences at seasonal markets came to hear exactly this. What is striking in the ayah is that it puts the same form in the mouths of people who read scripture.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah observes that people with no scripture at all made the same statement. The remark does not answer either party. It notes that the form of their argument does not require a book to produce, which removes the one thing both sides had been treating as the ground of their case, and commentators generally read it as the sharpest line in the passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes a third position that is neither adjudication nor even-handedness. It names the difference as real, names a judge, names a day, and declines to fill the interval with a verdict. That posture recurs wherever the Quran describes communities in dispute, and it has a consequence for how the interval is meant to be spent. What is left to people, in the meantime, is not the settling of the matter.

crossReferences.why: States the same deferral, that God will judge on the Day concerning what they used to differ about.
Says each community was given a law and a way, and directs them to compete in good instead.
Sets out earlier in this surah the criterion by which the deferred judgement will actually be made.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you describe a group's position as having nothing to it. That phrasing is a signal, not an assessment. State the strongest version of the position instead, in one sentence, and see whether the dismissal survives your own summary of it.

studies.title: Who Empties A House Of Prayer
studies.meaning: The question is put in the Quran's superlative form, which it reserves for a small number of offences, and here it is applied to obstructing worship rather than to any belief held. Two acts are named together: preventing God's name from being remembered in places of prostration, and working toward their ruin. The second follows from the first, since a building emptied of its use is already on the way down. Commentators propose several historical episodes for the ayah and record them side by side without deciding.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentaries offer more than one setting for this ayah, including the exclusion of the believers from the Sacred Precinct at Mecca and an ancient destruction of a place of worship far to the north. They set the proposals out and generally decline to choose, noting that the wording is plural and carries no restriction to one building, one city or one community.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a noun of place from the verb to prostrate. It names any spot where a person lowers himself in worship, which is why nothing in the word restricts it to a particular structure.
The word for a building falling to ruin, which in Arabic covers emptying as well as demolishing. A house nobody uses is described with the same term as one that has been pulled down.

A plural participle describing the state in which they would enter. The clause is a statement about their position rather than an instruction, and commentators read it as describing what became the case.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sanctuaries were real institutions across the peninsula and their protection was widely honoured. Inside the Sacred Precinct at Mecca, blood feuds were suspended and men who would have fought outside could trade. Other tribes maintained their own sacred places on the same understanding. Interfering with access to such a site was recognised as a grave breach regardless of what the interferer himself believed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word here is a plural, and nothing in the ayah limits it to one community's buildings. Another surah makes the breadth explicit, naming monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques together as places where God's name is much mentioned, and saying they would have been demolished were it not for God restraining some people by means of others.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The offence identified is not a belief but an obstruction, which places it in a different category from most of what this section of the surah has been describing. Emptying a place of worship and working toward its ruin are treated as one continuous act, so neglect and demolition sit on the same line. The superlative form of the question then sets the weight, since the Quran uses that construction sparingly.

crossReferences.why: Names several kinds of house of worship together and says restraint alone keeps them from being destroyed.
Describes who is fit to maintain the places of worship, tying it to belief and to practice rather than to lineage.
Concerns those who barred access to the Sacred Precinct while not being its rightful guardians.

studies.applyIt: Do one small thing for a place where people gather to pray: sweep something, fix something, pay for something, or simply turn up when the room is nearly empty. The ayah joins emptying a place to ruining it, which means that attendance itself is a form of upkeep.

studies.title: Whichever Way You Turn
studies.meaning: Two claims sit side by side. The first is that no direction is outside God's reach, so turning anywhere still faces Him. The second denies that God has taken a son. It answers that with ownership rather than argument: everything in the heavens and the earth already belongs to Him. Only someone who lacked something would need offspring. Early scholars read the pairing as one point. God is neither held in by place nor extended by family line.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines come shortly before the change of prayer direction toward Mecca, which the surah announces a few ayat later. Several occasions are reported for the first line. One is prayer on a journey, when the direction cannot be fixed. The classical sources record these without agreeing on which is primary. The setting is a community whose neighbours were disputing its standing and its direction.

keyTerms.note: Early scholars read it as His presence, His direction, or what is turned toward the worshipper. They are careful to add that the term carries no bodily sense and no place.
From a root for roominess and space, used of land wide enough to hold everyone. It answers the worry about direction by saying there is no edge to run past.
It describes standing in service over time, not a single act of obeying. Applied here to everything that exists, it makes obedience the ordinary state of creation, not a human achievement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Direction mattered enormously to people who navigated by stars and landmarks. Caravans crossed open country by reading the sky, and getting east and west wrong could cost lives. The two words also named the two halves of the known trading world, Syria and Persia one way, Abyssinia and the sea the other. Saying both belonged to God claimed the whole map a merchant could picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The denial that God has taken a son comes with a distinctive marker here. It is one of the few statements followed by the word for glorification used as an exclamation. That is a short interjection rather than a sentence. Early scholars note that the passage does not argue the point at length here. It answers with a single word and a statement of ownership.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting these two lines together separates God from the two ways people usually locate a thing: in space, and in a family. He is not somewhere. He is not descended from anyone, and nobody carries Him on. What replaces both is ownership and knowledge that covers everything. For a community about to be told to face a particular building, the order matters. The reminder that no direction holds God comes before the instruction about which way to stand.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction to turn toward the Sacred Mosque, which these lines prepare the ground for.
Answers the same claim about offspring by defining God entirely through denial.
States nearness from the other side: God is closer to a person than their jugular vein.

studies.applyIt: Next time you pray somewhere unfamiliar and are not sure of the direction, notice the small worry that rises before you settle on one. Face your best guess and let the worry go without arguing with it. These lines were given, among other things, for exactly that moment. The ease they offer is meant to be used rather than admired.
studies.explainEasier: Every direction belongs to God, so wherever you turn, He is there. Some people said God had a son. The answer is simple: everything in the sky and on earth is already His.

studies.title: Be, And It Is
studies.meaning: A name and then a sentence, and the two say the same thing in different registers. The name means originating with no precedent, not making something well but making something first of its kind, and the word is distinct from every Arabic term for shaping existing material. The sentence then removes process as the name removes material: a decree that requires only a word. Commentators are careful about an address to what does not yet exist, generally reading it as a figure for immediacy rather than as a report of an event.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering a claim about God taking a son, which the preceding ayah reports and rejects. Classical commentators read this ayah as the ground of that rejection rather than as an independent statement about creation, since a being who originates without precedent and produces by decree has no need of the relation being claimed. No separate occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to do something with no model in front of you. The same root gives the ordinary Arabic word for an innovation, something brought about that was not there before in any form.
The verb for bringing a matter to completion and closing it, used also of a judge giving a decision. It implies finality rather than intention, so what is decreed is already concluded.
The bare imperative of the verb to be, two letters in Arabic. It is the shortest possible command in the language, and the ayah pairs it with a verb of becoming built from the same root.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything a person in that world made was made from something. A potter had clay dug from a bank, a smith had ore carried in from a mine, a weaver had wool from an animal he could name, a builder had stone from a quarry. There was no craft anywhere in that life that produced from nothing and on no model, which is why the word chosen here has no analogue among human trades.
studies.didYouKnow: The divine name opening this ayah shares its root with the ordinary Arabic word for an innovation. The connection is the absence of a precedent in both cases. So the name does not say that the heavens and the earth were well made or made powerfully. It says specifically that they were made without anything to copy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two halves work together to describe a making unlike any a person has witnessed. Originating without precedent removes the need for a model, and a decree consisting of a single word removes the need for a process. The ayah's placement then does the arguing, since a being described this way requires nothing to complete Him, which is the claim the preceding passage was rejecting. The reply is made by definition rather than by dispute.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing as a general rule about His command whenever He wills a thing.
Uses the same divine name in the same argument, about a claim of offspring.
Applies the identical phrase to the announcement made to Mary about a birth without a father.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you made and trace what you started from. The materials, the tools, the instructions, the person who taught you. Follow it back four or five steps and notice that you never reach a beginning. That is the ordinary case, and this ayah is naming the exception to it.

studies.title: Their Hearts Resemble Each Other
studies.meaning: A request is quoted, for God to speak directly or for a sign to arrive, and the answer does not address the request at all. It observes that the same words were said by earlier people, and then makes the observation that carries the ayah: their hearts resemble one another. The subject has moved from evidence to disposition. If the identical demand recurs across centuries and communities, it belongs to the person making it rather than to a gap in what has been provided.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the phrase for those who do not know is generally read as naming people who had received no scripture at all. Classical commentators connect the demand to requests recorded elsewhere in the Quran, where a much longer list of specific signs is set out. They read this ayah as answering a pattern rather than an individual occasion, which is what the middle clause states directly.

keyTerms.note: From the root for likeness, which the surah has already used of fruit given in the Garden and of cattle indistinguishable to their owners. Here the resemblance is between hearts separated by centuries.
Left indefinite in the request, so what is asked for is not a particular proof but some sign, any sign. The vagueness of the demand is part of what the answer is responding to.
From a root carrying the sense of something settling until it becomes clear, as water clears when it stops moving. Certainty in the word is a condition arrived at rather than a conclusion reached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Requests of this kind were made and recorded. Another surah preserves a much longer list put to the Prophet: make a spring gush from the ground, produce a garden with rivers running through it, bring the sky down in pieces, produce angels, own a house of gold. The escalation in that list tells you something the single demand here does not, which is that no item on it was the real condition.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran preserves the escalated version of this demand in another surah, where five or six specific signs are named in succession. Each is more extravagant than the last. The fact that the list grows rather than settling on one item is itself informative, since a person who genuinely had a condition in mind would have stated it once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause runs in a direction most readers do not expect. It says the signs have been made clear for people who are certain, rather than that signs are given in order to produce certainty, and commentators discuss the order at length. What it establishes is that evidence and reception are not independent of one another. The same material can be clear or opaque depending on what is brought to it, which the surah has been demonstrating for a hundred ayat.

crossReferences.why: Records the escalated version of this demand, listing several increasingly extravagant signs in succession.
Answers the request for an angel to be sent down by describing what would follow if one were.
Notes that each of them wants to be handed scrolls of his own, spread open before him.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what would actually change your mind about something you are undecided on. Write the condition down in one line. Then notice whether it is a real condition you could recognise if it arrived, or whether it moves whenever you approach it. The ayah is about the second kind.

studies.title: Not Answerable For The Outcome
studies.meaning: A role is defined by two functions and then a third thing is explicitly excluded. Good news and warning are the task, covering both directions a message can run, and the closing clause removes responsibility for how any of it lands. The final phrase is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions, one making it a statement that he will not be questioned about them and the other an instruction not to ask about them, and both are preserved in the standard works.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, arriving after a long stretch of the surah describing refusal, dispute and demands for signs. Classical commentators read it as consolation placed where consolation is needed, and note that the two titles used here are among the Quran's most frequent descriptions of the prophetic role. No specific occasion is reported, though the placement itself is treated as significant.

keyTerms.note: From the root that also gives the word for skin. Lexicographers connect them through news that shows in the face, which is why the word cannot be used for ordinary information.
From a verb meaning to give notice of something coming. A warning in this sense is advance information rather than a threat, which is why the two titles form a matched pair rather than a contrast.
From a root describing a fire kindled to intensity, with the flames massed together. It is one of several distinct names the Quran uses, each drawn from a different aspect of burning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A herald went ahead of a caravan or an army to announce its coming. His job was to deliver, clearly and audibly, and then to withdraw; nobody held him accountable for what people did with the news. Tribes also sent criers to proclaim a truce, a market or a death. The two words this ayah uses name exactly the two kinds of announcement such a man carried.
studies.didYouKnow: The last clause of this ayah is read two ways in the recognised recitation traditions. One reading makes it a statement, that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) will not be questioned about those people. The other makes it an instruction, that he should not ask about them. Both are preserved in the standard works and the commentaries explain the ayah with each.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Defining a role by two functions and then naming a third that lies outside it sets a limit rather than adding a duty. Announcing is the task; outcomes are not. That relieves a burden the passage assumes was being carried, and it establishes something applicable well beyond prophecy, since nobody is answerable for a response they were never in a position to produce. The consolation works by narrowing the job description.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit plainly, that the task is reminding and not exercising control over people.
Divides the responsibilities explicitly: upon you the delivering, and upon Us the reckoning.
Asks whether he would compel people to believe, when belief is not something produced that way.

studies.applyIt: Identify one situation where you are carrying responsibility for another person's response rather than for your own conduct. A conversation you keep rehearsing, an outcome you are trying to engineer. Write down the part that is actually yours to do, and do only that part this week.

studies.title: God's Guidance Is The Guidance
studies.meaning: The subject is the terms on which approval is offered. Approval is described as conditional on adopting another community's way, and the sentence at the centre answers by defining rather than arguing: God's guidance is the guidance. What follows names the price of the exchange in the same two words the surah used a few ayat earlier for what a person has apart from God. Notice what is not disputed. The approval on offer is treated as real, and the objection is to what it costs.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to the Prophet in the singular during years of pressure from several directions in the city. Classical commentators read the ayah as concerning the condition attached to approval rather than as a general description of anyone, and they note that the Quran elsewhere describes an upright community among the people of earlier scripture who recite God's signs through the night and prostrate.

keyTerms.note: A community's defining path. The surah uses the same word a few ayat later for the way of Abraham, which was itself the disputed question, so the vocabulary already contains the reply.
From the root for contentment and acceptance. It describes settled approval rather than agreement on a point, which is why the condition attached to it is a whole way rather than a position.
The plural of a word whose verb also means to fall. Arabic pictures desire as the direction something drops in, and the plural here sets many inclinations against a single guidance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belonging was everything in that society, and belonging had terms. A person outside every group had no protection, no standing in a dispute and no share in anything. Conforming to a group's way was the ordinary price of acceptance, paid by everyone, and it was rarely experienced as a bargain because there was no alternative. The pressure described here was that mechanism applied to a messenger.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for their way is the same word the surah applies shortly afterwards to the way of Abraham. Several communities claimed that inheritance, and the surah is about to spend a long passage on the question. So the vocabulary of this ayah already points forward to the answer, since the disputed matter is precisely whose way Abraham's actually was.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The central sentence is a definition placed between a description of pressure and a statement of cost. It does not argue that God's guidance is better than the alternatives; it identifies guidance with it, which is a different kind of claim and cannot be met by weighing options. The passage also treats approval as a genuine good being offered, which is what makes it a temptation rather than a threat, and names what would be handed over in return.

crossReferences.why: States the same exchange later in this surah and answers it by naming the way of Abraham.
Describes an upright community among the people of earlier scripture, reciting God's signs in the night.
Tells each community to compete in good works rather than to seek one another's approval.

studies.applyIt: Notice one place where you have adjusted a position to keep someone's approval. Not a compromise you decided on, but a drift you have not examined. Name the approval and name what it cost in one line each. Seeing the two written side by side is usually enough.

studies.title: As It Deserves To Be Recited
studies.meaning: A positive statement placed in the middle of a long and often severe address, and commentators note its position. Those who recite the Book as its recitation deserves are said to believe in it, so proper reception rather than membership is what produces belief. The Arabic phrase for that recitation is glossed as following the text properly: reading it, understanding it, and acting on it, since the verb for reciting is also the verb for coming along behind. The second ayah then returns to a call made much earlier.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's long address to the Children of Israel. Classical commentators differ on who is meant by those given the Book here, some reading the earlier communities and some the recipients of the Quran, and they set the readings side by side. The second of these two ayat repeats an earlier one almost word for word, which is how the section's boundary is usually marked.

keyTerms.gloss: they recite it, they follow it
keyTerms.note: One verb covers reading aloud and coming after. Reciting in Arabic is following a text word behind word, which is why the same root gives both senses without any sense of metaphor.
Literally the right that its recitation has. Commentators gloss the phrase as reading, understanding and acting together, since a text has a claim on the person carrying it.
From the root meaning what exceeds a measure. The word describes a portion given beyond the ordinary share, which is why the surah pairs it here with a call to remember rather than with a title.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Texts travelled by voice, so the quality of a transmitter mattered enormously and everyone in a scholarly community knew who could be trusted. A man who reproduced sounds accurately without understanding them was known and discounted, and so was one who understood but altered as he went. The standard this ayah names would have been recognised at once by anyone who handled texts professionally.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat repeats, word for word, an ayah that appeared some seventy-five earlier in this same surah. The pair forms a bracket around the whole address to that audience, opening and closing it with the identical call to remember, and commentators use the repetition to mark where the section begins and ends.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a plainly positive statement here matters more than its content. After a hundred ayat describing refusal, distortion and dispute, the surah pauses to say that those who receive the text as it deserves believe in it, without qualifying the group or naming it. That makes the standard available rather than assigned. The closing repetition then ends the section where it began, on memory rather than on verdict.

crossReferences.why: Opens the long address with the identical call to remember, which this passage repeats to close it.
Gives the same positive assessment elsewhere, describing an upright community reciting through the night.
Says the reward of those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer is not allowed to be lost.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of scripture three times today: once for the sound, once for what it says, once for what you would do differently if you took it seriously. Five minutes in total. The phrase in this ayah is usually explained as those three things together, and doing them separately makes the difference visible.

studies.title: The Warning Said Again
studies.meaning: This warning appeared once before in the surah, and the second telling is not a copy. Two of its clauses have changed places, and one has changed its verb. Where the earlier version said that pleading on a soul's behalf would not be accepted, this one says it would not benefit. The first denial concerns whether such a plea is received; the second concerns whether it would do any good. Taken together the two versions close the same door from opposite sides.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the long address that the earlier version of this warning opened, so the section is bracketed by the same day named twice. Classical commentators note the repetition and the reordering, and read the pair as deliberate rather than as a duplication. Elsewhere the Quran speaks of pleading that takes place by God's leave, and the commentaries read the denials here alongside those passages.

keyTerms.note: The object of the verb is a day rather than a person. Guarding oneself against a stretch of time is an unusual construction, and the surah uses it in both versions of this warning.
The verb for something being taken and admitted. In this version it governs the ransom, whereas in the earlier telling it governed the plea, which is the exact point where the two differ.
To be of use to someone. Denying benefit is a wider statement than denying acceptance, since something can be admitted and still change nothing, and this version chooses the wider word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a world without books, important material was repeated on purpose and audiences expected it. A poet returned to his central line, a speaker restated a warning in altered words so the second hearing did not slide past, and a message carried between clans was said twice by the messenger before he left. Deliberate repetition with small changes was a technique of oral delivery, not a lapse in composition.
studies.didYouKnow: The two versions of this warning in this surah are not identical. Besides the clauses changing places, the verb attached to intercession changes from being accepted to being of benefit. Commentators noticed the difference early, and the effect is that a reader who has met the first version cannot let the second pass as something already known.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Repetition with alteration prevents a warning from hardening into a formula, which is a general feature of how the Quran restates things. The change of verb here also does real work, since it moves the denial from procedure to effect and leaves no version of the hope intact. Placing the second telling at the end of the section the first opened then frames everything between them with the same day, named twice.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first version of this warning, with two of the clauses in the other order.
States that no plea and no ransom would be accepted from those who let their faith become a game.
Describes the pleading that does occur, taking place only by the permission of the one who grants it.

studies.applyIt: Notice a warning you have heard so often that you no longer hear it. From a doctor, a friend, a text you know well. Say it back to yourself in different words, your own, once. The surah changes its own wording for exactly this reason, and the second version is what gets through.

studies.title: Leadership Earned Under Test
studies.meaning: Abraham is tested with words. He completes them, and God then appoints him a leader for humanity. He asks at once whether the appointment reaches his descendants. The answer allows it, but shuts out those who do wrong. Early scholars differ over what the words were. Some say the rites of pilgrimage, some the trials of his life, some commands that are not named. What the passage fixes is the order: testing first, appointment second, and no inheriting the office by blood alone.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line opens the surah's long treatment of Abraham, the Kaaba, and whose claim to him holds. It sits in a section arguing with communities in Medina that traced their standing to descent from him. The passage answers that argument at its root, without naming anyone. Early scholars read the exclusion in the last clause as the whole point of the exchange.

keyTerms.note: The root is used for wearing something out through use, as a garment wears. Testing here shows what a person is made of through repeated strain, not through a single exam.
