From a root associated with the left hand and with what comes without strain. Its opposite in the same sentence is built on a root for what is hard to handle, so the pair sets facility against friction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabian calendar was lunar and observed by eye. Someone had to see the new crescent and report it, which meant a month began on testimony rather than on calculation, and cloud could shift the start by a day. Naming a month by sighting made the community's shared time depend on people looking up together at the same hour, from different parts of the same town.
studies.didYouKnow: Ramadan is the only month named in the entire Quran. The sentence about ease and hardship in this ayah is quoted far outside its subject, in contexts that have nothing to do with fasting, and the classical commentaries already treated it as a general statement rather than one tied to the month.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The month is tied to a book rather than to an event in nature or a founding battle, which is unusual among religious calendars. What is being marked is a text arriving. The purpose clauses at the end order themselves: completing the count, then magnifying God, then thankfulness, so the practice is presented as leading somewhere rather than as an end in itself.

crossReferences.why: Names the night of the descent and describes what happens in it, without naming the month.
Calls it a blessed night in which every wise matter is distinguished, using the same root as criterion.
Repeats the principle of ease directly, saying no hardship has been placed on you in religion.

studies.applyIt: Take the sentence about ease and hardship out of its month for a moment and hold it against something you are making harder than it needs to be: a task you keep restarting, a standard you set for yourself alone. Ask what the easy version would look like. That question is not a concession; it is in the ayah.

studies.title: The Answer With No Go-Between
studies.meaning: A question is reported about God, and the reply is unusual in two ways. It drops the usual instruction to the Prophet to say something, and answers in the first person directly. And it does not describe God's location but His nearness, then His response, before asking anything of the questioner. Only after the assurance does the sentence turn to what people should do: answer Him, and trust Him. The order places the promise before the condition.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line sits among the ayat on fasting, right after the month is named and before the instructions resume. Several classical reports describe a question put to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). People asked whether God was near enough to be spoken to quietly, or far enough to need calling out. The reports differ in detail, and early scholars record them without settling which is primary.

keyTerms.note: Used of physical closeness and of kinship, since the related word means a relative. Nearness here is stated flatly, with no qualification. Early scholars contrast it with the distance the questioners assumed.
The noun for one act of calling out, not a general practice. Its use makes the promise specific: an individual call answered, rather than an assurance that God listens in general.
The same verb used a clause earlier for God answering, now turned back on the caller. The repetition makes the relationship two-directional in a single sentence, with the same word on both sides.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access to power in that world ran through go-betweens. Approaching a chief meant a relative to introduce you, a client relationship, or a gift. The sanctuary before Islam was full of objects thought to carry a request closer to a god. Asking was a chain of favours. A statement that the call goes straight, and the answer comes straight, removed every link in that chain at once.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the very few ayat where God answers a question about Himself without the usual instruction to the Prophet to say it. Elsewhere in this surah, questions are introduced with that formula again and again. Early scholars point out that the grammar drops it here, exactly where the subject is nearness. The shape of the sentence does what it says.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes asking direct, with nothing in between. That has consequences for how worship is understood: nothing is needed between a person and God at the moment of asking. It also ties God's answer to the caller's response, without making the second the price of the first. The promise is stated first, and without condition. And its place among the fasting ayat suggests hunger is meant to produce asking, not only restraint.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the invitation, call on Me and I will respond, and warns against disdaining it.
States the same nearness physically: closer to a person than their jugular vein.
Asks who answers the desperate when they call, and leaves the question standing.

studies.applyIt: Ask God for one specific thing today, out loud and in your own language, rather than in a borrowed phrase. Name it plainly: the actual worry, with its details. Many people find this harder than reciting, which is itself worth noticing. The promise in this line is attached to calling, and calling means saying what you actually want.
studies.explainEasier: Someone asked where God is. God answered Himself: I am close. When you call Me, I hear you and answer. You do not need anyone else to pass the message on.

studies.title: Until The Threads Can Be Told Apart
studies.meaning: A restriction the community had been keeping is lifted, and the reason given is that they had been straining against it in private. The passage does not scold. It names what happened, says the turning has already been accepted, and moves on. In the middle sits an image of husband and wife as garments for one another. The day's limits are then drawn by what the eye can see.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the second year after the migration. The classical sources report with reasonable agreement that in the first period of fasting the night was more restricted than it later became, and that some found the restriction beyond them. The ayah is reported as the response, and its opening is unusual in acknowledging the difficulty before removing it.

keyTerms.note: The everyday word for what is worn. Applied to two people about each other, it carries covering, warmth, closeness to the skin and the ordinariness of something put on daily without thought.
A reflexive form of the verb for betraying a trust, with the object being the people themselves. It describes a private inconsistency rather than a wrong done to anyone else.
An ordinary word for a thread of cotton. The image asks a person to look east and wait until two strands of colour can be told apart, which is a test anyone can perform without an instrument.

The word for the edge of a piece of land or the blade of a sword, so a line that is sharp rather than vague. The instruction that follows is about not approaching the line, not merely about not crossing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody in Medina owned a clock. The day was read off the sky: first light in the east, the sun's height at noon, the length of a shadow, the last colour going out of the west. Farmers and travellers knew these signs the way a modern person knows the time without looking. Defining dawn by two threads of colour used a measure everybody already carried.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the longest ayat in the surah, and it moves through four different subjects without a break. The mutual garment image occurs only here in the Quran. The phrase about the limits of God appears several times across the text, but the instruction not to come near them, rather than not to cross them, is distinctive to this place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are done at once that religious language usually keeps apart. A difficulty is admitted, and the admission is not turned into an accusation; the response is a turning and a pardon before anything else. Then the ordinary closeness of a marriage is given a warm image inside a passage about restraint, which refuses to treat the physical as merely tolerated. The ayah ends by explaining rather than commanding.

crossReferences.why: Describes marriage as tranquillity, affection and mercy placed between two people as a sign.
Uses the same phrase about the limits of God, there with a different instruction attached.
States the principle of ease that this concession puts into practice, a few ayat earlier.

studies.applyIt: Notice the moment today when the light changes and you can first tell colours apart, or the moment it goes. Stand still for it. This ayah measures a whole practice by something you can see with your own eyes, and most of us have stopped looking at the sky for anything except weather.

studies.title: Lowered To The Officials
studies.meaning: Two moves are described in one sentence, and the second is what gives the ayah its bite. Consuming property wrongly is named first, and then a specific method: handing some of it to those who decide cases, so that a larger share can be taken with a ruling behind it. The last three words close every excuse, since the whole thing is described as done knowingly rather than by confusion.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, among the practical instructions that follow the passage on fasting. Medina had judges and arbitrators, and disputes over palm groves, wells and debts were settled by men whose decisions carried weight. Gifts to such men were an ordinary part of the culture, which is what makes the ayah pointed: it names something with a respectable appearance and calls it consuming what belongs to others.

keyTerms.note: The verb describes lowering a bucket into a well. Used of a bribe, it pictures something let down quietly out of sight, which is a precise image for a payment nobody is meant to see.
Names what is void and comes to nothing, the opposite of the word for truth and rightful claim. Property taken this way is described as having no foundation, whatever paperwork supports it.
The plain verb for eating, used across the Quran for taking wealth. It makes the wrong bodily rather than abstract, and the same verb appears twice inside this one sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in Medina were settled face to face before an arbitrator both sides accepted, often a man known for judgement rather than an appointed official. His view decided who kept a well or a stand of palms. There were no written records to appeal to and no higher court, so a judgement was final and whoever influenced it took everything. Hospitality and gifts blurred easily into something else.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for consuming wealth appears at both ends of this sentence, framing the payment in the middle. The Quran uses eating as its standard image for taking property, and in this surah the same picture has already been used of those who swallow fire into their bellies, a few pages earlier.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A legal outcome is denied the power to make a wrong right. The property is called void before the ruling is even mentioned, so the judgement changes nothing about what the thing actually is. That is a claim about the limits of procedure, and it holds even where the process was followed correctly. The final clause locates the offence in knowledge: the person knew, and the knowing is part of the charge.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the warning against consuming wealth wrongly and sets trade by mutual consent against it.
Uses the same image of consuming, there for what is gained by keeping revelation quiet.
Addresses those who judge between people directly, asking that they judge with justice.

studies.applyIt: Look for the smallest place where you use an advantage that is not really yours: a connection who moves you up a queue, a form filled in loosely, a claim you know will not be checked. Pick one and do it the slow way this week. The ayah's last clause is about knowing, and you already do.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Approach The Houses By Their Doors
studies.meaning: A question about the moon is answered practically rather than astronomically: the phases are a calendar people can read. Then the ayah turns without warning to a custom about entering houses from behind, and states that righteousness is not located there. Commentators explain the custom as a practice of pilgrims in a state of consecration. The instruction that follows is short and literal: use the door.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, among the passages that answer questions the community had put. The classical sources describe a practice in which someone who had entered the state of pilgrimage would avoid the doorway of his own house and climb in from behind, treating the door as something to be shunned. The ayah is reported as an answer to that, and it declines to treat the practice as piety.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word for a new crescent, which shares a root with the shout that greeted its appearance. Naming the phases in the plural fits the answer, since it is the sequence rather than any one night that makes a calendar.
From a root for fixing a time or a place, and a related word later names the boundary points where pilgrims enter consecration. It covers scheduled moments rather than stretches of duration.
A broad word for upright conduct, connected to the word for dutiful kindness towards parents. The ayah defines it by removing a candidate first, then by naming awareness of God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Arabia was scheduled by the moon: markets, pilgrimages, the truce months when fighting stopped, the dates on a debt. A merchant who lent money reckoned repayment in moons, and a family knew when to expect a caravan by the same reckoning. The crescent was public information, visible to everybody at once, and it needed no expert to interpret.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of a series of ayat in the surah beginning with the words they ask you, which recur several times in this section on different subjects. The answer here is notable for not addressing what was asked: the question is about the moon's phases, and the reply is about what they are for.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two kinds of misplacement are corrected in one ayah. The first treats a question about the natural world by giving its use rather than its mechanism, which sets a tone about what revelation is for. The second refuses to let a physical detour count as devotion. Together they push in the same direction: religion is being separated from the decorative and the merely unusual.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same construction, denying that righteousness is a direction before defining what it is.
Describes the moon's phases as determined so that people may know the number of years.
Presents night and day as two signs made for reckoning time and seeking provision.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing you do the complicated way for no reason you can name: a route, a routine, a formality. This ayah answers a question about the sky and then, in the same breath, tells people to use the door. Take the direct route once this week and notice whether anything was actually lost.

studies.title: The Limit Given With The Permission
studies.meaning: Permission to fight is given with a limit attached in the same sentence, and the limit is stated twice: only against those who fight you, and no transgression. The classical commentators read the second clause broadly, covering excess of every kind, and they list what it was understood to exclude, including those who were not fighting. The ayah closes with a statement about what God does not love.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the period when the community, having been driven from Mecca, was permitted to defend itself after years in which fighting had not been allowed. The commentators treat this as among the earliest ayat on the subject and note that the restrictions arrive with the permission rather than after it. Reports about the exact occasion differ, and the classical works record more than one.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form describing two sides engaged with each other, rather than a verb for killing. The grammar assumes an opponent already fighting, which is why the following clause names them as those who fight you.
From a root meaning to cross over a boundary. The word covers going beyond in any direction, which is why the commentators read it as reaching well past the battlefield itself.

The clause states a divine disposition rather than a penalty, and the Quran uses this construction repeatedly to mark the outer edge of what is allowed. It closes the sentence without a threat attached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Warfare in Arabia had few restraints. A raid could take everything a settlement owned, cut down its date palms, and carry off its women and children, and the reprisal was expected to be larger. Fighting was seasonal and bound by the truce months, but within those limits scale was a matter of what a tribe could manage. A limit stated inside a permission would have sounded unusual.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about God not loving those who exceed appears several times in the Quran and always in the same shape, attached to an instruction that has just been given. Here it closes the first ayah of the surah's passage on fighting, so a restriction is the last thing said before anything else is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The structure matters as much as the content. Every clause that widens is followed by one that narrows, and the passage never lets a permission stand alone. That builds restraint into the same sentence rather than leaving it to conscience afterwards. And the closing statement grounds the limit in what God is like rather than in consequences, which places it beyond calculation about what an enemy deserves.

crossReferences.why: States the permission to fight in terms of having been wronged and unjustly driven from homes.
Insists that hatred of a people must not push anyone away from acting justly.
Directs that an inclination towards peace be met with the same inclination, and with trust in God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a conflict you are in, however small, and ask where your limit is. Not whether you are right, since most people can answer that quickly. Ask what would count as going too far, named in advance, before you are angry. This ayah puts the limit in the same sentence as the permission, which is the only moment it is easy to set.

studies.title: But If They Cease
studies.meaning: Hard instructions are given for a specific conflict, and each is paired with a condition. Expulsion is answered by expulsion, from where the expulsion happened. Fighting near the sanctuary is excluded unless it is begun there. Then the passage ends, twice in three lines, with a way out: if they stop, it stops. The final clause names God as forgiving rather than as victorious.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage that permitted the community to fight after it had been driven out of Mecca. The commentators tie the instructions to that particular conflict: a specific opponent, a specific expulsion, and a sanctuary in which fighting had been set aside for generations. The clause about persecution being worse than killing is read as referring to the pressure that had forced the emigration.

keyTerms.note: The root describes testing gold in fire, and the word covers persecution, civil strife and temptation together. Commentators here take it as the pressure applied to make people abandon their faith.
A verb for coming upon someone and getting the better of them, associated with skill and quickness. It describes an encounter in the course of a conflict rather than a search carried out at leisure.
From a root meaning to reach an end, and related to the word for being told to stop. The verb appears at the close of both ayat, and each time it ends the instruction that preceded it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary at Mecca had been a place where weapons were set aside for as long as anyone could remember. Tribes at war met there without incident, and the pilgrimage economy depended on that guarantee. A man could see the killer of his brother inside the sanctuary and do nothing. That restraint was one of the few things all of Arabia agreed on, which is why the exception here is stated so carefully.
studies.didYouKnow: The second ayah of this pair is six words long in Arabic and consists entirely of a condition and two names of God. It is among the shortest ayat in the surah, and it comes directly after one of the harshest, which the classical commentaries note as a deliberate placing rather than an accident of division.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Even at its hardest, the passage keeps an exit open and states it twice. Cessation ends the matter, and the sentence that describes the ending names God by mercy rather than by power. That places the purpose of the fighting in stopping something rather than in defeating someone. The classical readings hold to that distinction, and it is what keeps the passage tied to its occasion.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same condition: if they desist, what has already passed is forgiven them.
Says nothing prevents kindness and fairness towards those who did not fight you or drive you out.
The ayah immediately before, which sets the limit these instructions operate inside.

studies.applyIt: Notice how hard it is to let something end when you have been wronged and the other person stops. This passage says it twice in three lines, as if it expected the difficulty. Think of one grievance that is technically over and check whether you have actually put it down, or only stopped mentioning it.

studies.title: A Sentence That Contains Its End
studies.meaning: A purpose is stated for the fighting described in the preceding ayat, and it is a stopping point rather than a conquest: until the persecution ends and worship is free to be given to God. Then the same condition returns. If they stop, hostility stops, and the exception at the end restricts anything continuing to those still committing wrong. The sentence is built to close itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the short passage on fighting that began three ayat earlier. The commentators read the stated aim as the removal of the pressure that had made practising faith impossible in Mecca, rather than as the conversion of anyone, since the surah states a few dozen ayat later that there is no compulsion in religion. Reports on the specific occasion of the passage differ.

keyTerms.note: A particle marking a limit in time, and the whole shape of the ayah depends on it. What follows is the point at which the instruction expires, so the sentence carries its own ending inside it.

The word covers religion, obedience and the settling of accounts. Here the commentators read it as devotion offered freely, so the aim is that worship be possible rather than that anyone be made to offer it.
From the same root as the earlier warning against transgression, so the word is used consistently across the passage. Its repetition ties this ayah's ending back to the limit set at the start.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religion in Arabia was communal, not private. A person who changed allegiance lost his family's protection and often his livelihood, and pressure came through relatives rather than through officials. The early Meccan converts were boycotted, cut off from marriage and trade, and some were held by their own households. That is the situation the word for persecution names in this passage.
studies.didYouKnow: The condition about ceasing appears in both this ayah and the one before it, and in each case it is followed by a limit rather than by a further instruction. The word for hostility at the end shares a root with the word for transgression at the start of the passage, so the whole section opens and closes on the same idea.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A stated aim turns an open conflict into a bounded one, because a purpose can be reached. What is named is a condition of the world rather than the defeat of a party, which means the instruction ends when the condition changes and not when someone surrenders. The closing exception narrows the target one more time, and by the end of the sentence very few are left inside it.

crossReferences.why: States later in this surah that there is no compulsion in religion, which the commentators read alongside this aim.
Gives the same purpose in nearly identical wording, followed by the same condition about desisting.
Names monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques among what this kind of restraint protects.

studies.applyIt: Ask what would count as done in an argument you are still having. Not winning: done. If you cannot describe the state of affairs that would end it, the argument has no exit and will run until you are tired. This ayah gives its instruction an ending in the same sentence, which is worth copying.

studies.title: In The Same Measure As He Did
studies.meaning: The principle of equivalence is applied to the sacred months, and then to sanctities generally: what was violated may be answered in kind. The standard is stated as a measure, using the same verb on both sides so that the response is bound to the size of the original. Two clauses follow that pull in the opposite direction, asking for awareness of God and stating that He is with those who keep it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, connected by the classical sources to the year the community set out for the sanctuary and was turned back, and to the question of a sacred month in which they had been prevented. The commentators read the ayah as settling that a violated sanctity does not simply pass, while binding the answer to the same measure. Accounts of the details differ between the works.

keyTerms.note: The plural of what is set apart and protected: months, places and persons alike. Using the plural widens the sentence beyond the month just named, which is why commentators apply it to sanctities generally.

A word for exact likeness, used in the Quran for correspondence rather than approximation. Placed in the middle of the sentence, it turns a permission into a measurement, since anything beyond the like falls outside it.

From a root meaning to shield oneself, so the word describes someone guarding against harm rather than someone frightened. The closing promise attaches divine company to that guarding, not to the retaliation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Four months of the year were sacred across Arabia, and during them fighting stopped, markets opened and pilgrims travelled roads that were otherwise dangerous. The arrangement was old and universally kept, because everybody's trade depended on it. Breaking it was a serious matter, and a tribe that did so could expect to be remembered for it in poetry for generations.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for transgressing appears three times in this one ayah, twice describing the response and once the original act. Arabic uses that kind of repetition to bind two things to the same measure, and the classical commentaries note that the second use is called transgression only because it matches the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The measure is the whole point. Permission is given and immediately fixed to the size of the injury, which makes escalation the thing being prevented rather than the response itself. Then the ayah changes register: two clauses about awareness of God close a sentence about retaliation, and the promise of company is attached to restraint. What is permitted and what is commended are not the same thing here.

crossReferences.why: Permits a matching response and then says patience is better for those who are patient.
Sets an equal answer beside forgiveness and calls endurance a matter of firm resolve.
Applies the same principle of exact correspondence to a killing, earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: The next time you answer something unfair, decide the size of the answer before you give it. Say it to yourself: this much and no more. This ayah permits a response and then spends the rest of its length keeping it small, which is harder than either forgiving outright or escalating.

studies.title: Ruin Carried In Your Own Hands
studies.meaning: Two instructions and a warning sit in one short ayah, and the connection between them is what the commentators discuss. Spending is asked for; then hands are named as the means by which people throw themselves into destruction. Several classical readings are recorded, including withholding wealth when it is needed and going into danger unprepared. The ayah closes by asking for excellence and naming what God loves.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage that follows the instructions on fighting, where spending meant equipping and provisioning at real cost. The commentators record more than one reading of the middle clause, including an early report in which a companion applied it to withdrawing from effort rather than to recklessness. The classical works preserve the range rather than settling on one sense.

keyTerms.note: An unusual form from a root meaning to perish, and the word occurs only here in the Quran. Its rarity is part of why the classical commentaries discuss this clause at such length.
The phrase adds agency to the warning. Ruin is not described as arriving; it is described as something a person carries and drops, which makes the responsibility explicit without naming the act.
From a root for what is beautiful as well as good. The verb asks for quality in the doing rather than merely for the deed, and the noun formed from it closes the ayah as the thing God loves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Equipping a man for a journey or a campaign was expensive. A mount, water skins, provisions for weeks and a weapon added up to more than many households held, and those who could pay often paid for others as well. Refusing was easy and invisible, since nobody could see what a neighbour had put aside. The instruction to spend was aimed at a decision made privately at home.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for destruction in this ayah appears nowhere else in the Quran. Its single occurrence is one reason the classical commentaries record several readings of the clause side by side, and the early reports they preserve apply it in more than one direction, including to holding back rather than to rashness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses to let generosity and self-preservation be treated as opposites. Both appear in the same sentence, and neither is allowed to cancel the other. What holds them together is the final word, excellence, which names a quality of doing rather than an amount given. That leaves the reader with a judgement to make rather than a threshold to clear.

crossReferences.why: Describes what spending in the cause of God returns, using the image of a grain and seven ears.
Places a warning against killing yourselves directly after an instruction about handling wealth.
Lists spending in ease and hardship among the traits of those God is described as loving.

studies.applyIt: Give something today that you would notice giving. Not the amount that leaves no mark. Then check the other half of this ayah honestly: whether there is any place where being careful has quietly become the reason you never act. The two warnings in this sentence are aimed at the same person.

studies.title: Whatever Is Feasible Of Offerings
studies.meaning: The longest ayah in this section works through what happens when a pilgrimage cannot be completed as planned. Someone prevented, someone ill, someone with an ailment of the head: each is given an alternative, and the alternatives are graded so that a person without means still has a path. The recurring phrase is whatever is feasible. The ayah ends with two clauses about awareness and consequence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, connected by the classical sources to the year the community set out for the sanctuary and was turned back before reaching it. The commentators read the clause about being prevented against that experience. The detail of the ayah reflects a community learning the rites in practice, with questions arising as they went rather than settled in advance.

keyTerms.note: A passive form from a root meaning to be confined or hemmed in. The grammar makes the pilgrim the one acted upon, so the clause covers obstruction from outside rather than a change of mind.
Built on the same root as the word for ease used in the passage on fasting. The phrase recurs twice in this ayah, and each time it lets what is asked follow the person's actual capacity.
From a root meaning to guide or to lead, since the animal is led towards the sanctuary. The same root gives the word for guidance, so the offering is named by its journey rather than by its end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reaching Mecca was a serious undertaking. Pilgrims travelled for weeks in convoy, and an animal brought for offering had to be fed and watered the whole way. Illness on the road was common, and sores and lice on the scalp were a routine misery of long travel. Every situation this ayah names was something a caravan would meet in an ordinary year.
studies.didYouKnow: This is among the longest ayat in the surah, and it names three separate alternatives for people who cannot complete the rites as expected. The phrase about whatever is feasible occurs twice within it. The word used for the offering shares a root with the word for guidance, a connection the classical commentaries frequently note.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is built around exceptions rather than around the rite itself, which says something about how it is meant to be read. Difficulty is treated as normal, and the alternatives are graded downward until they reach someone with nothing at all. The final clause about consequence sits at the end of all that provision, and the classical commentators read the two halves together rather than separately.

crossReferences.why: Describes the call to pilgrimage and the rites, including the offerings and the circuits of the House.
States the principle these graded alternatives rest on: ease is intended for you, and hardship is not.
Describes the pilgrimage as owed to God by those who can find a way to make the journey.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you have postponed because you cannot do it properly: the visit, the course, the letter. This ayah spends most of its length on partial versions, graded down until nobody is excluded. Do the smallest feasible version of your postponed thing this week, without upgrading it in your head first.

studies.title: The Best Provision To Pack
studies.meaning: The months are named, and then three things are set aside for the duration: coarse talk, wrongdoing, and argument. Argument is the surprising item, since disputes are ordinary and not usually placed beside the other two. Then the register changes. Provisions are mentioned, as they would be for any journey, and the sentence turns the word into something else: the best provision is awareness of God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the sequence of instructions on the pilgrimage. The classical sources report that some pilgrims travelled without supplies, expecting to be fed along the way, and read the instruction to take provisions against that practice. The three things set aside are read as addressing what actually went wrong on crowded journeys, where tempers and close quarters met.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to twist a rope tightly, so the word pictures two parties pulling in opposite directions. It names contention rather than disagreement, which is why it can be set aside without ending discussion.
The ordinary verb for packing food for a journey. Its plainness is what makes the turn work, since the sentence uses a traveller's word and then names the best thing to pack as awareness of God.
From a root meaning to guard or shield. Calling it a provision changes the image: something carried and drawn on rather than a state of mind, and something that can run out if it was not packed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A pilgrim caravan was thousands of people moving slowly in heat, sharing wells and campsites with strangers from tribes they might have fought. Tempers were short, animals went missing, and precedence at water was a live question every day. Setting aside argument for the duration was not a spiritual abstraction. It addressed the most likely thing to go wrong in the next fortnight.
studies.didYouKnow: The address to people of understanding at the end of this ayah appears once before in the surah, in the line about life in retribution, and in both places it closes a passage rather than opening one. The three things set aside here are named in a descending order of drama, and argument, the least dramatic, is placed last.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A journey undertaken for God is protected from the ordinary friction of travel by naming that friction in advance. What is asked for is not extra devotion but the removal of three specific behaviours, which is a modest and achievable thing. Then the word for provisions is turned, and the passage suggests that what a person carries inwardly is the supply that actually decides how the journey goes.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same address to people of understanding, earlier in this surah.
Names the failures of speech that damage a community: mockery, nicknames, suspicion and backbiting.
Describes servants of the Merciful as those who answer the ignorant with peace.

studies.applyIt: Pick one setting this week where you will not argue: a particular meal, a particular hour, one recurring conversation. Not silence, and not agreement. Just no contention inside that window. This ayah fences off a period rather than a topic, which turns out to be much easier to keep.

studies.title: Leave From Where The People Leave
studies.meaning: Two worries are answered. The first is whether trading during the pilgrimage spoils it; the answer removes the blame without praising the trade. The second concerns a group who had kept themselves apart at one of the stations, and the instruction is to leave from where everyone else leaves. Then, immediately, comes a call to seek forgiveness, attached to the very act of standing where others stand.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that some families had held themselves above the general pilgrimage, staying within the sanctuary while others went out to the plain, and that this instruction placed them back among the crowd. They also report a hesitation about whether commerce during the season was appropriate. Both reports are widely recorded, though the details vary between the works.

keyTerms.gloss: you pour forth, you surge out
keyTerms.note: The verb describes water overflowing a vessel. Applied to a crowd leaving a place, it pictures a mass moving together rather than individuals departing, which is why the second ayah's instruction lands as it does.

The word means what is left over and abundant, and the Quran uses it for both divine favour and honest earnings. Using one word for both is what allows trade during the season to be described as seeking from the Lord.
From the same root as the word for the marks of God used earlier in this surah. It names a place by its function as something noticed, which is how the Quran describes several of these stations.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The pilgrimage season was also the largest market of the year. Caravans arrived with goods from Yemen and Syria, poets competed, debts were settled and marriages arranged. For many families the season's trade was a significant part of the annual income, and the two purposes were inseparable in practice. The question the ayah answers was therefore a practical one about livelihood.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the verb for pouring forth is used three times across these two ayat, and it is the word the Quran uses for pilgrims moving between the stations. The instruction in the second ayah, to leave from where the people leave, is one of the shortest correctives in the surah, and it is followed at once by a call to seek forgiveness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Standing apart is treated as something to seek forgiveness for. That is the striking move: the ayah does not argue that the separated group was mistaken about the ritual, it places them back in the crowd and then mentions forgiveness in the next breath. Distinction, even distinction with a religious justification, is being handled as a spiritual problem rather than a procedural one.

crossReferences.why: Grounds honour in awareness of God rather than in lineage, addressing the same instinct to rank people.
Describes pilgrims arriving on foot and on lean mounts from every distant road, answering one call.
Answers another practical question from this same section, also by removing a false form of piety.

studies.applyIt: Find one place where you quietly stand apart: a queue you get around, a room you leave early, a group whose company you accept but do not join. Stay this week. The instruction here asks nothing except that you go out when everyone else goes out, and it treats that as worth saying.

studies.title: As You Remember Your Fathers
studies.meaning: The comparison is unexpected and precise. Remember God the way you remember your fathers, or more strongly, which takes a habit already fully formed and points it somewhere else. Then a second sentence separates two kinds of asking. One person asks only for this world, and the ayah records what he receives and what he does not, without calling the asking itself wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the close of the pilgrimage instructions. The classical sources describe a practice after the rites in which men gathered and recited the deeds of their ancestors, competing in the honours of their line. Poetry contests of exactly that kind are well documented in the season. The ayah is reported as redirecting the gathering rather than abolishing it.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for an act of worship, which in the Quran attaches to the pilgrimage in particular. It shares a root with the word for a devout person, so the rites and the character are named together.
The comparative is built on the root for firmness, the same word used earlier in this surah for those stronger in love. What is being asked for is intensity rather than frequency.

An old word for an allotted portion, less common in the Quran than the usual term for a share, and used for a portion in the hereafter. Its rarity gives the closing clause a formal weight, like an entry in a ledger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Boasting of ancestors was a public art. After the pilgrimage, men would stand and recite what their fathers had given away, whom they had protected, which disputes they had settled, and a good performance raised a whole clan's standing for the year. Nobody thought this frivolous; it was how reputation was maintained. The ayah takes that scene and asks for the same energy in a different direction.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a share used at the end of this ayah is uncommon, and in the Quran it always names a portion in the hereafter that someone does or does not have. The sentence stops without saying what happens to the person described, which the classical commentaries note as deliberate restraint rather than an omission.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A comparison is used as a measure. The ayah does not describe what remembrance of God should feel like; it points at something the audience already did intensely and asks for that, or more. That is a practical standard rather than an ideal one. And the second half distinguishes not between good and bad requests but between narrow and complete ones, which the following ayah then illustrates.

crossReferences.why: Gives the complete request that this ayah's narrow one is set against, and states the outcome.
Describes what is given to whoever seeks only this world's harvest, and what is withheld.
Draws the same distinction between those who want the immediate and those who pursue what is beyond.

studies.applyIt: Notice something you talk about with real energy: a team, a project, a family story you tell well. Then notice the difference in your voice when you talk about God. The ayah does not ask you to manufacture feeling. It points at intensity you already have and asks where else it could go.

studies.title: Goodness Here And Goodness There
studies.meaning: A second kind of asking is quoted, and it has become the most repeated prayer in Muslim practice. Three requests sit in one line: goodness in this world, goodness in the next, and protection from the Fire. The word for goodness is left undefined, which the commentators note, since it covers whatever is genuinely good rather than a list. The following ayah says these have a share of what they earned.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the pilgrimage section by setting a second prayer against the first. The commentators record that this became the most commonly repeated supplication in the community, and that it was said at the circuits of the House and at the close of gatherings. Its brevity is part of the reason: it is short enough for a crowd to say together without instruction.

keyTerms.note: An indefinite noun, so what is asked for is a good rather than the good. Commentators list health, sufficiency, a righteous household, knowledge and forgiveness, and note that the word is left open deliberately.
An imperative from the same root as the word for God-consciousness, which describes shielding oneself. Here the shielding is asked of God, so the two uses of the root face each other.
From a root meaning to set something up in place, as a post is fixed upright. It names a portion assigned rather than won, which sits carefully beside the words about what they earned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prayers in Arabia were usually specific: rain, a safe return, a son, victory in a dispute. People asked for the thing they needed by name, and a vow often accompanied it. A supplication that asks for goodness without specifying it would have sounded unusually open-ended, and the commentators note that its generality is what let it become the prayer everyone could say.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the most frequently repeated supplication in Muslim practice, and it is quoted here as the speech of an unnamed person rather than given as an instruction. The word for goodness appears twice in one line, once for each world, and the classical commentaries decline to define it, listing possibilities instead of choosing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer refuses the choice between this world and the next, asking for both in the same breath and treating them as compatible. That shapes a whole attitude: material wellbeing is not made a rival of the hereafter, only insufficient by itself. And the following ayah ties the outcome to what was earned, so the prayer is not presented as a substitute for anything a person does.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the narrower request this one is set against, in the immediately preceding ayah.
Asks that the home of the hereafter be sought without neglecting one's portion of this world.
Another supplication quoted in the Quran, asking for what was promised and against disgrace.

studies.applyIt: Say this line once today, in English or in the recitation, and notice how little it specifies. Most of us pray for outcomes we have already chosen. Try one prayer this week that names no particular result, and see whether it changes what you are willing to accept as an answer.

studies.title: Two Days Or Three
studies.meaning: Remembrance is asked for during a set of counted days, and then the ayah does something unusual: it gives two options and clears both. Leaving after two days is not a fault, and staying longer is not a fault. A short clause attaches a condition to the whole arrangement, and the commentators read it as tying both choices to the same awareness. Neither option is presented as the better one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage on the pilgrimage rites. The days referred to are those spent camped after the main day of the rites, and the sources report that pilgrims differed over whether an early departure was a shortfall. The ayah settles that question by refusing to rank the two, and the classical works record the practice on both sides without preference.

keyTerms.note: A reflexive form of the verb for haste, so the person is described as hurrying himself rather than being hurried. Its pairing with the verb for delaying sets two deliberate choices side by side.
The counterpart verb, describing someone who puts himself later. The two verbs are built on the same pattern, which is how Arabic marks a matched pair rather than a preference and a fallback.
A passive verb used of a crowd driven together from every direction, and used of livestock as well as people. It ends a passage full of crowds moving between stations by naming one more gathering.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The days after the main rites were spent camped in a narrow valley with tens of thousands of others. Water was carried, tents were close, and the return journey ahead was long for anyone from Yemen or the north. Leaving a day early could mean joining a caravan that was setting out, or reaching home before supplies ran short. The choice was practical before it was devotional.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for counted days used here also opens the passage on fasting earlier in the surah, where it describes a different set of days entirely. The clause clearing the person from fault is repeated twice in identical wording, once for each option, which reads as a deliberate refusal to weight one above the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two acceptable options are given without either being commended, which is rarer in religious instruction than it sounds. The condition attached applies to both, so what decides the value of the choice is the state of the person making it rather than the choice itself. And the closing clause reframes the whole scene: a crowd dispersing in every direction will be gathered again into one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about counted days, there opening the passage on fasting.
Names the appointed days of the pilgrimage and what is done and eaten during them.
Handles the earlier stations of the same journey, also by removing a supposed fault.

studies.applyIt: Notice a decision you keep treating as a test of your seriousness: how long you stay, how early you arrive, how much you take on. This ayah gives two answers and clears both, then attaches its only condition to the person rather than to the choice. Take the shorter option once and see whether anything is actually lost.

studies.title: Speech That Impresses You
studies.meaning: A portrait is drawn in one sentence. Someone's talk about worldly matters is impressive, he calls God as witness to what is in his heart, and the last three words undo both. The oath is the telling detail: he swears about the one thing no listener can check. The final phrase names him the fiercest of disputants, which places the problem in argument rather than in belief.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentators record differing accounts of whether a particular individual is described here or a type is being drawn, and several works give both. The passage sits in a stretch of the surah that sorts people by what they do rather than by which group they belong to, and the portrait continues over the next three ayat.

keyTerms.note: The verb describes something that wins admiration, and it is addressed in the singular to the hearer. The reader is placed inside the scene as the person being impressed, rather than watching it from outside.

A superlative describing someone who twists and turns in a quarrel and cannot be pinned down. The root is connected to the side of the neck, suggesting a man who turns his head away rather than yield.

A word for parties in a dispute, used of litigants standing before a judge. It places the description in the setting of argument and claim, which is where the person in this portrait actually operates.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Eloquence was the highest public skill in Arabia. A man who could speak well settled disputes, negotiated for his tribe, and was believed before quieter men. Oaths were the currency of proof, since there were no documents to check, and swearing by God was the strongest thing a person could offer. Both of the tools in this portrait were exactly the tools a respected man used.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one that closes the group both begin with the same phrase, among the people is he who, and together they frame a contrast. The first names someone whose speech impresses; the last names someone who sells himself seeking God's approval, and nothing at all is said about that man's speech.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the impression a person makes from what they are, and it does so without giving the reader any way to tell the difference in advance. That is honest rather than useful: it warns that the tools of credibility can be held by anyone. What follows in the next ayat is not a test for detecting such a person but a description of what they do once they have power.

crossReferences.why: Continues the portrait directly and then sets its opposite against it in the same construction.
Describes an appearance that impresses and speech worth listening to, attached to the same warning.
Shows the same gap between what is said in a person's presence and what is planned afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you were persuaded by how something was said rather than by what it was. Not tricked, just carried. Try one thing this week: write down the actual claim, in your own plain words, before you agree with it. The gap between the two is what this ayah is describing.

studies.title: The Man Who Sells Himself
studies.meaning: The portrait continues and then breaks. The first man, once he has authority, works to ruin crops and offspring, and correction only stiffens him, since pride takes hold of him through the wrong itself. Then, with the same opening phrase, a second person is named: one who trades his own self seeking God's approval. Nothing is said about his speech, and the passage ends on God's kindness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section that sorts people by conduct rather than by affiliation. The classical commentators record differing accounts of whether particular individuals stand behind these portraits, and give more than one name for the second. The reading several works prefer is that two types are being set against each other for the listener to recognise wherever they appear.

keyTerms.note: Two words covering what is sown and what is born, so between them they name everything that grows. The pair describes ruin reaching the future rather than only the present, since both are next year's food and next year's people.

The word usually names honour and strength, and is used of God elsewhere in the Quran. Here it takes hold of a man through his own wrongdoing, so what could be dignity becomes the thing that stops him hearing.

The verb can carry both buying and selling in Arabic, and here the commentators read it as selling. What is traded is the self, which makes the transaction total rather than a portion of someone's wealth.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ruining crops and livestock was how conflicts were actually fought in Arabia. Burning a field, cutting date palms or driving off a herd destroyed a settlement without a battle, and the damage lasted for years. The pairing of what is sown and what is born names the two things a community could not quickly replace, and everyone hearing it knew a place emptied that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The two portraits open with the identical phrase, among the people is he who, three ayat apart. The first is given three ayat and the second only one, so the passage spends most of its length on the figure it warns about, and closes on the shorter description with a word about God's gentleness towards His servants.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is defined here by what it costs rather than by what it feels like. The second figure is described entirely by a transaction, and no claim about his inner state is reported at all. That inverts the first portrait, where the inner state was exactly what was sworn to. The passage suggests that a visible price paid is more informative than any account a person gives of themselves.

crossReferences.why: Opens this portrait, with the oath about what is in the heart that these ayat then answer.
Describes the same transaction from the other side, as God purchasing the selves of the believers.
Promises the final home to those who seek neither superiority on earth nor corruption in it.

studies.applyIt: Notice what your convictions have actually cost you this year. Not what you believe, what it cost. For most people the honest answer is very little, and that is worth knowing rather than being ashamed of. Pick one thing this week where holding to what you say will cost you something small and concrete.

studies.title: Enter It Whole
studies.meaning: One word carries the ayah: wholly, entirely, all of you. Commentators read it two ways, either as entering submission completely without keeping parts of one's life outside it, or as all of the believers entering together. Both readings are recorded and neither is dismissed. Then the warning about footsteps returns, and the second ayah handles what happens if someone slips after clarity has arrived.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to a community that had arrived from different backgrounds and brought its old arrangements with it. The commentators connect the ayah to believers who kept practices from before, holding parts of their earlier life apart from what they had entered. Reports about the exact occasion differ between the works, and several prefer the general reading.

keyTerms.note: The word covers peace and surrender together, and shares a root with the words for submission and for safety. Reciters differ over its vowelling, and the two readings pull towards peace or towards submission respectively.
The single word both readings turn on. Grammatically it can describe the peace as complete or the people as all of them, and Arabic lets the ambiguity stand without either sense cancelling the other.
The verb for a foot sliding on a smooth surface, not for a deliberate turn. Choosing it makes the failure an accident of footing, which is gentler than the alternatives the sentence could have used.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: New arrivals in Medina brought debts, alliances, feuds and marriages arranged under older rules, and none of it disappeared on arrival. A man might have sworn protection to a clan he no longer prayed with, or held a grievance his new brothers had no part in. Entering something wholly, in that setting, meant renegotiating relationships that had been settled for years.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the footsteps of Satan appears twice in this surah, here and earlier in the passage about food, and both times it follows an instruction that sounds entirely ordinary. The word the first ayah turns on is grammatically ambiguous, and the classical commentaries preserve both readings side by side rather than choosing between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Partial commitment is named as the problem rather than outright refusal, and the enemy is described as working by increments rather than by a single temptation. That is a particular account of how people go wrong: not a decision but a drift, one step at a time. The second ayah's response to a slip is not a threat but two names of God, which leaves the door where the first ayah left it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same warning about footsteps, there attached to food and to inventing rules.
Repeats the warning twice in one ayah and states what the following of those steps leads to.
Answers the anxiety a warning about slipping produces, addressed to those who went furthest.

studies.applyIt: Find the part of your life you keep in a separate room from the rest: the way you talk with one group of friends, a habit you would not describe out loud, a corner of your work. You do not need to fix it today. Just stop filing it separately, and start seeing it as part of the same life.

studies.title: Shadows Of Cloud
studies.meaning: A question is asked that expects no answer: is anything short of the final scene going to satisfy them. The image given is deliberately unelaborated, and the classical commentators are careful with it, affirming the coming without describing how. The verb in the middle is decisive: the matter is settled, in a form that reports the outcome without naming who brought it about.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the instruction to enter submission wholly. The commentators read the question as addressed to those who kept asking for one decisive sign, and note that the same demand recurs across the surah. No specific occasion is reported. The image of cloud shadow belongs to a family of descriptions of the final day found in several places across the Quran.

keyTerms.note: The plural of what casts shade, used of an awning and of anything overhead. Paired with cloud, it names the covered light of a heavy sky rather than a bright appearance, which is not what a listener would expect.
From a root meaning to cover or conceal. The word is used in this surah for the cloud that shaded a people in the wilderness, so the same term carries shelter in one place and finality in another.

A passive verb for a matter brought to its conclusion, used of judgements and of debts discharged. Its passive form leaves the settling without a described agent, which fits a sentence that refuses to elaborate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia a bank of heavy cloud was the most watched sight of the year. It meant rain, and rain meant the difference between a good year and a hard one, so people read cloud formations the way a sailor reads a sky. A dense cloud approaching drew everyone outdoors. That expectation of something enormous arriving overhead is the feeling the image borrows.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for cloud used here appears in only four places in the Quran, and one of them is earlier in this same surah, where it describes the cloud that shaded the Children of Israel in the wilderness. The classical commentaries note the recurrence, since the same covering appears once as mercy and once as the end of all matters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah answers a demand for proof by describing the moment when proof would finally arrive, and by noting that at that moment nothing remains to be decided. That makes the demand self-defeating, since the evidence being asked for comes only when it can no longer be acted on. The final clause widens from one scene to a general statement, that all matters return to God.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for cloud, there describing shade given to a people in the wilderness.
Describes the sky split open with cloud and the angels sent down in streams.
States that faith arriving on that day will not benefit a soul that had not believed before.

studies.applyIt: Notice a decision you are keeping open until you have more certainty. Some certainties arrive only when the decision has already been made for you. Ask honestly whether the evidence you are waiting for could still change anything by the time it comes, and if it could not, choose now on what you already have.

studies.title: Ask Them How Many Signs
studies.meaning: An instruction is given to ask a question whose answer everyone already knows: how many clear signs were given. The point is the number, and it is left unstated so the hearer supplies it. Then a general principle follows about altering a blessing after it has arrived. The word for altering is the one used elsewhere in this surah for changing a text, so what is described is substitution rather than neglect.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section where the surah keeps turning back to the history of earlier communities. The signs referred to are those recounted at length in the first part of this surah: the sea, the manna, the water from the rock, the covenant at the mountain. The classical commentators read the question as rhetorical, addressed to the audience through the request rather than answered by anyone.

keyTerms.note: An interrogative used in Arabic for large indefinite quantities as much as for genuine questions. Placed here it works as an exclamation, so the sentence says how very many rather than asking anyone for a figure.

The intensive verb for putting one thing in the place of another, used earlier in this surah of a word that was changed and of a testament altered. It describes replacement, which is more active than simply losing something.
The singular is used, as it is in the earlier promise of a favour completed. Naming it in the singular treats everything given as one gift, so exchanging any part of it touches the whole of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The stories of the earlier communities were not foreign in Medina. Jewish families in the city preserved them in detail, and Arab tribes had heard them for generations at markets and around fires. The sea, the mountain and the years of wandering were common knowledge, which is why the surah can ask about them without retelling. Everyone in earshot could have answered.
studies.didYouKnow: The imperative to ask, addressed in the singular, opens this ayah, and the same construction is used elsewhere in the Quran to introduce a question whose answer the audience already holds. The verb for altering appears in this surah applied to a word spoken, to a testament, and here to a blessing received.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A blessing is treated as something that can be swapped rather than merely lost, which is a sharper idea. The failure described is not forgetting but replacing: putting something else where the gift was. That makes ingratitude an act rather than an absence. And it explains why the ayah opens by asking how many signs, since the scale of what was given is what makes the substitution visible.

crossReferences.why: Describes people who exchanged the blessing of God for ingratitude, using the same idea.
Opens the surah's address to the same community by recalling the favour given to them.
Says they recognise the blessing of God and then deny it, most of them being ungrateful.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing that has been reliably good in your life for years: a person, a place, your health. Say what it is out loud today, in one sentence, to someone. Long-standing gifts are the ones that get quietly swapped for something else, mostly because nobody ever says their name.

studies.title: Made Beautiful To Them
studies.meaning: The verb at the start is passive and no agent is named: the worldly life has been made attractive to them. Then the ridicule is reported without a reply. The answer comes as a statement of position rather than an argument, that the mindful will be above them on the day of resurrection. The closing clause changes the subject entirely, and says God provides to whom He wills without measure.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators describe a community in which many early believers had little, while those who mocked them held wealth and standing, and read the ayah against that visible contrast. Reports naming particular individuals differ between the works. What is agreed is the situation: people whose position made the poverty of the believers look like a verdict on their choice.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb with no agent named, so the sentence declines to say who did the adorning. The classical commentaries record more than one view on that, and the grammar allows the question to stay open.

A word of physical position rather than of merit. Answering a social ranking with a spatial one is deliberate: the reply uses the same kind of language the mockery did, and simply reverses the arrangement.

The phrase can mean without limit or without being called to account for it. Both senses are recorded, and either way it detaches what a person receives from any calculation the onlookers could perform.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca and Medina was visible in a way it is not now. You could see it in the number of camels a man watered, the guests he fed, the clothes his household wore at the pilgrimage. Poverty was equally visible. In a small town where everyone knew everyone's circumstances, being poor was a public condition, and mockery of it needed no words at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The passive verb that opens this ayah is used across the Quran for things made to look attractive, and the one doing the adorning is almost never named. The closing phrase about provision without measure appears several times in the Quran, and always detaches what someone is given from what they appear to deserve.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two separate points are made, and the second is the more unsettling. The first reverses the ranking at a later date. The second says that provision in this life is distributed without a visible measure, which removes wealth from the evidence a person could use about themselves or anyone else. Together they take the whole subject out of the realm of what can be inferred from appearances.

crossReferences.why: Lists what is made attractive to people, and names the better return standing beside it.
Tells the story of two men and two gardens, where the ranking is reversed within a lifetime.
States that God allocates livelihood among people, raising some above others in degrees.

studies.applyIt: Notice one moment today when you measure yourself against what someone else has. Not to feel bad about noticing, just to catch it happening. This ayah answers that comparison by saying the distribution has no visible measure in it, which means the arithmetic you are doing does not work even in principle.

studies.title: Humanity Was One Community
studies.meaning: A whole history is compressed into one sentence. People were one community; prophets were sent with news and warning; scripture came to judge between them where they differed. Then the turn: those who differed over the scripture were the very people who had been given it, out of rivalry rather than confusion. The ayah ends with guidance described as given by permission, not achieved.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators differ over what the original single community was, some reading it as a period of agreement before division, others as a state of common ignorance before revelation. Both readings are recorded and neither is settled in the classical works. The ayah stands in a section of the surah that keeps returning to how earlier communities handled what they received.

keyTerms.note: The first word names a body of people with something in common, from a root connected both to a mother and to a direction. It describes belonging rather than agreement, which is part of why the commentators differ here.

From a root meaning to seek or desire, used for wanting beyond one's due. The word names the motive for the division, and it is placed in the sentence exactly where a reason for confusion might have gone.
The word for permission rather than for power. Placed at the end of a clause about guidance, it makes reaching the truth something granted rather than something the guided party managed on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held several communities reading scriptures they traced to overlapping origins, living in the same streets and disagreeing sharply. Arab tribes nearby had their own inherited accounts. Everyone could see that agreement had once existed somewhere back along the line and had not survived. The question this ayah answers was not academic for anyone hearing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for differing appears three times in this single ayah, twice about the people and once about the thing they differed over. That repetition is one reason the classical commentaries treat the ayah as the surah's compressed account of religious history rather than as a comment on any one community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Division is located after knowledge rather than before it, and the cause named is rivalry rather than obscurity. That removes the usual excuse in every direction, since nobody can then claim the message was insufficient. Then guidance is described as given by permission, which stops the ayah from becoming a claim that one party simply reasoned better than another.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing more briefly: people were one community, then they differed.
Names the religion enjoined on the prophets and repeats that division came after knowledge arrived.
Gives the same diagnosis earlier in this surah, calling the disagreement a deep split.

studies.applyIt: Think about a split you are close to: a family, an organisation, a group of friends. Try to describe the disagreement in one sentence both sides would accept. If you cannot, notice that. This ayah says the trouble usually starts after everyone has the facts, and it takes that seriously rather than blaming a misunderstanding.

studies.title: When Is The Help Of God
studies.meaning: A question is put to the community, and it is not gentle. Did you expect to enter the garden without what happened to those before you. What follows describes that experience, ending in a sentence spoken by a messenger and the believers with him, asking when the help of God will come. The reply is one short clause, and it does not dispute anything in the description of the hardship.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentators connect the ayah to a period of severe pressure, and several works place it around the difficulties of the early Medinan years, though they differ on which. What is agreed is that the ayah quotes earlier prophets and their followers rather than the present community, which is what gives the quoted question its weight.

keyTerms.note: A pair the Quran uses together, the first from a root for severity and harm arriving from outside, the second for damage and loss suffered. Between them they cover what happens to a person and what happens to their circumstances.

A doubled root that imitates the movement it names, used of an earthquake. The passive form leaves the shaking as something done to them, and the same word gives its name to a whole surah about the earth being shaken.
The plain interrogative for time. Its bareness is the point: what is quoted is not a complaint or a doubt but a question about timing, and it is placed in the mouth of a messenger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hardship in that world came without cushioning. A siege, a bad harvest or the loss of a caravan meant real hunger within weeks, and there was nowhere to appeal. The communities the ayah refers to had been driven out, imprisoned and killed. For an audience that had left Mecca with nothing, the comparison would have been recognised immediately rather than heard as history.
studies.didYouKnow: The question quoted here is asked by a messenger and the believers with him, which is unusual: the Quran rarely places a question of this kind in a prophet's mouth. The answer that follows is a single short clause, and the classical commentaries note that it corrects the timing without disputing the difficulty at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardship is presented as a normal feature of the road rather than as a sign that something has gone wrong. That reframes the whole experience, and it is done by comparison rather than by argument: this happened to them too. Then a question about timing is voiced by the most credible possible speaker, which makes the asking permissible. The answer is about nearness, not about meaning.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether people expected to say they believe and be left untested, recalling those before them.
Puts the same question about entering the garden, there tied to striving and to steadfastness.
States the relation between hardship and ease twice over, in two consecutive short lines.

studies.applyIt: If you are in something hard, write down the question you have actually been asking. Not the polite version. This ayah puts a blunt question about timing into the mouth of a messenger, which means the asking is not the failure. Then notice that the answer it gives is about how near, not about why.

studies.title: They Asked What, He Answered Whom
studies.meaning: The question asked is about what to give, and the answer changes the subject to whom. Five recipients are listed in a fixed order that starts at the nearest relation and moves outward to the traveller with no claim on anyone. The commentators note the redirection: nothing is said about amount or kind, and the ayah closes with a general statement covering any good done at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, one of a series in this section that begins with a reported question. Giving in Arabia was governed by kinship, and the obligation ran outward from close family. The list here follows that order and then extends it past where custom stopped, to the poor and the stranded traveller. The commentators read the ordering as deliberate rather than incidental.

keyTerms.note: Literally the son of the road, an idiom for someone whose circumstances are defined by being on a journey. The phrase makes the road itself his family, which is exactly why he has nobody else to ask.

The same word covers goodness and property, and it appears twice in this ayah, once for what is spent and once for what is done. That double use quietly ties giving and good conduct into one category.

From a root meaning to be still or motionless, so the word pictures someone brought to a standstill by need. It names a condition rather than a character, which is why nothing more is asked about them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller in Arabia was genuinely helpless. Away from his tribe he had no protection and no claim on anyone's hospitality beyond custom, and if his money ran out or his mount died he could not simply find work. Towns on the caravan roads dealt with stranded travellers constantly. Naming him last extends the circle of obligation to someone who will never repay it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of several ayat in this section that open with a question the community had put, and it is the one where the answer most clearly declines the question asked. The word for good is used twice within it, once for what is spent and once for what is done, so a single term covers wealth and conduct in one sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Redirecting the question is the teaching. A person asking what to give is thinking about the gift; the answer makes them think about people, and specifically about an order of nearness they may have skipped over.
