The closing clause then widens the subject past giving altogether, so that the whole matter is folded into a larger one: whatever good you do is known.

crossReferences.why: Names a similar circle of recipients inside its definition of righteousness, earlier in this surah.
Gives the near relative, the needy and the traveller their due, and warns against squandering.
Describes what giving returns, and what talk about it afterwards can undo.

studies.applyIt: Go through the list in order and stop at the first one where you cannot name a person: parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, someone far from home. That is probably where your giving stops. Find one name for that place this week. The ayah answers a question about amount by asking about people, and it is worth answering the same way.

studies.title: You Do Not Know What Is Good
studies.meaning: A hard instruction is given and the dislike it will provoke is acknowledged in the same breath. Then the sentence widens into a general principle that reaches far past its occasion: you may hate what is good for you and love what harms you. The final clause explains why, and it is not a comfort about outcomes. It is a statement about the limits of human knowledge, which is left as the last word.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. By then the community faced organised hostility from Mecca and was being told to defend itself. During the Meccan years they had been forbidden to fight. Early scholars describe real reluctance among believers, some of it moral and some of it fear. They read the opening concession as taking that reluctance seriously, not brushing it aside. The ayat that follow deal with specific questions from the same conflict.

keyTerms.note: Not mild dislike. The word covers what is hateful and forced on you against your will. The Quran uses it here of the believers themselves, granting their feeling rather than criticising it.
A particle of hope and possibility. It keeps the two clauses that follow from becoming a rule. The passage says this can happen, not that every dislike hides a benefit.
The comparative and the plain adjective share a form, so the word slides between good and better. What is being contrasted is not pleasure and pain but two assessments of the same thing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The emigrants in Medina had left houses, businesses and family behind. They arrived depending on hosts. Conflict with Mecca threatened the caravan trade that many of their relatives still worked in. Fighting meant facing cousins and brothers across a field. Reluctance in that setting was not squeamishness. It was the reasonable response of people who could name, one by one, the men they might meet.
studies.didYouKnow: The two middle clauses of this ayah are among the most quoted lines in Arabic. People use them outside religion too. It is plain comfort after a lost job or a broken engagement. Early scholars already treated the idea as one you could lift from its setting. That is why the wider statement is put as a chance. It is not a claim about every case.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the gap between God and the human being in knowledge, not in power. That is a specific claim. It does not say that everything painful turns out well. It says your judgement is made with less information than you assume. That leaves room for grief to be real while the verdict waits. And by admitting the dislike first, it shows a faith that does not require pretending to want what you do not want.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same principle to marriage: you may dislike something in which God places much good.
Dramatises the point at length, three acts that look wrong until their reasons are given.
Shows Jacob holding hope against every visible sign, and refusing to despair of God's relief.

studies.applyIt: Think of something from five years ago that you did not want and now would not undo. Write down one sentence about it. Then think of something you are resisting now and put the two beside each other, without concluding anything. The point is not to talk yourself into liking it. It is to remember, accurately, that your reading of events has been wrong before.
studies.explainEasier: God says people will be asked to do things they hate. Sometimes you hate what is good for you. Sometimes you love what will hurt you. God knows how things will turn out, and you do not.

studies.title: Weighing One Wrong Against Another
studies.meaning: A question about fighting in a sacred month is answered in two stages. The act is called grave, which concedes the question rather than dismissing it. Then a list is set beside it of things called graver, and the comparison is what the ayah is doing: not excusing the first but placing it on a scale. The passage then describes the aim of the pressure being applied to the community.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report an incident in which a small party sent out by the community encountered an opposing group near the boundary of a sacred month, and that the resulting controversy prompted the question this ayah answers. Accounts of the details differ across the works, but the setting is well attested and the ayah is read against it.

keyTerms.note: The plain word for large, used here of the seriousness of an act. The comparative form of the same word then appears twice for the items set against it, so the whole comparison is built on a single root.
A verbal noun for blocking someone from a path, covering physical obstruction and persuasion alike. It heads the list of graver things and names an act of prevention rather than one of violence.
The verb is used of an animal that swells from eating a poisonous plant and then dies of it. It describes something that looked like growth and turns out to have been the cause of the ruin.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sacred months were the infrastructure of Arabian life. Trade, pilgrimage and safe travel all depended on the guarantee that fighting stopped, and a violation was talked about across the peninsula. Access to the sanctuary was a related guarantee, and barring someone from it was a serious act with no remedy anyone could seek. This ayah weighs one such guarantee against another.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative form appears twice in this ayah, each time raising something above the act the question was about. The clause about persecution weighing heavier than killing has already appeared a few ayat earlier in a slightly different wording, so the surah states the same weighting twice within a short passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A comparison is used where a denial might have been expected. The ayah does not say the objection was wrong; it says the objection was smaller than what the objectors themselves were doing. That is a demanding form of argument, because it requires both sides of a scale to be named honestly. It also means the concession stands: the act was grave, and saying so is part of the answer.

crossReferences.why: States the same weighting of persecution against killing, in a slightly different wording.
Names the sacred month and the offerings among what is not to be violated, alongside a warning about hatred.
Describes those who bar people from the Sacred Mosque although they are not its rightful keepers.

studies.applyIt: When you next weigh a complaint made against you, try answering it the way this ayah does: concede the part that is true first, in plain words, before you say anything else. Most arguments lose their heat at that point, because the concession is what the other person was actually waiting for.

studies.title: They Look Forward To Mercy
studies.meaning: Three groups are named in one line, and the verb attached to them is the surprising part. They hope for God's mercy, and the sentence stops there. Nothing is guaranteed. Those described have believed, migrated and struggled, which is as much as a person could do, and what they are said to have at the end of it is hope. Two names of God close the ayah.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed directly after the hard ayah about the sacred month. The commentators read the placement as answering the anxiety the previous passage would have produced among those who had taken part in the disputed incident. The people described are the emigrants who had left Mecca, and the reports agree on that while differing over the details.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cut off or abandon, so the word carries the severing of ties as much as the journey. It names leaving a place behind rather than arriving somewhere new.

A verb sitting between hoping and expecting, used of someone who anticipates something without holding a guarantee. Placing it after everything these people had done is what gives the ayah its restraint.

The word appears in the construct form, so it is God's mercy specifically rather than mercy in general. What they hope for is not a verdict or a reward but a relation, which is a smaller and a larger thing at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The emigrants had left houses, businesses and graves behind, and most arrived in Medina with nothing. Some had been traders in Mecca and now worked as labourers. Their old property was occupied by others, and there was no expectation of getting it back. What this ayah calls migration was, for those hearing it, a specific memory of a specific week when they loaded what they could carry.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here is one of hope rather than of certainty, and the classical commentaries pause on it. They note that the people described had done everything asked of them, and that the sentence still stops short of a guarantee, ending instead with two names of God about forgiveness and mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Certainty is withheld from the people best placed to claim it, and the withholding is the point. Hope is presented as the correct posture even after a maximal effort, which keeps the relationship from turning into an account settled. At the same time the two closing names make that hope well-founded rather than anxious. The ayah holds both of those together in one line.

crossReferences.why: Asks that God be called on in fear and hope, naming both postures together in one clause.
Describes the hardship these same people had been through, a few ayat earlier.
Names the same three actions and states the rank given to those who took them.

studies.applyIt: Think about something you have worked hard at and now feel entitled to an outcome from. This ayah takes people who had given up everything and describes them as hoping. Try holding your own effort that way for a day: real, costly, and still not a claim. Most people find it lighter rather than heavier.

studies.title: Weighed, Not Simply Declared
studies.meaning: Two questions are answered in one ayah. The first is met with a weighing rather than a verdict: both things carry serious harm and some benefit for people, and the harm is the heavier. The second question, about what to give, is answered with a single word the commentators read as what is left over beyond need. The ayah closes by naming reflection as its purpose.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the run of ayat answering questions the community had put. The commentators describe this as one stage in a sequence of passages on the subject, coming before the later and more decisive ayat in another surah, and they read the weighing here as preparing for what followed. The second half continues a question about giving that was answered a few ayat earlier.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for advantage or profit. Its presence is striking: the ayah concedes real benefits rather than denying them, and then places them on the lighter side of a scale.

A comparative rather than an absolute. The sentence is built as a measurement rather than a declaration, which is why the classical works describe this ayah as a stage rather than the end of the matter.
The same root gives the word for pardon and for what is left over easily. Answering a question about giving with this word ties generosity to what a person can spare without strain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both practices were woven into Arabian social life. Wine circulated at gatherings and was celebrated in poetry, and the arrow game divided a slaughtered camel by lot, with the losers paying and the winners often feeding the poor from the meat. That is the benefit the ayah concedes: real people were fed. Naming it honestly is what makes the weighing land.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places where the Quran answers a question by conceding the other side of the argument before making its own point. The word given as the answer to the second question is a single word in Arabic, and the same root produces the word for pardon, so the vocabulary of giving and of forgiving overlap.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A judgement is presented as a comparison, and the reader is left holding the scale. That is unusual, and the closing clause explains it: the purpose named is thinking, not compliance. It also models a kind of honesty about mixed goods. Something can be genuinely useful and still not worth what it costs, and the ayah refuses to make the case easier by denying the usefulness.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same two subjects later and states the outcome the classical works read as decisive.
Answers the earlier form of the same question about giving, there by naming the recipients.
Uses the same word for what comes easily and is left over, there about how to deal with people.

studies.applyIt: Take one habit you defend by naming its benefits, and write those benefits down honestly. Then write the cost beside them, in the same detail. This ayah does not tell you the answer comes out one way. It shows you the method, and it names thinking as the point of the exercise.

studies.title: Then They Are Your Brothers
studies.meaning: A question about orphans is answered in two moves. The first names the standard: whatever improves their situation is best, which leaves the method open and fixes the aim. The second addresses a practical worry about mixing households and property, and answers it with a word about kinship rather than about accounting. Then a clause notes that God distinguishes the one who spoils from the one who repairs.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that after severe warnings about consuming the property of orphans, guardians began separating their food and belongings entirely, which made caring for them impractical and left the children isolated. The ayah is reported as the answer to that, and the sources are broadly agreed on the setting even where details differ.

keyTerms.note: From the root for mending what is broken, used earlier in this surah of repairing a testament and of reconciling people. Naming the aim rather than the method leaves the guardian to judge each case.

The verb for blending two things together, used of mixing property and of sharing a household. It describes an intermingling rather than a transaction, which is exactly what the questioners were worried about.
From a root meaning hardship and being brought into difficulty. The clause states what was not done, so the ease of the arrangement is presented as a deliberate restraint rather than an oversight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Orphans in Arabia were common and vulnerable. Conflict, disease and hard travel left children without fathers, and their property, often a share of palms or animals, passed into the hands of a relative to manage. Households were shared: the same cooking fire, the same herd, the same store of dates. Separating an orphan's food completely from the family's meant something close to excluding him.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah calls orphans in a shared household your brothers, using the ordinary word for a sibling. The clause about God distinguishing the one who spoils from the one who repairs is built on two roots already used across this surah, so the sentence sorts guardians with the same vocabulary it has been applying to whole communities.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The standard given is an outcome rather than a procedure, which places the burden on the guardian's judgement and then names the one who can tell the difference. That is a demanding arrangement, because it removes the safety of a rule followed exactly. And the clause about not being overburdened suggests that a stricter arrangement was possible and was not chosen, which frames the whole answer as a relief.

crossReferences.why: Warns against substituting the bad for the good and consuming orphans' property along with your own.
Sets out testing orphans before handing over their property, and warns against consuming it hastily.
Puts the same concern in one short line, in a Meccan surah addressed to an orphan.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you help at arm's length: a relative you send money to, a neighbour you check on from the doorway. This ayah answers a worry about getting too involved by naming the person as family. Do one thing this week that mixes your life with theirs rather than keeping the accounts separate.

studies.title: Even If She Pleases You
studies.meaning: Two parallel statements are made, one about women and one about men, in almost identical wording. Between them sits a comparison that does the work: a believing servant is better than an idolater, however attractive. The ayah is built to set attraction against direction, and it explains the reason at the end, that one side calls towards the Fire and the other towards the Garden and forgiveness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section on households and their arrangements. Marriage in Arabia was an alliance between families as much as a bond between two people, and it carried religious consequences, since a household's practices followed its arrangement. The classical commentators discuss the scope of the terms used here at length and record differences over how widely they extend.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used a few ayat earlier of speech that impresses a listener. Its recurrence links the two passages: in both, something admirable on the surface is set against what lies underneath it.

The feminine of the word for one who has faith, from a root meaning safety and trust. The comparison applies it to someone in the lowest social position of that time, which is what gives the sentence its force.

The ordinary verb for calling someone towards something. Using it of both sides is deliberate: the passage describes two invitations rather than a threat and a promise, so the difference lies in the destination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A marriage in Arabia joined two lineages, and it decided which gods a household honoured, which feasts it kept, and which side it took in a dispute. Children followed the arrangement. Marrying across a religious line was therefore not a private matter, and both families would have weighed the alliance in terms of protection, trade and standing before anything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The two halves of this ayah mirror each other almost exactly, with the same clause about being pleased repeated for each. That kind of full symmetry is uncommon in the Quran's passages on household arrangements. The comparison in each half reaches for the person of lowest standing in that society and places them above the alternative.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage rearranges a social hierarchy without arguing against it directly. Standing, wealth and beauty are not denied; they are simply outweighed by something that society did not rank at all. And the closing image reframes the whole subject: what is described is not a matter of status but two directions of travel, with a household understood as moving in one of them together.

crossReferences.why: States a matching principle about who is suited to whom, in the language of good and bad.
Denies that lineage or origin decides rank, and grounds honour in awareness of God.
Handles a related question about households divided by belief, in a later Medinan passage.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of a first impression you form from things you would not defend out loud: appearance, accent, the confidence in someone's voice. This ayah names attraction honestly and then sets it beside something else. Try describing one person this week by what they are pointed at rather than by how they come across.

studies.title: A Question Answered With Restraint
studies.meaning: A question is put about menstruation. The answer is kept narrow. It calls the condition a discomfort, not an impurity in the person. It sets apart marital intimacy for as long as it lasts, and nothing more. Then the sentence lifts: God loves those who turn back to Him, and those who keep themselves clean. Early scholars read that closing line as the point of the whole ayah. A matter of the body is turned into a matter of love.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line sits among a run of ayat that begin with reported questions from the community. The classical sources describe the practice around them. Some neighbouring communities kept a menstruating woman from eating and sitting with the household at all. Other Arabian custom made no distinction whatever. Early scholars read the answer as taking a middle position between two customs the audience already knew.

keyTerms.note: A mild word, used elsewhere for an irritation, a nuisance, or hurtful speech. Early scholars note it is much weaker than the words for defilement available in Arabic, and that the choice is deliberate.
An intensive form, describing people who return repeatedly rather than once. It is paired here with cleanliness, which links an inward habit to an outward one in a single clause.
A reflexive form: the action is done by the person to themselves. The root covers physical washing and inward clearing alike, and Arabic keeps both senses in play at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households in Medina were close quarters. Families ate from a shared dish, slept in one or two rooms, and drew water together. A rule of complete separation meant a woman spending several days each month outside her own home. Reports from the period describe exactly that arrangement among some communities in the town. Against that background, an answer that touched only one part of married life was a large narrowing.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of a run of ayat in the surah that open by reporting a question to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). That formula occurs about fifteen times across the Quran, and it clusters heavily here. Early scholars use these openings to work out what the first community was actually asking about. It turns out to be mostly practical matters of daily life.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to treat a natural function as a stain on the person. The wording carries that refusal. It then attaches God's love to two ongoing habits, not to a state reached once. Repentance and cleanliness are set side by side, as if they were versions of the same movement. What could have been a note about restriction becomes a statement about what God is drawn to.

crossReferences.why: Uses the image of spouses as garments for one another, describing the same relationship at its warmest.
Names tranquillity, affection and mercy as the purpose of the marital bond.
Repeats God's love for those who purify themselves, in an entirely different context.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you speak about bodies, your own and other people's, when something is uncomfortable or awkward. The words chosen here are careful, and the care is the lesson. This week, when illness or a bodily limit comes up in your household, pick the gentler word rather than the blunter one. See whether the conversation goes differently.
studies.explainEasier: Someone asked about a woman's monthly period. God says she is not dirty. It is just something that hurts. Husbands and wives wait a few days before being close again. God loves people who keep themselves clean.

studies.title: Send Something Ahead For Yourselves
studies.meaning: An image from farming is used for the marital relation, and the commentators are clear about its scope: it names the bearing of children, the ground on which the next generation grows. Then the sentence turns without pause to something else entirely. Send ahead for yourselves, and know that you will meet Him. What began as a private matter ends facing a meeting.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the sequence on households. The classical sources record that a question was raised about a particular matter and that this ayah was the reply, and the works differ over the details. What they agree on is the shape of the answer: an image, then an immediate turn to conduct and to accountability, ending with an instruction to give good news.

keyTerms.note: The word for ploughed land, used earlier in this surah for the crops a corrupter destroys. The commentators read it as naming what grows rather than the standing of the ground, so the image is about offspring.
A verb for sending something in advance of yourself, used of provisions dispatched before a traveller sets out. It moves the sentence from the present into what a person will find waiting for them.
A participle rather than a verb, so it names a settled fact rather than a future event. Placing it here attaches the most private part of a life to the most public reckoning of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agriculture in Medina was the centre of life, and the vocabulary of sowing and harvest ran through ordinary speech. A field was tended over seasons, watered, protected and depended on for years, and a farmer's relation to his land was long rather than transactional. That is the register the image belongs to, and it would have sounded like patience rather than possession.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for cultivated ground appears earlier in this surah in a completely different setting, describing what a corrupter destroys along with the next generation. The two occurrences are eighteen ayat apart, and both pair the field with offspring, so the surah reuses one image on opposite sides of a contrast.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The turn in the middle of the ayah is the teaching. Something intimate is named and then immediately connected to a meeting with God, which refuses to leave private life outside the account. What is asked for is not restraint but forethought: send something ahead. And the last clause changes the addressee entirely, ending a passage about the household with good news.

crossReferences.why: Names tranquillity, affection and mercy between spouses as a sign to be reflected on.
Uses the image of a garment for the same relation, earlier in this surah.
Uses the same verb about a soul considering what it has sent forward for tomorrow.

studies.applyIt: Take one relationship you are inside every day and ask what you are sending ahead in it. Not what you are getting. This ayah moves in a single sentence from something private to a meeting, and the move is worth copying: choose one small thing today that the other person will still be glad of in ten years.

studies.title: An Oath Laid Across The Road
studies.meaning: A specific trap is named. Someone swears by God not to do something, and then finds the oath itself standing between him and doing good, keeping ties, or making peace between people. The ayah does not discuss the technicalities of oaths; it points at what this one is being used for. The construction covers both a genuine bind and a convenient excuse without distinguishing them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, among the instructions on households and disputes. Oaths were the strongest verbal commitment available in a society without documents, and men swore readily and publicly. The commentators record that some treated an oath sworn in anger as grounds for staying estranged from a relative, and read the ayah as addressing that. The ayat that follow continue with unintended oaths.

keyTerms.gloss: an obstacle, a thing set up
keyTerms.note: The word means something laid across a path, and also something exposed and put on display. Both senses fit here: the divine name is placed across the road, and held up as the reason for staying put.
From the same root as the word for righteousness used earlier in this surah, and applied especially to kindness towards parents. It names the ordinary good that an oath in this case is preventing.

The verb for repairing, appearing here for another distinct time in this surah, after a testament and an orphan's affairs. Each time it names putting something back rather than starting something new.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath in Arabia bound a man publicly and was expected to hold. Swearing by God in front of witnesses made it a matter of honour, and backing down cost standing. A quarrel between relatives could therefore be frozen permanently by a few words spoken in temper, with neither side able to move without looking weak. Everyone knew a family in that position.
studies.didYouKnow: Three good things are named in this one short ayah as what an oath might be blocking: doing good, mindfulness of God, and making peace between people. The ayah then closes with two names of God about hearing and knowing, which sit pointedly at the end of a sentence about words spoken aloud.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A religious commitment is described as capable of becoming an obstacle to religion, which is a sharp observation. The divine name is exactly what makes the oath binding, and exactly what is being misused. The passage does not resolve this by adjusting the rules about oaths; it names the purpose the oath is serving and leaves the person to see it. The following ayat then deal with what oaths actually bind.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately, distinguishing unintended oaths from what the heart actually resolved.
Sets out what is done about an oath deliberately made, rather than leaving it standing forever.
Addresses someone who withheld from a relative, asking whether they would rather be pardoned themselves.

studies.applyIt: Think of a position you have taken that you would not take today, and that you are holding because you said it out loud. Not a principle, a position. This ayah is about the moment a commitment starts working against the thing it was meant to protect. Say the harder sentence this week: I have changed my mind.

studies.title: What Your Hearts Have Earned
studies.meaning: A distinction is drawn between words said without weight behind them and what the heart actually resolved, and only the second is held against a person. Then a specific situation follows: a vow of abstention from one's wife, with a waiting period of four months and two possible endings. Each ending is met with names of God rather than with a verdict, one pair about mercy and one about hearing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section on households. The classical sources describe a pre-Islamic practice in which a man could swear off his wife indefinitely, leaving her neither married in any real sense nor free to remarry. Setting a limit of four months put an end to an indefinite suspension. The commentators are broadly agreed on that background.

keyTerms.note: Names speech with nothing behind it, the filler phrases people use without meaning them. The word is used elsewhere in the Quran for what is absent from the Garden, so it carries a sense of the pointless.

The verb is the ordinary one for earning wages. Applying it to hearts treats an intention as something worked for and acquired rather than as a passing state, which is why it can be held against a person.

A reflexive form describing someone holding themselves in expectation. The same root is used for the waiting period after a separation, so the vocabulary of this whole section is built around suspended time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman in that position had no way out. She could not remarry, her family could not press the matter, and she had no income of her own. An indefinite vow left her in a state that could last years, and it was a known instrument of pressure inside a marriage. Setting a fixed limit turned a permanent condition into a bounded one with a required outcome.
studies.didYouKnow: These three short ayat close with three pairs of divine names in a row: forgiving and forbearing, forgiving and merciful, hearing and knowing. The last pair arrives at the moment a separation is decided, and the classical commentaries note that hearing is named there rather than any word about judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is located in what was actually resolved rather than in what was said, which is a claim about how a person is read. Words spoken carelessly do not create obligations; the heart's intention does. Then the passage takes an open-ended cruelty and puts a clock on it. What was indefinite becomes finite, and both possible endings are named without either being condemned.

crossReferences.why: Precedes this directly, naming the misuse of an oath that these ayat then take apart.
Draws the same distinction between idle oaths and deliberate ones, and sets out what follows.
Applies the same principle to an honest mistake, holding a person only to what the heart intended.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between something you said and something you meant, in one conversation this week. Most of our speech is the first kind, and this ayah says it is not being counted against us. Then find the one thing you did mean and have not acted on. That is the part the ayah is actually interested in.

studies.title: What God Created In The Womb
studies.meaning: A waiting period is set, and then the most striking clause arrives: what is in the womb may not be concealed. The ayah puts that in terms of belief rather than of procedure, which makes honesty here a matter of faith. Then rights are described as mutual, in a phrase the commentators discuss closely, and the closing word about a degree is read in more than one way across the classical works.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the surah's passage on separation. Before this, arrangements afterwards were governed by custom and by whichever family had more standing. A pregnancy decided inheritance, lineage and a child's claims, so concealing one could change a family's future. The commentators read the clause about honesty against that, since the disclosure often ran against a woman's immediate interest or her family's.

keyTerms.note: A word carrying two opposite senses in Arabic, covering both a monthly period and the interval between them. The classical commentators record both readings, and the difference affects the length of the waiting.

keyTerms.gloss: in what is recognised as right
keyTerms.note: Literally what is known, meaning conduct a community would recognise as decent. The phrase recurs throughout this section, tying the standard to something people can see rather than to a fixed list.

The word for a step or a rank. The classical commentators read it in more than one way, most often of the husband's responsibility for maintenance or of his standing in the matter of return, and they record the range.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A separation in Medina reorganised a woman's whole position: where she lived, who supported her, whether she could remarry, and what her children could claim. All of it was decided in front of families who had their own interests. A waiting period created a fixed interval in which nothing could be rushed, and it gave a pregnancy time to become known before arrangements were settled.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the waiting period belongs to a small class of Arabic words that carry two opposite meanings, and the classical commentaries record both readings without one displacing the other. The clause about not concealing a pregnancy is stated as a matter of believing in God and the Last Day rather than as a procedural requirement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truthfulness is placed at the exact point where a concealment would be most useful and least detectable. Nobody else could know, and the ayah answers that by attaching the disclosure to belief rather than to enforcement. That is a pattern the Quran uses repeatedly: where verification fails, the standard is raised rather than lowered. The description of rights as mutual then sets a baseline the passage works within.

crossReferences.why: Opens a later surah on the same subject and repeats the concern with counting the period carefully.
Continues directly, setting limits on what may be taken back and calling them the limits of God.
Addresses the same relation and states that women are not to be inherited against their will.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing you know and have not mentioned because mentioning it would cost you something and nobody would ever find out. That is the exact situation this ayah describes. You do not have to announce it publicly. Just tell the one person whose decision actually depends on it.

studies.title: Retention Or Release, Both Kindly
studies.meaning: A count is set on how far a separation can be reversed, and each stage is given two possible endings named with the same weight: keeping the arrangement decently, or releasing it with kindness. The two are presented as equal options rather than as a good outcome and a failure. Then a narrow exception is described about what may be returned, and the passage closes by naming limits.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources describe a practice in which a man could separate and take back repeatedly without limit, keeping a woman suspended indefinitely, and report that this ayah set the count. The reports are widely recorded. The passage sits in a long stretch of the surah working through the arrangements that a separation produces.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of turning livestock loose to pasture in the morning. The image is of release into open ground rather than of expulsion, and the word carries none of the harshness the English can.
The noun from the verb meaning to do something well and beautifully. Attaching it to the release rather than to the retention puts the higher of the two standards on the harder option.
The word names a boundary line around a piece of ground. The passage repeatedly asks that people stay inside rather than test the edge, and the phrase built on it dominates this whole section.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Repeated separation and return was a recognised way of controlling a woman without releasing her. She could not remarry, her family could not intervene, and the cycle could continue for years. Everyone in Medina would have known of a case. Setting a number turned an open loop into something with an end, and the counting is what made the difference.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the limits of God appears four times within this single ayah, more than in any other ayah of the Quran. Both of the endings offered are named with a positive word, one about decency and one about kindness, so the language does not mark the separation as the worse outcome.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending something well is treated as an achievement rather than as a failure to continue. The passage gives release its own standard, and the higher of the two words is attached to it, which changes what a person is aiming at when a relationship ends. The repeated language of limits then frames the whole arrangement as a marked-out space that both parties are standing inside together.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same pair of options and warns against holding on in order to cause harm.
Uses the same two options in a later surah and adds the calling of two just witnesses.
States that if the two do separate, God will enrich each of them out of His abundance.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are ending or have ended: a job, a friendship, a project. This ayah gives the ending its own standard and uses the warmer of its two words for it. Ask what a good ending would look like in your case, and do one part of it this week rather than letting the thing trail off.

studies.title: A Door That Does Not Reopen Easily
studies.meaning: A limit is described that closes the loop the previous ayah opened. After a final separation the arrangement cannot simply be resumed, and the condition stated makes an immediate reversal impossible. A return becomes possible again only under a further condition, that the two of them think they can keep within the limits. The ayah ends by saying these boundaries are made clear to people who know.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing directly from the ayah that set the count. The commentators describe the effect rather than debating the purpose: what had been a reversible cycle becomes final at a defined point. The classical works discuss the details of this ayah extensively, and much of that discussion belongs to legal literature rather than to a study note.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for entering a marriage. Its use here is what makes the condition substantial, since what is described is a genuine second arrangement rather than a formality arranged for the purpose.

A verb sitting between thinking and being fairly sure, short of certainty. The condition asks for a reasonable expectation rather than a guarantee, which the commentators note as realistic about what anyone can know.

keyTerms.gloss: the two return to each other
keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form, so both parties return rather than one taking the other back. The grammar makes the reunion mutual, which is not how such arrangements had worked in practice before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Words spoken in anger were binding in Arabia, and a man could dissolve a marriage in a moment and reverse it the next week. Households lived close together, so quarrels were public and reconciliations were performed in front of everyone. A limit that made the third separation final introduced a cost into a sentence that had previously been cheap to say.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah closes a passage in which the phrase about the limits of God appears repeatedly across consecutive ayat. It ends with the words for people who know, one of several closing formulas in this section, each naming a different faculty: those who know, those who believe, and those with understanding.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A boundary is placed where reversibility would otherwise be unlimited, and the effect is to make an easy word expensive. That says something about how the passage understands human behaviour: what can be undone cheaply will be done carelessly. The mutual form of the verb for reunion then quietly changes the shape of the arrangement, since the return now requires both of them and not one.

crossReferences.why: Sets the count that this ayah completes, and introduces the language of limits it uses.
Continues the passage, addressing pressure applied after a separation has already been made.
Opens a later surah on the same subject and asks that the counting be done carefully.

studies.applyIt: Notice a sentence you say easily when you are angry, and that you then have to take back. This passage works by making a cheap word expensive, which is a strategy rather than a scolding. Choose one such phrase and take it out of your vocabulary for a month. The cost will land somewhere better.

studies.title: Do Not Hold On To Cause Harm
studies.meaning: The two options return, and this time both are named with the same word, so neither is presented as the better. Then the specific abuse is named: holding on in order to cause harm. The ayah calls that wronging yourself rather than wronging her, which is a deliberate reversal. It closes by recalling what was given and warning against treating revelations as a plaything.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that some men would take a woman back near the end of the waiting period and separate again, restarting the count purely to prolong the suspension. The ayah names that use of the arrangement directly. The commentators read the warning about treating revelations lightly as addressed to exactly that manipulation of a protective procedure.

keyTerms.note: A form describing mutual or deliberate harm, from the root for damage. Placed as the purpose of the holding on, it names the intention rather than the act, so the same action is right or wrong by what it is for.

The passage does not say he wronged her, which the commentators notice. The construction turns the harm back on the person doing it, a move the Quran uses repeatedly for wrongs committed against others.
The word for something taken as a joke or a toy. Used of revelations, it names the treatment of a protective arrangement as a device, which is a specific kind of contempt rather than open rejection.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The waiting period was a woman's protection: a fixed interval after which she was free. Restarting it repeatedly turned that protection into a cage, and there was no authority she could appeal to. Her family could argue, but the man held the procedure. Naming this in revelation gave the situation a public description it had not had before, which is often the first thing that changes anything.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names three things in sequence at its close: God's favour, the Book, and wisdom, all as things sent down to teach. The same three appear together earlier in this surah in the description of what a messenger does among people. Here they arrive at the end of a warning about manipulating a procedure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The wrong is located in the intention rather than in the action, since taking someone back is otherwise exactly what the passage encourages. That makes identical conduct acceptable or not by what it is for, which is a demanding standard and an unenforceable one. And by saying the person wronged himself, the ayah declines to leave the injury as only the victim's problem.

crossReferences.why: Introduces the same two options and the language of limits that this ayah returns to.
Warns against coercion undertaken in order to take back part of what was already given.
Repeats the instruction not to cause hardship in order to constrain someone's choices.

studies.applyIt: Ask what one of your ongoing commitments is actually for. Not what it was for originally, what it is doing now. This ayah judges an identical action by its purpose, which means the audit has to be internal. If you find something you are holding on to in order to make a point, let it go this week.

studies.title: Do Not Stand In Their Way
studies.meaning: The address turns from the two people involved to everyone around them. When a waiting period has run and both parties want to resume, the surrounding family is told not to obstruct it. The verb used describes preventing something by force of position rather than by argument. The ayah ends with a comparative, that this is purer for you, and then plainly: God knows and you do not.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report a case in which a man's sister had separated and then wished to return to her husband, and her brother refused out of anger on her behalf, and they report this ayah as the answer. Accounts differ in detail across the works, but the situation described is consistent: a relative blocking a reconciliation both parties wanted.

keyTerms.note: An uncommon verb describing obstruction by someone who has the power to obstruct, and used of a difficult birth. It names blocking rather than advising, and its rarity gives the instruction a precise target.

A reciprocal form of the verb for being pleased, so agreement on both sides is written into the word itself. The condition is that the two are content, which is what makes the outside objection an intrusion.

A comparative from the root that joins cleansing and growth, used earlier in this surah for what a messenger does. Naming the outcome as purer answers the objectors in the terms they cared about, which was honour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage was a family matter, and a brother or father spoke for a woman in negotiations. When a marriage failed, the family that had given her felt the insult, and letting her return could look like accepting humiliation. Honour was a real currency, and refusing was the respectable choice. That is the pressure this ayah is speaking into.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction here is addressed in the plural to the people around the couple rather than to either of them, which is unusual within this passage. The ayah closes with two comparatives in a row, purer and more decent, and then with a short clause saying that God knows and you do not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Third parties are named as a real obstacle, which is an honest observation about how relationships actually end. Family honour is not argued with; the ayah simply asserts a different measure of what is cleaner. And the closing sentence sets a limit on the objectors' confidence, since the outcome they are protecting against is one they cannot actually see.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same kind of obstruction from those holding power over a woman's arrangements.
Handles the mirror case, where the husband rather than the family is the one causing harm.
Warns against acting on suspicion, which is usually the material an objection like this is made of.

studies.applyIt: Think of a reconciliation between two other people that you are, quietly, not helping along. Perhaps you heard the story from one side and took it up. This ayah addresses the bystanders, not the couple. Step back once this week from a dispute that is not yours, and say nothing where you would usually add something.

studies.title: Neither Parent Harmed Through The Child
studies.meaning: A period is named for nursing, and then everything else in the ayah is about protecting the people inside the arrangement. The father provides; nobody is burdened beyond capacity; neither parent is to be harmed through the child; the same responsibility passes to an heir. Weaning earlier is cleared if both agree after consulting one another, and hiring a nurse is cleared if payment is fair.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the passage on separation, since nursing arrangements were exactly what became contested when a household split. In Arabia, infants were often nursed by women other than their mothers, and the arrangement created lasting bonds recognised as a form of kinship. The ayah addresses a situation the community faced constantly rather than a rare one.

keyTerms.note: A dual form with an adjective for completeness attached to it. The precision is the point: naming a full term gives both parents something fixed to measure an agreement against rather than a matter of opinion.
A form that carries both harming and being harmed, so the clause covers each parent using the child against the other. Arabic lets a single word do what English needs two separate clauses for.

A reciprocal noun from a root connected to drawing out honey, and so to drawing out an opinion. Requiring consultation alongside agreement means the decision has to be talked through, not merely conceded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nursing was a serious economic arrangement. A wet nurse was paid, and Meccan families often sent infants to be nursed among the desert tribes for the health of the child and the language it would learn. A nursing woman had a claim on the household. When a marriage ended, the question of who paid for what was immediate and could turn bitter quickly.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about no soul being burdened beyond its capacity appears here in the middle of a passage about nursing arrangements, and it returns in almost identical words at the very end of the surah, inside the closing supplication. The same principle is stated once as an administrative point and once as the ground of a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The whole ayah is arranged around preventing a child from becoming an instrument. Both parents are protected by the same clause, in the same word, which refuses to assign the fault in advance to either of them. And the requirement of consultation makes the decision joint even after the relationship has ended, which quietly keeps a form of partnership alive past the point where everything else has been divided.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the clause about capacity at the very end of the surah, there inside a prayer.
Recalls a mother's carrying and her weaning over two years as grounds for gratitude.
Repeats the instruction about payment for nursing and about consulting one another properly.

studies.applyIt: If you share a responsibility with someone you no longer get on with, look at how decisions between you actually get made. This ayah asks for agreement and for consultation, which are two different things. Do the second one this week: ask before you decide, even where you could reasonably decide alone.

studies.title: Four Months And Ten
studies.meaning: A period is set for a widow, and its length is stated oddly precisely: four months and ten. Then the sentence releases her. When the term has run, no blame attaches to anyone for what she does with herself within what is recognised as decent. The clause is addressed to the community rather than to her, which is where the pressure in such situations actually comes from.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Before this, a widow in Arabia could be held in mourning for a full year, secluded and set apart, in a custom the classical sources describe as severe. The passage that follows a few ayat later refers to a year of support, and the commentators discuss the relation between the two at length. What is agreed is that a long confinement was shortened.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb from a root meaning to receive something in full. Death is described as a soul being collected rather than as an ending, and the passive leaves the one collecting unnamed in the sentence.

A reflexive form: the women hold themselves in waiting rather than being held by anyone. The same verb is used earlier in this section for a different waiting, so agency stays with the person waiting.
A name of God for one who knows the inside of a matter, from a root connected to testing soil by ploughing it. It closes a sentence about what people around a widow might do or say.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A widow's mourning in pre-Islamic Arabia could involve a year in a small hut, wearing the worst clothes she had and touching no perfume, and the sources describe the ritual that ended it in unpleasant detail. Neighbours watched and enforced it. A woman's family had a stake in how long she was seen to grieve, since her conduct reflected on them.
studies.didYouKnow: The period given here is four months and ten, not five months, and the classical commentaries note the precision. The clause releasing people from blame is addressed in the masculine plural, so it speaks to those around the widow rather than to her, which is where objections to a woman remarrying actually originated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A limit on grief is set in both directions. There is a period, so a bereavement is given real time and is not rushed; and the period ends, so nobody may extend it on her behalf. The release is phrased as removing blame from onlookers, which quietly names the actual obstacle. And the closing name for God is one about knowing the inside of things.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same situation a few ayat later, with a year of support and no eviction.
Continues directly, handling what may and may not be said during such a period.
Sets out waiting periods for other circumstances, and promises ease to whoever is mindful of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are keeping someone else's grief on your own timetable: expecting them to be over it, or expecting them not to be. This ayah sets a period and then ends it, and it speaks to the onlookers rather than to the bereaved. Ask the person what they want rather than deciding for them.

studies.title: What You Keep Inside You
studies.meaning: A narrow space is described with unusual care. During a waiting period, an indirect indication of interest is cleared, and so is keeping it entirely to oneself. Then a line is drawn: no private undertakings, and no concluding of the arrangement until the term has run. Between the permissions and the limit sits a sentence conceding the obvious, that people will be thinking about each other.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing from the ayah on a widow's waiting period. The classical commentators explain the situation practically: a woman in that period would receive interest, and the question was what could be said without pressuring her or pre-empting the term. The passage answers by distinguishing indirect speech from a commitment rather than by prohibiting contact altogether.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for approaching a subject from the side rather than head on. The word names indirect speech precisely, and the ayah's whole distinction rests on the difference between hinting and undertaking.
From a root meaning to shelter or house something, which gives the words for a cupboard and for a covering. What is described is not hiding a wrong but keeping a thought in its proper enclosure.
The word for a knot tied in a rope. Marriage is named by that image throughout this section, so what is postponed is the tying itself rather than the intention that precedes it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in a Medinan neighbourhood was known. A visit was noticed, a conversation at a doorway was reported, and a woman without a husband was watched more closely than anyone. A widow with property or standing would attract approaches immediately, some from men her family had reason to prefer. The distinction this ayah draws was a real protection from being committed before she was ready.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah concedes what people will be thinking before it sets any limit, using a clause that begins with God knowing. That order recurs across this section of the surah, where the difficulty is often named before the instruction. Two names of God close the ayah, one about forgiveness and one about forbearance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A thought is separated from a commitment, and only the second is restricted. That is a specific view of the inner life: what passes through a person is not held against them, and the line falls at what they do with it. Then the sentence about God knowing what is inside a person is placed on the other side, so the concession does not become licence. Both halves are needed.

crossReferences.why: Sets the waiting period whose conduct this ayah then describes in detail.
Draws the same line between what is said carelessly and what the heart has actually resolved.
States in one short line that God knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret.

studies.applyIt: Notice a thought you have been treating as a failing simply because you had it. This ayah clears the thought and draws its line at the commitment. Try separating the two this week: let the thought be there without arguing with it, and watch what you actually do next. That second part is what is being asked about.

studies.title: According To His Means
studies.meaning: A situation is described where nothing was owed and nothing had been settled, and the ayah still asks for something to be given. The amount is not fixed; it is scaled twice, once for the person with room and once for the person without, using the same word for both. That word means capacity rather than obligation. The closing phrase attaches the whole thing to those who do good.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the sequence on the arrangements a separation produces. In Arabia a woman leaving a marriage that had barely begun would have nothing, and no custom required anything to be given. The commentators read this ayah as creating a provision where none had existed, and note that it is framed as a due upon those who do good rather than as an enforceable claim.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb from the root for what is enjoyed and made use of, which also gives the noun for goods and provisions. It asks for something usable rather than a token, and the root recurs across this section.
From a root meaning wide and roomy, so wealth is named as having space rather than as having much. Its counterpart in the same sentence comes from a root for narrowing and being pinched.
The word for what is true and what is owed, the same term used for truth elsewhere in this surah. Placing it at the end turns a recommendation into something the giver owes rather than confers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman returning to her family after a marriage that produced nothing brought back no property and a diminished position. Her prospects depended partly on what she arrived with. A provision of clothes, dates or a little silver was not symbolic in that setting; it was the difference between arriving as a burden and arriving with something in her hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah uses the same word twice, once for the wealthy and once for the constrained, so the measure is identical while the amount is not. The closing phrase names it a due upon those who do good, using the word for excellence that also appears in the ayat on release, so this section keeps returning to a standard above the minimum.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An obligation is created at the exact point where none could be claimed, which is the interesting move. Nothing had been agreed and nothing had happened, and the ayah still asks. Scaling it to capacity rather than fixing an amount keeps it real for the poor and prevents the rich from discharging it cheaply. And attaching it to those who do good makes the giving a matter of character.

crossReferences.why: Handles the neighbouring case where an amount had been set, and prefers foregoing to claiming.
Extends a comparable provision more widely a few ayat later, again as a due upon the mindful.
Repeats the scaling of what is given to a person's means, and promises ease after hardship.

studies.applyIt: Find one place where you have given the minimum because that is what was agreed. A tip, a fee, a favour returned. This ayah asks for something where nothing was owed at all, and scales it to what you actually have. Add something small this week to a transaction that was already settled.

studies.title: To Forego Is Nearer
studies.meaning: A precise arrangement is stated, half of what was set, and then two ways out of it are named, one from each side. Either party may waive their share. The ayah then does something a legal sentence usually does not: it says which of the options is better, without making it required. The final instruction is broader still, that generosity between people should not be forgotten.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately following the case where nothing had been agreed. Here a sum had been set, and the ayah divides it. The commentators differ over who is meant by the one in whose hand the tie is held, some reading the husband and others a guardian, and the classical works record the range without settling it. Both readings leave the ayah's preference in place.

keyTerms.note: From the root for pardon and for what is easily spared, used earlier in this surah as the answer to a question about giving. Waiving a claim and forgiving an offence are named by one word in Arabic.
A comparative rather than a command. The ayah says foregoing is nearer to mindfulness of God, which recommends without requiring, and leaves both parties free while telling them which way is which.
The word for what is over and above, used elsewhere for divine favour and for honest earnings. Naming it as something between people makes generosity a shared space rather than one person's virtue.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dowry was a real transfer of wealth, often camels, silver or a piece of land, and it was negotiated between families before anything else. When an arrangement ended before it began, the money was already spoken for on both sides. Waiving a claim in that setting cost something visible, and everyone who knew the families would hear about it either way.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for waiving used here comes from the same root as the word given a few ayat earlier as the answer to a question about what to spend. The ayah names the better option with a comparative rather than a command, which is uncommon in this section, and closes with an instruction about generosity addressed to both parties at once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An exact entitlement is stated and then, in the same breath, both sides are invited past it. That combination is the passage's method: a floor for those who need one, and a direction for those who can go further. Naming which option is nearer to mindfulness of God without requiring it leaves the choice real. Nothing is enforced, and the better path is still marked.

crossReferences.why: Handles the neighbouring case where no amount had been agreed, and asks for provision anyway.
Uses the same appeal, asking whether you would not rather be pardoned yourselves.
Sets an equal response beside forgiving, and places the reward with God for whoever pardons.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are owed, exactly and defensibly. This ayah agrees that you are owed it and then says letting it go is nearer to something you want more. It does not tell you to. Sit with that for a day before you decide, which is longer than most of us give the question.

studies.title: Keep The Prayers Through Everything
studies.meaning: Two lines about keeping going. The first asks for guarding the prayers, singles out a middle prayer, and describes the posture: standing before God in devotion. The second removes the last excuse. Under threat, pray on foot or from the saddle, and make it up in remembrance once you are safe. Early scholars differ over which prayer the middle one is. The afternoon prayer is the most widely held view, and they set out the range without agreeing.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, and this passage is placed unexpectedly. These two ayat break into a long, detailed section on divorce, waiting periods and provision for widows. The subject then resumes at once. Early scholars discuss the placement rather than explaining it away. Their common reading is that a passage about households under strain is exactly where a reminder about prayer belongs.

keyTerms.note: The verb used for protecting property and for memorising the Quran. It implies active care of something valuable that can be lost through inattention, not through a single decision.
The feminine form of the word used earlier in the surah for a balanced community. It can mean central in order or best in quality, and that double sense is part of why scholars differ.
Describes sustained, quiet obedience while upright. The word suggests attentive stillness rather than fervour, which is why it is used of the posture rather than of the feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Danger was ordinary. Travellers between settlements risked raiding parties, and a merchant on the road kept watch through the night. Dismounting in open country was the moment you were most exposed, since a camel takes time to kneel and rise. Permission to pray while walking or riding was framed for people whose actual choice was between stopping in the wrong place and not praying at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The middle prayer named here became one of the most discussed questions in early Quranic commentary. The classical works list several candidate prayers and the arguments for each. Al-Tabari gives an unusually long section to weighing the reports. The Quran leaves it unnamed. One practical result of that is that all the prayers get guarded more carefully.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prayer is shown as something that bends rather than lapses. The standard is keeping it up, not perfecting its form. Naming a middle prayer without saying which one creates an attentiveness that a clear answer would have narrowed. And the closing clause frames the whole practice as taught, not invented: remember God as He taught you what you did not know. That makes worship itself part of the gift.

crossReferences.why: States that prayer is fixed on believers at appointed times, including after fear has passed.
Describes what the prayer does, restraining from indecency, which is why it is worth guarding.
Identifies those constant in their prayer as the exception to human anxiety and impatience.

studies.applyIt: Identify the prayer you most often lose: the one that falls in a meeting, a commute, or the middle of a task you hate interrupting. Do not resolve to be better generally. Decide now where you will pray that one tomorrow, physically, and what you will say to whoever is with you. These two lines are about arrangements more than intentions.
studies.explainEasier: Keep up your prayers, especially the middle one, and stand before God with care. If you are in danger, pray while walking or riding. When you are safe again, remember God as He taught you.

studies.title: A Year Of Support, No Eviction
studies.meaning: Provision is made for a widow: a year's maintenance, and specifically that she is not to be turned out of the house. Then the same release appears as before, that if she leaves, nobody is answerable for what she does within what is decent. The commentators discuss at length how this ayah relates to the shorter period set earlier, and the classical works record more than one account.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical commentaries differ over the relation between this ayah and the four months and ten set a few ayat before it, and over which arrangement stands. Several read this as an earlier provision and the shorter period as what followed; others read them as addressing different aspects. The works preserve the disagreement rather than resolving it.

keyTerms.note: The same word used earlier in this surah for the testament made before death. Here it names a provision for a widow, so the vocabulary of what a person arranges in advance runs through both passages.
A short phrase attached to the provision, naming the specific harm being prevented. The word for expulsion is the same one this surah uses of communities driven out of their homes.
From the root for what is used and enjoyed, appearing repeatedly across this section for what is given to a woman after a marriage ends. It names goods rather than a cash settlement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A widow's most immediate problem was the roof. A house belonged to her husband's family, and after his death the heirs had a claim on it, so she could find herself asked to leave within days of the burial while still in mourning. Naming eviction explicitly addresses the thing that actually happened, and a year gave a family time to arrange something.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for the provision is the same one the surah used earlier for the testament made before death, so a bequest and a widow's maintenance are named by one term. The clause releasing the community from blame is repeated here in almost the same wording as six ayat earlier.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The provision is directed at the two things that fail first: money and shelter. Naming the house separately shows the passage working from what actually went wrong rather than from a principle. And the repeated clause about no blame for what she does keeps returning to the same point, that a woman's choices after a bereavement were being decided by other people.

crossReferences.why: Sets a shorter waiting period for the same situation, which the commentaries read alongside this.
Introduces the word used here for a bequest, earlier in this surah in its usual sense.
Sets out the shares an heir receives, which the classical works discuss in relation to this provision.

studies.applyIt: Think about what would actually be hard for someone close to you in the first month after a loss: not the grief, the logistics. Where they sleep, who pays a bill, whether a car gets moved. This ayah is unusually concrete about that. Ask one such practical question next time, instead of asking how they are.

studies.title: A Due Upon The Mindful
studies.meaning: A provision described earlier for particular cases is now stated generally: divorced women are to be provided for, decently. The short ayah carries no conditions and names no amount, and it closes by calling this a due upon those mindful of God. The ayah after it steps back from the whole section and names the purpose of the explanation: that you may use your reason.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's long passage on marriage and separation. The commentators differ over whether this repeats an earlier instruction or extends it to cases the earlier ayat did not cover, and the classical works record both readings. The second ayah functions as the section's closing formula, of a kind the surah uses at several points to end a run of instructions.

keyTerms.note: The same word used twice earlier in this section, so its third appearance generalises what had been described case by case. It names usable goods rather than a settlement figure.
The passage places the due on a class of people described by their awareness rather than on a legal category. That framing recurs across this section, where the standard is named by character.
From the root meaning to tie or tether. Closing a long run of practical instruction with a word about reasoning suggests the details are meant to be understood rather than only followed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The end of a marriage in Medina left a woman dependent on her father's household or on a brother, and she arrived with whatever she had been given. Nothing in custom required a departing husband to add anything. In a town where households were small and margins thin, a provision of goods changed a woman's standing in the family she returned to.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat is a closing formula the surah uses several times, each with a different final verb: reflecting, remembering, mindfulness, and here reasoning. The same construction appears in the passage on intoxicants and again at the end of the ayah about attraction and marriage, so the surah marks the end of an answer this way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a due on the mindful rather than on everyone has a specific effect: it cannot be enforced and it cannot easily be evaded either, because the person who declines has told you something about themselves. That is how this whole section works. Then the closing ayah names reasoning as the point, which treats the instructions as something to be understood rather than simply obeyed.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same provision for one particular case, scaled to the giver's own means.
Names the two ways an arrangement can end, both with a positive word attached to them.
Uses the same closing formula, there ending with reflection rather than with reason.

studies.applyIt: Look at something you do only because someone can check. Then look at something you do that nobody would ever know about. This section places its duties in the second category on purpose. Pick one obligation you could quietly drop without consequence, and keep it this week, deliberately, because it is yours.

studies.title: Thousands Who Fled Death
studies.meaning: A compressed story is told in one line. Thousands left their homes to avoid death, God said die, and then revived them. No names, no place, no date. The commentators record differing accounts of who they were, and several works note that the point is the pattern rather than the identification. Then a general statement about grace, and an instruction that ties the story to what follows.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a run of narrative in the middle of the surah's legislative section. The commentators record more than one account of the people referred to, some connecting them to an epidemic and some to a summons to fight, and the classical works preserve the alternatives without deciding. What they agree on is the shape: flight from death did not prevent it.

keyTerms.note: A plural of a plural, so the number is deliberately large and deliberately vague. Naming a crowd rather than individuals fits a story told without names, where the scale is what carries the point.

The word describes caution and taking precautions rather than terror. What is named is a reasonable protective instinct, not cowardice, which is what makes the outcome instructive rather than a punishment.
The causative of the verb to live. The story turns entirely on this word, and the surah has already used the same root for the earth revived after its death, in the long ayah of signs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Flight from an epidemic was the ordinary response in the ancient world, and whole settlements would empty when sickness arrived. Leaving was what a sensible head of household did. Arabia knew both plagues and the summons to defend a settlement, and in each case a family had to decide quickly whether to stay. The story names a decision everyone hearing it could imagine making.
studies.didYouKnow: The story is told in a single ayah with no names, no place and no date, which is unusual even by the Quran's compressed standards. The instruction that follows it, one short line, links the narrative directly to the surah's earlier passage on fighting, and the run of stories that follows continues the same theme.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Precaution is not criticised, and that matters. The people described did something reasonable, and the outcome shows that the thing being avoided was not in their hands either way. What follows is not fatalism but a rearrangement of where control actually sits. The closing clause about most people not being grateful attaches the story to a return that was itself a favour.

crossReferences.why: States that death will catch up with you wherever you are, even inside fortified towers.
Says those destined to be killed would have gone out to their places regardless of any precaution.
Tells another story of death and revival further on in this surah, there about one man.

studies.applyIt: Notice one precaution you take that has quietly become a way of not living: a risk you never take, a conversation you never start, a plan you never commit to. This ayah does not criticise caution. It just shows that caution did not decide the outcome. Take one small thing off the avoided list this week.

studies.title: The Loan That Comes Back Larger
studies.meaning: God asks a question rather than giving an order, and the question uses the language of money. Someone is invited to lend to the one who owns everything, on terms where the repayment is multiplied many times over. The phrase for a good loan means one given without interest and without pressure. The line then adds that God both withholds and expands. That puts the multiplying, and any tightening of your means, in the same hand.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina.
