This line sits right before the account of Saul, Goliath and the small band that held its ground, and just after an instruction to spend in God's cause. Early scholars read the placement as pairing two kinds of commitment, wealth and life, in one passage. No single occasion is agreed for the ayah. Several reports connect it to appeals for supplying the community's expeditions.

keyTerms.note: The trade verb for lending, from a root meaning to cut off a portion. Using it of giving to God turns charity into a deal with an expected return, not a loss.
Early scholars gloss the adjective as given willingly, from lawful earnings, with no demand for thanks. It describes the manner of the lending, which the passage treats as part of what is lent.
A pair of opposites: closing a hand and opening it flat. Putting both under one subject answers the fear behind holding back, that giving makes you smaller, by naming who governs that.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lending ran the trade of Mecca and Medina. Caravans went out on advances. Harvests were paid for against dates not yet grown. Much of it carried heavy interest that ruined debtors. Everyone in the audience knew how it worked, and how cruel it was. A loan with no interest, no security and no risk of default took their most familiar tool and removed everything that made it dangerous.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a good loan appears six times across the Quran. It is always about giving in God's cause, never about ordinary borrowing between people. Early scholars observe that God, who owns everything, has no need to borrow. They read the image as chosen for the giver's sake. It lets a person picture their charity as an asset rather than a cost.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Framing charity as a loan changes how giving feels without changing the act. It grants that people part with money more easily when they expect a return. Then it supplies a return that is real but delayed. The clause about withholding and expanding takes the sum away entirely, since the wealth you are guarding was never under your control. Generosity turns into a matter of accurate accounting.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the offer of a good loan and attaches a generous reward to it.
Adds forgiveness to the multiplication, and names God as appreciative and forbearing.
Gives the multiplication a picture: one grain producing seven ears of a hundred each.

studies.applyIt: Give something this week at the point where it is slightly inconvenient rather than out of what is left over. The amount matters less than the timing: before the month's spending, not after. Notice the small resistance when you do it. That resistance is the thing this ayah is addressing, and it is answered by the last clause rather than by the first.
studies.explainEasier: God asks who will lend Him some money. That means giving in His cause. He promises to pay it back many times over. He is the one who makes money tight or easy anyway.

studies.title: They Asked, Then They Turned Away
studies.meaning: A request is made and a question is put back to the askers, almost gently: is it possible that if this were required of you, you would not do it. They answer with an argument, and it is a good one, since they had been driven from their homes and their children. Then the outcome arrives in half a line. When the thing was required, they turned away, except a few.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a run of narrative addressed to a community that had itself been driven from its homes and was being asked to fight. The commentators note the parallel and read the story as placed here for exactly that reason. The prophet in the account is not named in the Quran, and the classical works record differing identifications without insisting on any.

keyTerms.note: A word for the leading men of a people, those whose word carries in council. Naming them rather than the people generally locates both the request and the failure in the same group.
A particle of possibility inside a question, so the prophet's reply is a suggestion rather than an accusation. It leaves them room to answer, which is exactly what makes their answer count.

The verb for turning one's back, used across the Quran for withdrawal from something previously accepted. It describes a movement rather than a refusal, so the failure is shown as a departure rather than an argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Asking for a king was asking for something Arabia largely did not have. Tribes were led by chiefs whose authority rested on consent and lineage, and nobody could compel anyone to fight. A standing command structure meant giving up the right to walk away, which was the freedom a tribesman valued most. The request in this story was a serious surrender of something.
studies.didYouKnow: The prophet in this account is not named anywhere in the Quran, and no period is given. The story is told across several ayat and includes a request, a warning, an argument and an outcome, all before the king is even appointed, which the classical commentaries note as an unusually detailed narrative frame.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The gap between an intention and its execution is put on display, and the intention was sincere. Their argument was true: they had been driven out. What the story adds is that a real grievance does not by itself produce endurance. The prophet's question anticipates this before it happens, so the failure was foreseeable and was foreseen, and the story is still told without contempt.

crossReferences.why: Precedes this directly with another story about flight, and with the instruction it prepares for.
Describes a similar gap between what was said and what happened when the moment came.
Continues this same story, where the few who held are separated from the many who did not.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you said you would do if a particular situation arose, and then the situation arose. Not to condemn yourself: to notice the size of the gap. This story shows that gap in people with a genuine grievance and a genuine intention. Naming yours honestly is the only thing that ever narrows it.

studies.title: He Was Not Given Wealth
studies.meaning: A king is appointed and the objection is immediate, naming two things: our own claim, and his lack of money. The reply does not argue with either. It states that the choice was made, and then adds two qualifications the objectors had not thought to weigh: knowledge and physical stature. The ayah closes by placing sovereignty entirely in the giving of God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the story that began with the request for a king. The commentators describe the objection as arising from lineage: leadership was expected from particular families, and the person named came from outside that expectation. The account is given in the Quran without the detail found in other traditions, and the classical works are cautious about supplementing it.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the word for truth and rightful claim. The objectors are not merely expressing a preference; they are asserting an entitlement, which is why the reply speaks about choosing rather than about merit.
From a root meaning to spread out or extend. Applied to knowledge and to the body, it describes reach and capacity rather than quantity, and the same word is used elsewhere of an open hand.
A name of God from the root for width and room. Its placement after a dispute about who deserves what suggests the supply being argued over is not scarce in the way the argument assumed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leadership in Arabia followed lineage and wealth together. A chief needed the standing of his family and the means to feed guests, settle blood claims and equip men, since authority without resources could not act. The objection in this story would have sounded entirely reasonable to anyone listening, which is why the reply names two other qualifications instead of denying the first.
studies.didYouKnow: The two qualifications named in the reply are knowledge and physical stature, in that order, and the pairing is unusual. The classical commentaries note that the second mattered in a leader expected to fight at the front, and that naming knowledge first sets the priority even while conceding that the body counts for something.
studies.theologicalSignificance: An appointment is defended by widening what counts rather than by denying the objectors' criteria. Their claim about lineage is not answered at all, and their point about wealth is passed over. What replaces both is a statement about who gives authority, which relocates the whole question. The dispute is not settled on its own terms; it is moved to different ground entirely.

crossReferences.why: States that sovereignty is granted and stripped away by God, in the language of a prayer.
Describes wisdom as given to whomever God wills, and calls it abundant good.
Shows another figure asking for office on the grounds of honesty and knowledge rather than standing.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you objected to, and write down the criteria you were using. Then ask what someone might have been weighing that you were not. This story does not say the objectors were wrong about wealth. It says they were working from a shorter list than the one being used.

studies.title: Tranquility Inside The Chest
studies.meaning: A sign is given for a contested appointment, and it is an object rather than an argument. What arrives is a chest containing tranquility from the Lord and a remnant of what two families left behind. The word for tranquility is the one the Quran uses elsewhere for what descends on hearts. The ayah closes with a condition rather than a claim: a sign for you, if you are believers.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the account of the appointment of a king. The commentators identify the chest with an object the community had lost, and describe differing accounts of what it contained and how it returned. The classical works record the range and are careful not to go beyond what the ayah states. The sign is given to people who had objected on grounds of lineage and wealth.

keyTerms.note: An ordinary word for a box or coffer, used elsewhere in the Quran of the container an infant was placed in. Its plainness is part of the point, since the sign arrives inside something rather than as a display.
From a root meaning to dwell and to be still, which gives the words for a home and for calm. The Quran uses it for what God sends down on hearts in danger, so it names composure rather than comfort.
The word for what is left over after most of something is gone. Naming the contents this way is modest: what returns is a remainder rather than a restoration, and the sign is carried by that modesty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Objects carried authority in the ancient world. A tribe's standard, a chief's sword, an inherited seal: these settled arguments that words could not, because everyone recognised them. In Arabia a family's possession of such a thing was recited in poetry. Making the sign of a disputed kingship an inherited object rather than a miracle placed it in a language the audience already used.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for tranquility appears in only a handful of places in the Quran, and elsewhere it always describes something sent down onto hearts rather than contained in an object. Here it is said to be inside the chest, which the classical commentaries discuss carefully, several of them reading the containment as accompaniment rather than as physical.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sign given is not a demonstration of power but the return of something the community had lost. That is a particular kind of evidence, and it works by memory rather than by spectacle. Then the closing condition qualifies the whole thing: it is a sign for you, if you are believers, which admits that the same object would prove nothing to someone unwilling.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same tranquility sent down on a companion in a cave, in a moment of real danger.
Names it as what God sends into the hearts of believers so that faith may increase.
Uses the same word for a chest, there the one an infant was placed in and cast into a river.

studies.applyIt: Notice what actually steadies you when something goes wrong. For most people it is not a reason but an object, a room, a routine, a voice. This ayah names calm as something sent rather than manufactured. When you next find yourself steady, take a moment to notice where it arrived from.

studies.title: A River And A Smaller Army
studies.meaning: Two tests are set in a single scene. The first is a river, and the sorting is done by thirst: most of the army drinks and is dismissed, a few take only a handful and cross. The second comes at once, when even those who crossed lose heart at the size of the enemy. The answer is given not by the commander but by ordinary soldiers who expect to meet God, and it is arithmetic rather than encouragement.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This sits in a long account of the Children of Israel asking for a king, then failing what a king demanded. The Quran does not name the prophet who appoints Saul. Early scholars identify him with Samuel, while noting that the text is silent. The passage comes in a surah addressing a community newly required to defend itself, and it works as a mirror held up to that situation.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used of Abraham's trials, from a root meaning to wear out through use. A test in this sense reveals what is already there rather than adding a new difficulty.
One cupped hand of water. The word measures the exemption precisely, which is the point: the test is not abstinence but whether a person can stop at what was allowed.

Used of a detachment of fighters rather than a crowd. It carries organisation and purpose, which is why the contrast in the sentence is between a small band and a large one, not between a few people and many.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water discipline was a survival skill in Arabia and everyone listening had practised it. A traveller who drank his fill at a well and then found the next one dry was already dead. Guides rationed by the mouthful and judged a companion by whether he could be trusted at a water source. The river test would have read, to that audience, as a straightforward test of competence as much as of obedience.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where Saul and Goliath are named. The passage is also one of a small number of long stories inside surah al-Baqarah, which is otherwise mostly instruction. David appears two ayat later, killing Goliath before he is a king or a prophet. It is a single clause, which early scholars fill out from the wider tradition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Numbers are put in their place without being denied. The small band still knows it is small. What changes the sum is the conviction that they will meet God, so a view that reaches past death alters how the odds look now. The passage also shows commitment thinning under pressure in two stages, not one. That is a realistic account of how resolve fails. The remedy comes from inside the ranks, not from above them.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same principle of small numbers prevailing, and then adjusts it for weakness.
Shows large numbers failing at Hunayn, the reverse of this lesson.
Completes the scene: the prayer before battle, and David killing Goliath.

studies.applyIt: Find the small test in front of you today rather than the large one. It is usually the equivalent of the handful of water: the second helping, the extra hour, the reply you could send but should not. Pass that one deliberately. The story puts the river before the battle because that is the order in which people are actually sorted.
studies.explainEasier: Saul told his army not to drink from the river, except one handful. Most drank anyway and were sent home. The few left were scared of a bigger army. Some of them said God has often let a small group win.

studies.title: Pour Patience Over Us
studies.meaning: A prayer is quoted at the moment of confrontation, and it asks for three things in a specific order: patience, firm footing, and then support. Patience comes first, before any request about the outcome. The verb used for it is unusual, describing something poured out over a person from above, which makes endurance an arriving thing rather than a quality summoned from within.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the story of the small force that crossed the river and faced a much larger one. The words are given as the prayer of those who went forward, and the commentators note that they are quoted rather than prescribed. The account belongs to the run of narratives placed here before the surah returns to its own community's situation.

keyTerms.note: The verb for emptying a vessel completely over something, used elsewhere of pouring molten metal into a mould. Asking for patience in this word makes it arrive from outside and cover the person rather than be produced by them.
An intensive verb for fixing something firmly, with feet as its object. The image is of ground that will not slide, which is a specific and modest request compared with asking for victory outright.

keyTerms.gloss: and help us, give us victory
keyTerms.note: The verb covers both aid and the granting of victory, so a single word carries assistance and outcome together. It comes last in the sequence, after two requests about the people praying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ancient battle lines were decided by whether men held their ground. A formation that broke was cut down from behind, and everyone who had fought knew it. Prayers before an engagement were common across the ancient world, and they usually asked for victory. Asking first for patience and for footing names the two things that actually decided whether a line held.
studies.didYouKnow: The three requests in this prayer are ordered from the inside outwards: a state of the heart, then the body's position, then the outcome. The verb for pouring occurs only three times in the whole Quran, once here, once in an almost identical prayer elsewhere, and once of molten metal being poured out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is asked for first is not the result. Two of the three requests are about the people praying, and only the last concerns what happens. That order is itself instruction: the prayer treats endurance and steadiness as things that must be given before an outcome is worth asking about. And by describing patience as poured, it removes the assumption that a person simply has it or does not.

crossReferences.why: Records almost the same words in a different setting, asking that patience be poured out on them.
Quotes a similar prayer from earlier followers, asking for firm feet and for forgiveness.
Describes the crossing and the small number who went on, immediately before this prayer.

studies.applyIt: Next time you are about to do something difficult, ask for the state you will need rather than for the result. Steadiness, patience, a clear head. It sounds like a smaller request and it is usually the one that decides everything. Say it in those words once this week and notice the difference.

studies.title: The Earth Would Have Gone To Ruin
studies.meaning: The story ends in three quick clauses: they defeated them by God's leave, David killed Goliath, and David was given sovereignty and wisdom and taught. Then the narrative stops and a general principle is stated that reaches far beyond it. Without God restraining people by means of one another, the earth would be ruined. The particular story becomes an instance of something continuous.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the run of narratives that began with the request for a king. The commentators read the closing principle as the reason the whole story was told at this point in the surah, since the community was itself being asked to hold a line. The Quran gives the encounter in a single clause, without the detail preserved in other traditions.

keyTerms.note: The same phrase used earlier in this surah about guidance given to those who differed. Placing it before the outcome of a battle attributes the result without removing the fighting from the people who did it.

The verbal noun for pushing something away, an ordinary physical word. Used of God working through people, it describes a restraint applied continuously rather than an intervention at one moment of crisis.

From the root for corruption and spoiling, used of food that has turned. The word appears throughout this surah for what a corrupter does, so the general principle is stated in the surah's own vocabulary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Balance between tribes was what kept Arabia habitable. No single group could dominate the peninsula, and the knowledge that a raid would be answered restrained most of them most of the time. The system was violent and it also prevented worse. An audience living inside that arrangement would have recognised the principle immediately rather than needing it explained.
studies.didYouKnow: David is named here for the first time in the order of the Quran's text, and the encounter itself is given in a handful of Arabic words. The closing principle about people being restrained by one another appears once more in the Quran, at 22:40, where it is attached to the protection of places of worship.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The story is given a general reading in its own last sentence, and the reading is unexpected. What the encounter illustrates is not the reward of the faithful but a permanent arrangement in which no power is allowed to become total. That places restraint at the centre of how the world is kept liveable, and it makes the checking of power a mercy rather than an accident.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle and attaches it to the protection of places of worship of every kind.
Describes the small force and the river crossing that lead directly into this outcome.
Describes what David was given, including sound judgement and decisive speech.

studies.applyIt: Look for a place where something you dislike is holding something worse in check: an awkward colleague who asks the questions nobody else will, a rule that slows you down. This ayah reads a battle as an instance of restraint keeping the world liveable. Notice one such restraint today and let it stand.

studies.title: Recited To You In Truth
studies.meaning: Two short clauses close the run of narratives that began several ayat earlier. The first names what has just been recited as signs of God, given in truth, which stops the stories from being read as history for its own sake. The second is addressed directly to one person and states his position among the messengers. The whole ayah is confirmation rather than argument.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the account of the king, the river and the encounter that ended it. The commentators read the ayah as a closing seal on that section, and note that the surah uses similar formulas elsewhere to mark where a passage ends. The address in the second half is to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), at a point when his position was being disputed.

keyTerms.note: The verb for following one thing with another, which is also the word for reciting. Recitation in Arabic is named by sequence, so the word implies a text unrolled in order rather than delivered all at once.

The phrase can mean both truthfully and for a true purpose. Both senses fit at the close of a narrative section: the accounts are accurate, and they were told for a reason rather than as entertainment.
A passive participle: those who have been sent. Naming them by the sending rather than by any quality of their own places the whole emphasis on who did the sending.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stories were the main medium of the age. Poets and tellers carried the histories of tribes, the deeds of ancestors and the fates of vanished peoples, and a good telling drew a crowd at a market. What separated one account from another was the teller's reliability. Ending a run of narrative by naming its source addresses exactly the question an Arabian audience would have asked.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the shortest ayat in this part of the surah, and it comes directly after one of the longer narrative sections. The surah uses a similar closing sentence at other points, naming the recitation and its purpose, so a reader following the text can see where one section ends and another begins.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Narrative and revelation are joined explicitly. The stories just told are called signs, which means they are being offered as evidence rather than as memory. That places a claim on how they should be read: not as the past but as a pattern still running. And the direct address at the end ties the reliability of the account to the standing of the one reciting it.

crossReferences.why: Uses a similar formula, naming an account as news of the unseen revealed to the one reciting.
States why the accounts of the messengers are told: to make the heart firm with them.
Says there is a lesson in their stories for those with intelligence, closing a long narrative.

studies.applyIt: Notice which stories you retell about your own life, and what each one is for. Most of us keep a small set and run them without asking. This ayah names a purpose for the stories it has just told. Pick one of yours and ask what you are proving with it, and whether it is still true.

studies.title: An Unfinished Ranking
studies.meaning: Differences among the messengers are stated plainly, and examples are given without the ranking being completed: some were spoken to directly, some raised in degrees, and one was given clear signs and strengthened. Then the sentence turns to what happened afterwards. Those who came later fought one another, though the evidence had reached them, and the ayah says twice that this was not prevented.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the narrative section and opening onto the surah's later passages. The commentators are careful here, noting that a difference of gift is not a difference of standing in the essentials, and that the ayah does not complete the ranking it begins. The second half addresses something the community could see: peoples divided after receiving the same message.

keyTerms.note: From the root for what is over and above. It describes something added rather than a hierarchy of worth, which is why the commentators read it as a difference of gift and of role.

The classical commentators most commonly identify this as the angel Gabriel, and the phrase appears elsewhere in this surah in the same connection. Other readings are recorded, and the works do not insist on one.

A reciprocal form, so the fighting is mutual rather than one side attacking. Its subject is those who came after the messengers, not the messengers themselves, which the sentence is careful to separate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The audience in Medina lived among communities that traced themselves to the same prophets and disagreed sharply. That was not an abstraction: it decided alliances, marriages and who traded with whom. The observation in this ayah, that division followed rather than preceded the arrival of clear evidence, described something the listeners could verify by walking through their own town.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about God's will and the fighting is repeated twice within this one ayah, in almost identical wording, with the human disagreement named in between. The Quran rarely repeats a clause at that distance, and the classical commentaries treat the repetition as framing the human choice between two statements of divine permission.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together that are hard to hold. Division after clear evidence is attributed to people who disputed, and the sentence still says twice that it was not prevented. Neither half is dropped. The ayah also declines to complete its own ranking of the messengers, which leaves a difference acknowledged without turning into a hierarchy anyone could use.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same account of division arriving after knowledge, a few dozen ayat earlier.
Repeats that some prophets were given advantage over others, and names one gift specifically.
States that no distinction is made between any of His messengers, as part of what believers affirm.

studies.applyIt: Think of two people you admire who are genuinely different in what they are good at. Notice how quickly the mind wants to rank them, and how little that ranking would actually help you. This ayah names the differences and then stops. Try leaving one comparison unfinished this week.

studies.title: Neither Trade Nor Friendship
studies.meaning: An instruction to spend is given a deadline, and the deadline is described by what will not be available. Three things are named, and each is a way people normally get out of a shortfall: buying your way clear, calling on a friend, or having someone speak for you. The ayah closes them one after another. What is left is only what was sent ahead.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the surah's long passage on giving. The commentators note the placement, since the ayat that follow work through the subject at length with parables. The three things named were the actual mechanisms of a merchant society: credit, personal ties and the intercession of a patron, and all three were how difficulties normally got resolved.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary commercial word, used across this surah for exchanges of every kind. Naming it first places the day beyond the reach of the mechanism a merchant audience trusted most.

From a root meaning to penetrate or run through something, so the word names a friendship that has got inside a person. It is much stronger than acquaintance, and it is the tie a person calls on last.

From a root meaning to make something even by pairing it, so an intercessor joins himself to the one he speaks for. It is denied here without qualification, and the surah revisits it shortly with a condition attached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant in Mecca or Medina lived on credit, connections and reputation. A bad season was survived by borrowing, and a legal difficulty by finding someone whose word carried. Everybody had a patron or a relative who could speak on their behalf, and knowing whom to ask was a skill. The ayah names each of those three resources and removes them in sequence.
studies.didYouKnow: The three things denied here are named in a rising order of intimacy: a transaction, a friendship, and someone speaking on your behalf. The ayah of the Throne, a few ayat later, returns to intercession and qualifies it rather than denying it, so the surah states the point twice with different precision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is about giving, and it argues for it by describing a moment when nothing can be arranged. That is a specific way of motivating generosity: not by promising a return but by removing the alternatives. The three denials also say something about the social world, since each names a real form of help that works here and will not work there.

crossReferences.why: Returns to intercession a few ayat later and places it under permission, rather than denying it.
Repeats the instruction to spend before a day comes with neither trading nor friendship in it.
Warns that no parent will avail a child on that day, nor a child a parent, in anything.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself who you would call if something went badly wrong tomorrow. Most people can name two or three. Now notice how much of your security rests on that list rather than on anything you have done. This ayah does not take the list away. It just points at a place where it does not reach.

studies.title: The Living And The Sustaining
studies.meaning: The ayah is built from denials and possessions. God is alive and stands without support, so nothing outside Him holds Him up. Neither drowsiness nor sleep touches Him. That rules out the lapse in attention every ruler and guardian eventually has. Everything belongs to Him. No one speaks up for anyone before Him without His leave, and human knowledge reaches nothing of His except what He allows. It closes by saying that holding the heavens and the earth does not tire Him.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This ayah sits between an appeal to spend before a day when no bargaining is left and the statement that religion is not forced. Early scholars note the sequence rather than reporting a particular occasion for it. Read in place, it gives the reason the instructions around it carry weight. The one issuing them neither sleeps, nor forgets, nor tires.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the verb to stand. It joins two ideas the English needs two words for: standing without support, and holding everything else upright at the same time.
The state just before sleep, when attention slips but the eyes are open. Naming it separately from sleep closes the gap a listener might have left, since a watchman can nod without lying down.
Early scholars read it as His knowledge, His rule, or a created thing beneath the greater Throne, and they record the range without insisting. All agree it implies no bodily sitting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sleep was the vulnerability of that world. Caravans posted watches through the night, and a sentry who dozed could lose the whole company to a raid before dawn. A chief slept and his authority paused; a guardian slept and the herd was unguarded. Everyone listening had lain awake keeping watch or had trusted someone else to. Denying drowsiness to God was denying the one failure they most feared in a protector.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical tradition keeps a report in which the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) asked a companion which ayah of the Book he thought greatest, and accepted this one as the answer. It sits at number 255 of 286 in the longest surah. It contains no command, no story and no address to a human being. It is entirely description.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah describes God mostly by taking limits away. It does not add up a list of qualities. That keeps the description from settling into a picture. Speaking up for someone before God is allowed, but only with His leave. So both hope and His rule are kept intact. The last clause answers a human hunch: that holding up something so vast must cost something. It denies that any effort is involved at all.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same two names, the Living and the Sustaining, at the head of another surah.
Defines God by denial in the same way, at the shortest possible length.
Expands the theme of knowledge that reaches everything, down to a falling leaf.

studies.applyIt: Say this ayah once tonight before you sleep, and let the line about drowsiness land on your own tiredness. You are about to stop paying attention for eight hours, and something you have no part in will keep running. Most people find that the ayah works differently at that hour than at any other. Try it at the point where you are least capable.
studies.explainEasier: God is alive and never sleeps, not even for a second. Everything in the sky and on earth is His. He knows what is ahead of us and behind us. Holding it all up never tires Him.

studies.title: No Compulsion In Religion
studies.meaning: The opening clause denies that religion can be made by force. The reason follows at once: the difference between guidance and error has been made clear enough that force is not needed. The second half describes what belief actually is, using a physical image. Someone who turns down false objects of devotion and trusts God has taken hold of a handle that will not snap. Faith is presented as a grip, not a place.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. The classical sources report an occasion among the Helpers there. Families whose children had been raised in other faiths asked whether they could force them, and this ayah answered. The reports vary in detail, and early scholars record several versions. What they agree on is the setting: a mixed town where the question was practical and domestic, not theoretical.

keyTerms.note: From the same root as the word for aversion, so it names making someone do what they find repugnant. The negation is absolute in form, denying the thing itself rather than restricting it.
From a root meaning to overflow or exceed a limit. It covers idols, oppressive rulers and any power claiming what belongs to God, so the rejection named is wider than rejecting statues.
The loop or handle on a bucket, a saddlebag, or a garment, the part you grip when the weight is on you. The image is of holding rather than standing, which implies suspension over something.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Handles were everyday hardware in that life. A leather bucket lowered into a well hung from a loop. A rope or handle that gave way lost the water, and sometimes the bucket. Saddlebags carrying a family's goods across open country depended on the same fittings. When an Arabian audience heard of a handle that does not break, they pictured a specific relief: the moment you pull hard and it holds.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase for the firmest handhold appears twice in the Quran. It is here, and in surah thirty-one, where it describes the person who hands their face over to God. Both times it follows a rejection of false authority. Early scholars treat the repetition as one image used twice, not two images, which is unusual for a picture this specific.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes clarity, not force, the way truth spreads. It grounds that in the nature of belief itself. A conviction produced by pressure would not be the thing being asked for. Placing this right after the great ayah of God's sovereignty is pointed. The one who holds up the heavens without effort is shown declining to force a single human mind.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether the Prophet would compel people to believe, when God did not make them one community.
States the truth plainly and leaves belief or rejection to the hearer.
Uses the same image of the firmest handhold for one who surrenders to God.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose religious practice you have tried to change by pressure: a sibling, a child, a friend you argue with. Drop the pressure for a month, deliberately, and keep the relationship. Clarity was named here as the alternative to force, and clarity takes longer. Decide now what you will do instead of the argument you usually have.
studies.explainEasier: Nobody can be forced to believe. The right way is already clear enough to see. If you turn away from false gods and trust the real one, you are holding a handle that will never break.

studies.title: Out Of The Darknesses Into Light
studies.meaning: The ayah is built on a deliberate lopsidedness that the English can miss. Darkness is plural and light is singular. God brings believers out of many darknesses into one light. False authorities bring people out of the single light into the many. Early scholars read the number as the argument. Error has countless forms and truth has one. What the two halves contrast is the direction of travel, not the starting point.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line comes straight after the denial that religion can be forced, and early scholars read the two together. Having said belief cannot be forced, the passage describes what actually moves a person: God's guardianship. No particular occasion is reported. The image of leading out of darkness runs across the Quran, used elsewhere of Moses and of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), sent for the same purpose.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning nearness. It names the relative or ally who stands up for someone unable to defend themselves, so the word carries both intimacy and legal responsibility at once.
A plural, and it shares its root with the word for wrongdoing, which Arabic pictures as putting something where it does not belong. Darkness and injustice are linguistically the same failure.
Always singular in the Quran when set against darkness. Early scholars note the pattern across the text and treat it as meaningful rather than a matter of style.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night in the desert was absolute in a way that is hard to recover now. Without a moon a traveller could not see a hand, and the standard advice was to stop moving until dawn rather than risk walking off a ridge. A single lamp in a doorway was navigation for a whole quarter of a town. Being led out of the dark was not an image about mood. It was about not dying between one settlement and the next.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of plural darkness with singular light holds throughout the Quran without exception. It holds in every context where the two appear together. Classical scholars from al-Tabari onward remark on it. The same lopsidedness governs the description of God creating the heavens and the earth in the opening ayat of surah six.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What the passage gives God is guardianship, not just instruction. That makes guidance a relationship, not a delivery of facts. The reverse movement is active too. False authorities do not simply fail to help. They lead people out of light they already had. So error is a journey, not a starting condition, and light once received can be walked away from.

crossReferences.why: Opens with God appointing the darknesses and the light, using the same asymmetric pair.
Describes the Book as sent so people may be brought out of darkness into light by God's leave.
Develops light into an extended image of lamp, glass and oil, and calls God the light of the heavens.

studies.applyIt: Notice one place where you were given clarity and have drifted back. A practice you kept and dropped, an honesty you used to manage. The ayah describes movement in both directions, which means the drift is not permanent. Name the one thing you would need to change to reverse it. Start it today rather than working out the whole route.
studies.explainEasier: God is the friend of those who believe. He leads them out of the dark and into the light. False powers do the opposite. They take people who had light and lead them back into the dark.

studies.title: Bring It From The West
studies.meaning: An argument is reported, and its structure is what matters. Abraham names God by two continuing acts, giving life and causing death. The opponent answers with a demonstration that meets the words without meeting the claim. Rather than explaining the difference, Abraham moves to something the man cannot imitate at all. The sentence ends with a single word: the one who denied was confounded.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a run of three passages about life and death that follow the ayah of the Throne. The opponent is not named in the Quran, and the classical commentators record more than one identification without insisting. The ayah notes that he had been given sovereignty, which the commentators read as the reason he could answer a claim about life and death with a display of power.

keyTerms.note: The verb from which the word for a proof or an argument comes, used earlier in this surah of a case pressed in public. It names formal dispute rather than conversation, so the scene is a contest.

Two verbs in the present tense, describing continuing action rather than single events. That is what the opponent's reply misses: he can produce an instance, but the claim was about what is always happening.
A passive verb describing someone stopped in confusion, unable to answer. It is the last word about him in the ayah, and it names the end of an argument rather than a change of mind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A king who could pardon a condemned man and execute another had, in the plainest terms, the power of life and death. The demonstration reported here was not a trick; it was how authority actually looked to everyone watching. Arabian audiences knew rulers of that kind from the Persian and Byzantine borders, and the exchange would have sounded like a real confrontation.
studies.didYouKnow: The second challenge is not an argument but a request, and the ayah reports no reply to it at all. This is one of three consecutive passages in the surah about the giving of life, the others describing a ruined town and a request made by Abraham himself, so the theme is turned over three times in a row.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange demonstrates a specific method: when an opponent redefines the terms, the claim is restated in a form that cannot be redefined. Abraham does not accuse the man of cheating. He moves to ground where a demonstration is either possible or it is not. And the closing clause attributes the failure not to bad argument but to a refusal that guidance does not overrule.

crossReferences.why: Continues the sequence with another scene about the giving of life, there to a passing traveller.
Shows Abraham reasoning about a lord that sets, in a very different argument from this one.
Records another exchange in which Abraham answers with a question his opponents cannot answer.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often an argument is won by shifting what the words mean rather than by meeting the point. This ayah shows a reply that does not fight over the definition and simply restates the claim somewhere it cannot slide. Try that once this week: ask for the same thing in a form that has only one meaning.

studies.title: A Hundred Years, Or Part Of A Day
studies.meaning: A man passing a ruined town asks how it could ever be revived, and the answer is given to him rather than explained. He dies for a century, wakes, and guesses he slept a day. Three things are then shown in order: his food unspoiled, his animal, and bones being assembled and clothed. The ayah ends with his own words, his question turned into a statement.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the second of three passages on the giving of life. The man is not named in the Quran, and the classical commentators record several identifications without settling on one. The commentaries note that the question he asked was not a denial but a wondering, and read the answer as given to genuine perplexity rather than as a punishment for doubt.

keyTerms.note: A vivid phrase for a building whose walls have fallen inward onto the roof beams. The image is precise: not a ruin worn down slowly but a structure that came down and stayed where it fell.

keyTerms.gloss: it has not turned or spoiled
keyTerms.note: A rare verb connected to the passing of years. What is denied is the change food undergoes with time, so this part of the sign is described by an absence rather than by an event.
A verb for raising and joining, used here of bones being brought together. Reciters differ over one letter of it, and both readings describe the same picture of a structure being reassembled.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ruined settlements were a common sight in Arabia. Trade routes moved, wells failed, and a place that had supported hundreds became a scatter of walls within a generation. Travellers passed such sites regularly and named them. The question the man asks is the question anyone would ask standing in one, and the ayah reports it without any tone of denial.
studies.didYouKnow: The proofs are shown in a deliberate order: food that should have spoiled and did not, an animal, and then bones being assembled and covered. Each addresses a different span of time, and the classical commentaries note that the man is shown the evidence in ascending difficulty before he says anything at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A question about how something could happen is answered by making it happen to the questioner. That is the shape of the passage, and it treats the doubt as reasonable enough to deserve an answer rather than a rebuke. What changes at the end is not the information but the position: the man who asked from outside now speaks from inside the thing he was asking about.

crossReferences.why: Precedes this with the first of three scenes about the giving of life, there as an argument.
Completes the sequence with a request made by Abraham, answered with a demonstration.
Sets out the same argument from the stages of growth and from the earth reviving after rain.

studies.applyIt: Think of a question you have carried for years without an answer arriving. This passage does not resolve the man's question by explanation; it puts him inside it. Notice whether the questions that eventually settled for you settled by argument or by something happening. Then hold the current one a little more patiently.

studies.title: To Put My Heart At Ease
studies.meaning: Abraham asks to be shown how the dead are given life, and the reply is a question: have you not believed. His answer is the interesting part. He says yes, and then adds a reason that is not about belief at all but about the state of his heart. The request is granted, and what he is asked to do with four birds is described briefly and without explanation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the third of three consecutive passages on the giving of life. The commentators are unanimous that the request was not doubt, and they take the answer at face value: a wish for the settling that comes from seeing. Several classical works record differing accounts of the details of what was done with the birds, and the Quran itself gives only the outline.

keyTerms.note: A verb for something that has settled and stopped moving, used of a heart and of ground alike. What is asked for is not information but the end of a restlessness, which is a different request entirely.
A particle used specifically to answer a negative question in the affirmative. Its force is emphatic: not a simple yes but a contradiction of the doubt the question might have been taken to imply.

keyTerms.gloss: incline them, draw them to you
keyTerms.note: A verb the commentators read in more than one way, some as inclining the birds towards him and others as cutting them up. The classical works record both readings, and the Arabic supports each of them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Birds were part of daily life and daily observation. People knew the flight paths of pigeons, kept them, and used them to carry messages, and a bird released could be expected to return. Hills stood visible from any settlement in that country. The elements of the demonstration were entirely ordinary things, arranged into something that could not happen by itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The exchange contains a question, an emphatic particle answering it, and then a reason, all within a few words. The classical commentaries frequently pair this ayah with the story a few lines earlier, since one man asked how and was made to experience it, while here a prophet asks how and is shown. Both questions receive an answer rather than a reproof.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A distinction is drawn between believing something and being settled about it, and the second is treated as a legitimate thing to want. That is unusually generous, and it comes with the highest possible credentials, since the person asking is a prophet. The passage does not suggest the request was a weakness. It records the question, the answer, and the fact that it was granted.

crossReferences.why: Precedes this with a man asking a similar question and being answered by experience rather than sight.
Records another request for a sign made by believers who wanted their hearts reassured.
Names what settles hearts, using the same root as the word Abraham uses in his answer here.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between something you believe and something that has settled in you. They are not the same, and this ayah does not treat wanting the second as a failure of the first. Name one thing you hold that has not settled, and stop apologising for the gap. Ask for it instead.

studies.title: Seven Ears Of A Hundred Grains
studies.meaning: A single grain is described producing seven ears, with a hundred grains in each. That image is offered as the shape of spending in God's cause. Then the multiplying is widened further: God multiplies for whom He wills. The second line attaches a condition, and it is not about the amount. Giving followed by reminders of your generosity, or by insult, is shut out. So what is being measured is how the receiver is treated afterwards.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines sit in a run of ayat on giving that goes on for most of a page and includes several farming pictures. The community was funding expeditions and supporting emigrants who had arrived with nothing. Appeals for money were frequent and public. Early scholars note that this section is about how to give, not whether to, which suggests giving itself was not the difficulty.

keyTerms.note: The seed head at the top of a wheat or barley stalk. The image is agricultural and slow: nothing about it is instant, and the return arrives after a season of waiting rather than at once.
The specific act of bringing up a kindness you did in order to make the other person feel it. Arabic has a single word for it because the behaviour was recognised and despised.
A general word for harm, here covering the words and manner that wound a recipient. Pairing it with the previous term names two ways generosity turns into humiliation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The audience knew the sums were generous but not fantastic. A good grain of wheat could split into several stalks in watered Medinan soil, and a heavy ear held dozens of grains. The picture stretches a real yield rather than inventing one. It also carries the farmer's experience of delay. You bury something you could eat, see nothing for months, and are not certain of the harvest when you do it.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about spending in God's way is repeated word for word at the start of both these ayat. Classical rhetoricians treat that as deliberate. The identical opening makes the difference between the two endings impossible to miss. The first ends in multiplying and the second in safety. The only thing that changes between them is how the giver behaves afterwards.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The return on charity is put entirely outside the giver's control. The multiplying is God's, and its size is not stated. That takes charity out of the logic of investment, even while borrowing its words. The receiver's dignity is made a condition of the reward. So the passage treats a poor person's self-respect as something God protects. That raises the stakes of a passing remark far past ordinary politeness.

crossReferences.why: Gives the reverse image: charity ruined by reminders, like soil washed off bare rock.
States the comparison directly, kind words being better than charity followed by injury.
Shows the manner the passage asks for: feeding others while wanting neither reward nor thanks.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you helped someone and later mentioned it, even lightly, even to a third person. That is the specific behaviour these lines exclude. This week, when you give something, decide in advance that you will never refer to it again, to anyone. Keeping that decision is harder than the giving, which is why the passage spends a whole ayah on it.
studies.explainEasier: Giving money to help others is like planting one seed. It grows into hundreds. But do not remind people of what you gave them, and do not hurt them with your words.

studies.title: Kind Words Over Wounding Charity
studies.meaning: A comparison is made, and one side wins outright. A decent word, together with letting an offence go, is better than money given and then followed by injury. The claim is startling because it ranks something free above something costly. The closing names for God explain the ranking. He is beyond need, so a transfer of wealth adds nothing to Him. And He is slow to anger, which is the quality the giver failed to show.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line sits inside its long treatment of giving, placed between the picture of the multiplied grain and the image of charity washed off bare rock. Early scholars read the three together as one argument. No particular occasion is reported for this line. It reads as the principle the parables around it are illustrating.

keyTerms.note: The adjective means known or recognised as good, from the root for knowledge. Decency in speech is treated as something a community already recognises rather than something requiring definition.
The root means to cover or conceal, as a helmet covers a head. Here it likely means overlooking the offence of being asked, which is the small resentment a request for help can produce.
Describes someone with the power to punish who withholds it. Naming God this way at the end of an ayah about wounding speech places the giver's impatience against a standard set very high.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Asking for help in that society cost something visible. A man approached another in front of witnesses, in a market or a courtyard. The exchange was public property within the hour. Poets made reputations by praising open-handedness, and destroyed them by recording a slight. A donor who gave and then spoke sharply did not merely hurt one person. He set the story loose in a town where everyone would hear it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a kind word is the same term the Quran uses across dozens of ayat for what is commonly recognised as right. It appears in contexts from marriage to inheritance to speech with orphans. Early scholars treat that consistency as significant. The Quran keeps appealing to a standard of decency it expects the audience to know already. It does not define it fresh each time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Charity is measured here by its effect on the person receiving it, not by the cost to the giver. That reverses the usual accounting. The ayah also puts speech inside the category of charitable acts. So a decent refusal can outrank a grudging gift. The two names of God at the close ground the ethic in His own conduct. He needs nothing and is not in a hurry, and that is what the giver is being asked to be.

crossReferences.why: Shows what the alternative destroys, comparing spoilt charity to soil stripped from a rock.
Instructs a gentle word when you have nothing to give and must turn someone away.
Pairs the provision of the vulnerable with speaking to them kindly, as a single obligation.

studies.applyIt: The next time you cannot give someone what they ask for, spend the thirty seconds you would have spent apologising on something warm and specific instead. Then say nothing about it afterwards. This ayah claims that exchange is worth more than money handed over with a sigh. It is one of the few claims here you can test directly on someone's face.
studies.explainEasier: A kind word, and letting something go, is worth more than money you give and then throw back in someone's face. God is rich. He does not need your money.

studies.title: Rain On A Bare Rock
studies.meaning: A warning is given about what can undo a gift after it has been made: a reminder of the favour, and a wounding word. The comparison that follows makes the point physical. A smooth stone with a layer of soil on it looks like ground until rain arrives, and then it is bare again. What is lost is not the reward alone but the appearance that anything was ever there.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the long passage on giving that runs through this part of the surah. The commentators read the two failings named as the ordinary temptations of a generous person rather than the faults of an obvious hypocrite, and note that the ayah is addressed to believers. The parable that follows in the next ayah is its exact counterpart.

keyTerms.note: From a root for conferring a benefit, which in this form means holding it over someone afterwards. Arabic uses the same root for genuine grace, so the word marks the point where giving turns into a claim.
A slab of bare stone with nothing to hold water. The word is chosen for its surface: soil sits on it convincingly and nothing can root in it, which is the whole comparison in a single image.
An uncommon word for a surface left clean and hard. It is the last word of the image, and it describes not damage but exposure, which is what the parable is actually about.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In that country a sudden downpour was the most testing thing that happened to land. Soil that had blown across rock looked exactly like a field until it rained, and then a farmer discovered what he had. Anyone who had planted in the wrong place knew that discovery. Rain, which everywhere else in the Quran is a mercy, is here the thing that reveals.
studies.didYouKnow: The same word for a downpour appears in this ayah and in the next, once stripping a surface bare and once doubling a garden's produce. The surah sets two parables side by side using the identical element, so the difference between them lies entirely in what the rain lands on rather than in what arrives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A completed good deed is described as reversible, which is a demanding idea. What undoes it is not a later sin but words spoken about the deed itself, so the giving and the talking about it are treated as one act extended over time. And the comparison to someone giving to be seen suggests the two failings work the same way: in both, the audience has become the point.

crossReferences.why: States the same condition positively: those who do not follow their giving with reminders or hurt.
Gives the matching parable, where the same downpour doubles a garden's produce instead.
Describes those who spend to be seen by people, and pairs it with not believing.

studies.applyIt: Think of a favour you have mentioned more than once to the person who received it. Once is a story; twice is a bill. This ayah is unusually specific about how that undoes the thing. Choose one such favour and decide, deliberately, never to mention it again, then notice how quickly the impulse comes back.

studies.title: And If Not, Then Dew
studies.meaning: The counterpart parable arrives, and its terms are the same but the outcome inverted. A garden on high ground receives the same downpour and doubles its yield. Then the sentence adds something the first parable had no need of: if the heavy rain does not come, dew is enough. The comparison is not between success and failure but between soil and stone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage on giving. The commentators note that this ayah names two motives together, seeking God's approval and strengthening one's own soul, and read the second as the settling that giving produces in the giver. The pairing with the previous parable is deliberate, since both turn on the same word for the rain that falls.

keyTerms.note: The noun comes from the verb for making something firm, used in the prayer for steady feet earlier in this surah. Giving is described as producing that firmness rather than only expressing it.

keyTerms.gloss: on a rise, on high ground
keyTerms.note: Elevated land, which drains well and catches both rain and dew. The detail is agricultural: a garden placed there is well sited, so the parable's outcome follows from the ground it stands on.
The gentlest form of moisture, what settles overnight without a cloud. Naming it as sufficient changes the parable's claim: good ground does not depend on abundance, only on being what it is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gardens in Arabia were built where water could be managed: on terraces, near a spring, above the flood line. Dew mattered more than a traveller might expect, since in some seasons it was all the moisture a crop received, and farmers built low walls to catch it. The parable's detail about high ground would have read as competence rather than luck.
studies.didYouKnow: The two parables share the same word for a heavy downpour, and the difference between them lies entirely in what receives it. This one adds a second, lighter form of rain that the other has no use for, so the passage ends with the good ground being productive in abundance and in scarcity alike.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The measure of a gift is placed in the giver rather than in the amount. A garden on good ground yields in a downpour and yields in dew, which detaches the outcome from whatever happens to arrive. And by naming an inward strengthening as one of the two motives, the passage treats giving as something that forms the giver rather than only transferring wealth.

crossReferences.why: Gives the matching parable, where the same downpour leaves bare stone behind it.
Opens this passage with the image of a grain producing seven ears of a hundred grains each.
Uses another agricultural image for a good word, a tree yielding its fruit in every season.

studies.applyIt: Give something small this week in a season when you feel you have nothing to give. Not the large gesture when things are going well. This parable's point is that good ground produces in dew as well as in downpour, and the only way to find out which ground you are is to try it when the weather is poor.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Garden Burned In Old Age
studies.meaning: A question is put rather than a statement made, and it is designed to be answered from inside. Would any of you want this: a garden of palms and vines, every kind of fruit, rivers underneath, and then old age arrives, and weak children, and a fiery whirlwind takes it. The details are stacked so the loss lands at the worst possible moment, when nothing can be rebuilt.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the sequence of parables about giving. The classical commentaries record a report that a companion was asked about this ayah's meaning and connected it to a man whose deeds were undone at the end of his life. The commentators generally read it against the preceding warning about reminders and hurtful words rather than as a separate subject.

keyTerms.note: The verb is one of affection and wishing rather than of choosing. Putting the parable as a question in this form invites the listener to answer from feeling before any reasoning arrives.

Literally largeness, used of age as the accumulation of years. Its arrival in the sentence is what makes the loss final, since the same disaster earlier in a life would be a setback rather than an ending.
A wind that turns on itself and lifts what it passes over. The word occurs only here in the Quran, and the fire inside it makes the image specific rather than a general storm.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A garden of palms and vines was the work of decades. Palms take years to bear, irrigation channels are dug and maintained by hand, and a man planted for a son as much as for himself. Fire in a dry palm grove moves faster than anyone can run. Everything in this parable would have been familiar, including the particular horror of losing it late.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the whirlwind in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The parable is built entirely from good things, a garden, fruit, children, long life, and the disaster arrives only in the last clause, so a listener has fully imagined the possession before losing it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues by imagination rather than by assertion. Nothing is claimed; a scene is built and the listener is asked whether they would want it. That works because the answer is obvious and the application is not. Placing the parable after the warnings about undoing a gift suggests that a lifetime of good can be arranged so that it is not there at the end.

crossReferences.why: Names the two things that undo a gift, which this parable then dramatises as total loss.
Tells a longer version of the same scene, a garden destroyed and its owner left with nothing.
Describes a garden's owners who planned to withhold its harvest and found it stripped by morning.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are building that could still be undone at the end. Not by disaster, by your own hand. This parable is placed immediately after a warning about spoiling a gift by talking about it. Look at one thing you have built and check whether the way you speak about it is quietly burning it down.

studies.title: What You Would Not Take Yourself
studies.meaning: Two sources are named for what is given: what you have earned and what the earth produced for you. Then the instruction narrows to quality. Do not aim at the poor part of it, and the reason given is a test anyone can apply, since you would not accept this yourself except with your eyes shut. The ayah closes with two names of God about sufficiency and praise.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage on giving. The classical sources report that some brought the poorest of their dates to be distributed, and that this ayah addressed the practice. The commentaries note that the giving referred to covers both trade income and the produce of land, which between them accounted for nearly every household in Medina.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to head for something on purpose. It names a choice rather than an oversight, so what is described is someone selecting the poor portion rather than simply giving carelessly.
The direct opposite of the word for wholesome used at the start of the same ayah. Placing the two in one sentence sets a scale, and the giving described sits at the wrong end of it.
A verb for closing the eyes, used of overlooking a fault in a transaction. It names the exact behaviour of a buyer accepting poor goods to end a negotiation, which is the standard the ayah applies.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date harvests were sorted carefully. The best fruit was kept or sold, the middling eaten, and the poorest dried hard and fed to animals or held for lean months. Everyone in Medina could grade dates by sight. Bringing the lowest grade to a public distribution was therefore visible to everybody present, and the ayah names something people could watch happening.
studies.didYouKnow: The test the ayah proposes is a buyer's test rather than a moral one: would you take this in a trade. The word for shutting the eyes belongs to the language of a market transaction, so the standard for giving is set by what a person would accept in a deal rather than by what they consider generous.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The standard is made self-administering. Rather than fixing a quality, the ayah asks a person to apply the judgement they already use when they are on the receiving end, which nobody can be mistaken about. And the closing names remove the obvious objection: the giving is not needed by the one it is offered to, which means its quality is entirely about the giver.

crossReferences.why: States that virtuous conduct is not attained until you give from what you cherish.
Names another way a gift is spoiled, there by what is said afterwards rather than by what is given.
Describes the one who gives and is mindful, and the ease that is made for him afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Look at what you last donated: the clothes, the food, the furniture. Ask honestly whether you would have accepted it. Not whether it was usable, whether you would have taken it. If the answer is no, give one thing this month that you would actually have wanted, and notice how differently it feels.

studies.title: Two Promises, Two Directions
studies.meaning: Two voices are set against each other, and each is described as making a promise. One promises poverty and urges indecency; the other promises forgiveness and abundance. The parallel is exact, which is the point, since both work by expectation. Then the second ayah turns to wisdom, given to whom God wills, and calls receiving it much good.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage on giving, where the fear of running short was the practical obstacle. The commentators read the first ayah as naming that fear precisely and attributing it, and note that the promise on the other side is not of wealth but of forgiveness and favour. The second ayah widens the subject and closes the passage's argument.

keyTerms.note: The same verb is used of both sides, which is the ayah's structure in a single word. Arabic uses it for a promise and, with a different construction, for a threat, so the doubling here is exact and deliberate.

From a root connected to a broken spine, so the word names being unable to stand rather than merely having little. What is promised is not modest means but collapse, which is why it works as a deterrent.
From a root meaning to restrain, as a bridle restrains a horse. Naming it here, straight after a contrast between two promises, suggests wisdom is what lets a person tell one from the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poverty in Arabia was not an abstraction but a specific sequence: the animals go first, then the stored dates, then the land, and then a family becomes dependent on relatives. Everyone had watched it happen to someone. A man deciding whether to give away a portion of his stores was calculating against that sequence, and it was a reasonable calculation.
studies.didYouKnow: The same verb is used for both promises in the first ayah, so the sentence is built as a matched pair. The second closes with a phrase about those with insight that recurs across this surah, and the word it uses for wisdom appeared earlier in the description of what a messenger teaches a community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear of scarcity is not dismissed as foolish; it is attributed to a source and set beside another expectation. That framing treats the calculation as real and asks which projection you are working from. And what is offered on the other side is not a guarantee of wealth, which would answer fear on its own terms, but forgiveness and favour, which changes the terms instead.

crossReferences.why: Names another failure in giving, there in what is said afterwards rather than in what is feared.
States that whatever you spend, He will replace it, addressing the same fear directly.
Names the same fear of poverty in another setting, and answers it with a statement about provision.

studies.applyIt: Notice the sentence your mind says when you are about to give something away and hesitate. Write it down in the exact words it uses. This ayah says that sentence is a promise being made to you by something. Reading it back in that form is usually enough to see it for what it is.

studies.title: The Case For Giving Quietly
studies.meaning: The first line says that nothing given or pledged escapes God's knowledge. That sets up the second. Public giving is called good, with no qualification. Then private giving to the needy is called better for you. The comparison is not between right and wrong but between good and better. The reason given is the effect on the giver, not on the person receiving. Hidden giving is said to cover over some of your own failings.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines sit in the long section on spending that runs through the middle of it. The community was raising funds openly for emigrants and expeditions, so public giving was both necessary and easy to see. Early scholars note that the passage does not discourage the public appeal it sits inside. It adds a second track alongside it. No single occasion is agreed for these two lines.

keyTerms.note: A binding promise to God to do something, often conditional on an outcome. Listing it beside ordinary charity brings private undertakings nobody witnessed into the same account as public ones.
Shares a root with the word for truthfulness. The connection is deliberate in Arabic: giving is treated as evidence that a stated commitment is genuine rather than as a separate virtue.
From a root meaning to conceal, the same root that gives the word for denial of faith. Here the covering is God's, hiding a person's failings in the way the giver hid the gift.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving in a town like Medina was almost impossible to hide. Households were close, markets were small, and a sack of dates arriving at a poor family's door would be noticed and talked about. Hiding it therefore took effort. You sent a gift at night, or through a third person who would not name the source. Reports from the period describe both methods, which suggests the instruction was taken practically, not as an ideal.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for covering over the giver's failings is built on the same three letters as the Quran's word for rejecting faith. That word literally means to bury or hide something. The early Arabic dictionary writers connect the two senses through farming: a sower covers seed with soil. The same image sits behind the early Arabic word for a farmer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses the simple rule that hidden charity always wins. It calls the public act good in its own right. That protects communal fundraising from suspicion. It then puts the advantage of secrecy in what it does to the giver, not in the receiver's dignity. The ayat around it handle that separately. God's knowledge is the premise for both. Since nothing is unseen, there is no audience worth performing for.

crossReferences.why: Widens the same point across every setting, spending by night and day, secretly and openly.
States that God is the one who receives charity, which is why the human audience is optional.
Shows giving done wanting neither reward nor thanks from those who receive it.

studies.applyIt: Give something this month that nobody will ever know about, including the person receiving it if you can manage it. Do not tell your family, and do not record it anywhere someone might read. Notice the small urge to mention it, and let it pass unspoken. That urge is precisely what this passage is offering to relieve you of.
studies.explainEasier: God knows every gift you give and every promise you make. Giving in the open is good. Giving quietly, so nobody sees, is even better for you. It helps wipe away some of your bad deeds.

studies.title: Their Guidance Is Not On You
studies.meaning: A burden is lifted before anything else is said. Their guidance is not on you, which the commentators read against a reluctance to give to people outside the community. Then three statements about spending follow, each beginning the same way: what you give is for yourselves, is sought only for the face of God, and will be repaid in full. The reason for giving moves entirely to the giver.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that some hesitated to give to relatives and neighbours who had not joined the community, hoping that withholding would apply pressure, and report this ayah as the answer. The accounts are widely recorded, though the details differ. The opening clause addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and through him the practice itself.

keyTerms.note: A phrase of removal: something is being taken off a person rather than added to them. Placing it first means the instruction that follows arrives after the weight has already been lifted.
